lessons.title: How macroeconomic models work
lessons.subtitle: Translate assumptions into equations, diagrams and economic mechanisms.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 1 - Module Info and Introduction.pdf

concepts.title: A model is a conditional argument
concepts.explain: A model simplifies reality to isolate a mechanism. This course derives consumers’ and workers’ utility-maximizing choices and firms’ profit-maximizing choices, then combines markets to explain short-run output, unemployment and inflation. General equilibrium tracks how one market affects the others. Its main models are closed economies; long-run growth and open-economy theory belong to EC3102. Different adjustment assumptions can produce different predictions from the same shock.
concepts.formula: Assumptions → optimal choices → market equilibrium → prediction
steps: State the question and maintained assumptions.
Identify which agents choose which variables and which constraints they face.
Derive behavior, combine market conditions and solve.
Translate the result into a graph and an economic mechanism; check how changing an assumption changes the prediction.
concepts.increase: Allowing more adjustment, such as flexible wages, can remove an imbalance that persists under fixed wages.
concepts.decrease: Restricting adjustment, such as fixing prices, can make output respond to demand.
concepts.edge: A mathematical solution need not fit the situation if an assumption fails.
concepts.example: A demand increase raises output in a fixed-price model. With flexible prices and fixed productive capacity, the same demand change may instead raise prices.

check.prompt: Why can two models give different answers to one shock?
check.answer: Their assumptions can allow different adjustment mechanisms.

concepts.title: Endogenous and exogenous depend on the model
concepts.explain: An endogenous variable is solved inside the model. An exogenous variable is taken as given. The labels belong to a particular model, not permanently to a variable.
concepts.formula: c = a + b y, with a, b and y given
steps: List the equations.
List the unknowns solved by them.
Treat remaining inputs as exogenous.
concepts.increase: If given income y rises, this consumption rule predicts higher c when b > 0.
concepts.decrease: If given income y falls, c falls when b > 0.
concepts.edge: In a larger model that determines income, y becomes endogenous.
concepts.example: With a = 10, b = 0.6 and y = 100, c = 70. Here c is endogenous; y is an input.

check.prompt: Is the real wage always exogenous?
check.answer: No. A price-taking worker takes it as given, while a labor-market equilibrium model determines it.

concepts.title: Autonomous does not mean zero
concepts.explain: An autonomous component is unexplained by the variables included in a model. It can be positive and can change between scenarios. A slope measures a response to an included variable.
concepts.formula: C = C₀ + cY − br
steps: Hold Y and r fixed.
Change C₀ to isolate an autonomous demand shift.
Change Y or r to move through the existing relationship.
concepts.increase: Higher C₀ raises desired consumption at every Y and r.
concepts.decrease: Lower C₀ lowers desired consumption at every Y and r.
concepts.edge: Autonomous consumption is a model component, not a claim that people can consume indefinitely without resources.
concepts.example: With C₀ = 20, c = 0.5, Y = 100 and br = 10, C = 60. Increasing C₀ to 25 raises C to 65.

check.prompt: Does a higher Y count as higher autonomous consumption?
check.answer: No. It is the income-induced component cY.

concepts.title: Real purchasing power
concepts.explain: Nominal values use current money prices. Real quantities remove the price component: a real wage measures the output bought by an hour of work. Nominal GDP values current production at current prices; real GDP uses constant base-year prices to track physical production. The course assumes choices depend on real opportunities, so scaling all relevant nominal prices and income equally leaves the real budget unchanged.
concepts.formula: w = W/P; real balances = M/P; 1 + g_real = (1 + g_nominal)/(1 + g_P)
steps: Identify the nominal amount.
Identify the matching price measure.
Divide and compare purchasing power.
concepts.increase: At fixed P, higher W raises w. At fixed W, higher P lowers w. If W rises faster proportionally than P, the real wage rises.
concepts.decrease: At fixed P, lower W lowers w. At fixed W, lower P raises w. If W falls faster proportionally than P, the real wage falls.
concepts.edge: Equal proportional changes in W and P leave w unchanged. Subtracting growth rates is an approximation; the exact ratio matters for large changes. A price index reported with base 100 must be normalized consistently when converting levels.
concepts.example: W = 180 and P = 6 give w = 30 units of output per hour. If W then rises 8% and P rises 10%, w changes by 1.08/1.10 − 1 = −1.818%, not exactly −2%.

check.prompt: A nominal wage rises 10% and prices rise 10%. What happens to the real wage?
check.answer: It is unchanged because 1.10/1.10 = 1.

concepts.title: Stocks accumulate flows
concepts.explain: A stock is measured at a date; a flow is measured over a time interval. Saving changes wealth, investment changes capital, and a budget deficit adds to debt, subject to valuation and other adjustments.
concepts.formula: Ending stock = beginning stock + net inflow
steps: Check whether the quantity has a time interval.
Separate gross additions from removals.
Reconcile the change in stock.
concepts.increase: Positive net saving increases wealth when there are no valuation changes.
concepts.decrease: Dissaving reduces wealth, through asset sales or increased debt.
concepts.edge: Capital gains can raise wealth without saving. Gross investment can coexist with falling capital if depreciation is larger.
concepts.example: Wealth starts at 100, saving is 8, and assets lose 3 in value. Ending wealth is 105, not 108.

check.prompt: Is an account balance of 500 a flow?
check.answer: No. A balance at a moment is a stock.

concepts.title: Income, saving and net worth
concepts.explain: Income is a flow earned over a period. Saving is the part not consumed. Wealth is assets minus liabilities. Repaying debt with unconsumed income raises net worth just as acquiring an asset does.
concepts.formula: Wealth = assets − liabilities; saving = income − consumption
steps: Calculate total income.
Subtract consumption.
Trace saving into higher assets or lower liabilities.
concepts.increase: Higher income with unchanged consumption raises saving and wealth accumulation.
concepts.decrease: Higher consumption with unchanged income lowers saving; saving becomes negative when consumption exceeds income.
concepts.edge: Borrowing itself does not increase net worth when it raises cash assets and debt equally.
concepts.example: Assets of 200 and debt of 80 imply wealth of 120. Repaying 10 of debt using 10 of existing cash leaves wealth at 120.

check.prompt: Does taking a 20 loan immediately make someone 20 wealthier?
check.answer: No. Their assets and liabilities both rise by 20.

concepts.title: Movement along a curve versus a shift
concepts.explain: A curve records combinations of its axis variables while other determinants are held fixed. An axis-variable change creates movement along it. A change in a held-fixed determinant changes the relationship itself.
concepts.formula: y = mx + b: slope m, vertical intercept b; if m ≠ 0, horizontal intercept −b/m
steps: Name both axes and what is held fixed.
For a straight line, identify its slope and intercepts; solve intersections as simultaneous equations.
Changing an axis variable moves along a fixed relationship. Changing a held-fixed determinant changes the relationship.
An upward shift means higher y at a given x. A rightward shift means higher x at a given y. For a downward-sloping curve these can describe the same change.
concepts.increase: Higher productivity raises labor demand at every real wage, shifting the curve right.
concepts.decrease: Lower productivity lowers labor demand at every real wage, shifting the curve left.
concepts.edge: A shift need not be parallel. For Y = A F(K,N) with F(K,0) = 0, higher A raises output at each positive N but leaves the origin fixed. For an upward-sloping curve, a rightward shift corresponds to a downward, not upward, shift.
concepts.example: On a graph with w vertical and N horizontal, a lower w moves down the labor-demand curve. Higher A shifts the whole curve.

check.prompt: Why is a higher wage not a labor-demand shift?
check.answer: The wage is an axis variable on that demand curve.

concepts.title: Marginal conditions and constraints
concepts.explain: An interior optimum equates marginal benefit and marginal cost. A first-order condition locates a stationary point, while curvature and feasibility determine whether it is an optimum.
concepts.formula: dπ/dN = MPN − w = 0; d²π/dN² < 0
steps: Write the objective and feasible choices.
Differentiate including all indirect effects.
Check curvature and boundaries.
Translate the condition into economics.
concepts.increase: When marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost, increasing the choice raises the objective locally.
concepts.decrease: When marginal benefit is below marginal cost, reducing the choice raises the objective locally.
concepts.edge: At a boundary, equality need not hold. A desired negative quantity is infeasible when quantities must be nonnegative.
concepts.example: For π = 10N − N² − 4N, dπ/dN = 6 − 2N gives N = 3 and the second derivative is −2.

check.prompt: Does a zero first derivative always prove a maximum?
check.answer: No. Check the second derivative or global shape and feasible boundaries.

concepts.title: Partial derivatives and direct plus indirect effects
concepts.explain: A partial derivative varies one independent argument while holding the others fixed. After a constraint makes one argument depend on another, the total response must include every route. Subscripts on a function name identify argument positions, not dates: u1(c2,l2) differentiates with respect to consumption, its first argument, evaluated in period 2.
concepts.formula: If v = g(x) and y = f(v,x), dy/dx = f1(v,x)g′(x) + f2(v,x). If y = f(g(x)) only, dy/dx = f′(g(x))g′(x).
steps: Write the inner dependency v = g(x).
Differentiate f with respect to v and multiply by dv/dx for the indirect effect.
Add any direct partial derivative with respect to x.
Evaluate derivatives at the same stated point; interpret signs and units.
concepts.increase: A small rise in x raises y when the sum of the direct and indirect effects is positive, even if one component is negative.
concepts.decrease: A small fall in x lowers y when that sum is positive; when the sum is negative, a fall in x raises y. Always recompute the signed sum.
concepts.edge: If the two routes cancel, the first-order change is zero; this does not prove the function is constant for a finite change. Holding v fixed would deliberately omit the indirect route.
concepts.example: Let c = 12 − 2l and u(c,l) = cl. At l = 2, c = 8: uc = 2, ul = 8 and dc/dl = −2, so dU/dl = 2(−2) + 8 = 4. Direct leisure utility exceeds the consumption-utility loss.

check.prompt: For f(g(x),x), why is f2 alone insufficient when g′(x) is nonzero?
check.answer: x also changes the first argument through g; add f1g′ to the direct effect f2.

concepts.title: Total differentials, indifference curves and implicit slopes
concepts.explain: A total differential adds the first-order contribution of every changing argument. Along an indifference curve utility stays constant, so the total differential equals zero. Solving that relation gives the slope without needing an explicit formula for the curve. This is the same logic used to differentiate a firm’s implicit optimality condition.
concepts.formula: du = uc dc + ul dl; along fixed u, dc/dl = −ul/uc; MRS of leisure for consumption = ul/uc > 0. For H(x,y) = 0, dy/dx = −Hx/Hy if Hy ≠ 0.
steps: State which relation is held constant.
Differentiate every term affected by the change.
Set the total differential equal to zero for a fixed level.
Solve for the desired ratio and check its denominator and economic meaning.
concepts.increase: With positive marginal utilities, increasing leisure along one indifference curve requires reducing consumption. The forgone consumption per extra leisure unit is the positive MRS.
concepts.decrease: Reducing leisure along the same curve requires increasing consumption to preserve utility. The trade-off is local because the MRS usually changes along the curve.
concepts.edge: An indifference-curve slope holds utility fixed; a budget slope holds resources and market prices fixed. They coincide at an interior tangency, not at an arbitrary feasible bundle. If the denominator derivative is zero, the usual finite implicit slope formula is unavailable.
concepts.example: For u = ln c + 2 ln l at c = 10 and l = 4, uc = 0.1 and ul = 0.5. Hence dc/dl along the IC is −5. A budget with wage 3 instead has slope −3, so this point is not a tangency.

check.prompt: Why is the MRS positive although the indifference curve slopes downward?
check.answer: The course defines MRS as the amount of the vertical-axis good forgone per extra horizontal-axis good, the negative of the curve slope.

lessons.title: Production and the labor market
lessons.subtitle: From production and individual choices to full employment and unemployment.

concepts.title: Output, technology and inputs
concepts.explain: Output is Y = A F(K,N). Capital K consists of produced goods used in production over more than one period, such as machines; material completely used up this period is an intermediate input. N is labor. A summarizes technology, management, energy availability and other influences not separately represented by K and N. A graph against one input holds the other input and A fixed.
steps: Choose the input on the horizontal axis.
Hold the other input and A fixed.
Separate a movement along production from a productivity shift.
concepts.increase: More N raises Y at fixed K and A. Higher A raises Y at every N.
concepts.decrease: Less N lowers Y at fixed K and A. Lower A shifts production down.
concepts.edge: The Cobb–Douglas example assumes A > 0, K > 0, N > 0 and 0 < α < 1 for the derivative formulas. Output is zero if an essential input is zero; marginal-product formulas at zero may be undefined or unbounded. F(K,N) denotes a function, not F multiplied by K.
concepts.example: With A = 1, α = 0.5 and K = 100, Y = 10√N. Increasing N from 25 to 36 raises Y from 50 to 60.

check.prompt: What must be held fixed when reading MPN from a production graph?
check.answer: Capital and technology.

concepts.title: Diminishing marginal products
concepts.explain: Each marginal product is the partial derivative of output. With the other input fixed, adding an input raises output but reduces the extra output from another unit of the same input.
concepts.formula: MPK = αY/K; MPN = (1−α)Y/N; ∂MPK/∂K = α(α−1)Y/K² < 0; ∂MPN/∂N = −α(1−α)Y/N² < 0
steps: Differentiate Y with respect to one input.
Differentiate again to assess curvature.
Keep the other input fixed in both steps.
concepts.increase: Increasing K alone raises Y but lowers MPK. Increasing N alone raises Y but lowers MPN. The production curve rises while flattening in either graph.
concepts.decrease: Reducing K alone lowers Y but raises the MPK of remaining capital. Reducing N alone lowers Y but raises the MPN of remaining labor.
concepts.edge: Diminishing marginal product is not negative marginal product. A derivative is the limiting tangent slope; a finite change is an average slope over an interval. Y/N is average labor productivity, not MPN.
concepts.example: For Y = 10√N, MPN = 5/√N. At N = 25, MPN = 1; at N = 100, MPN = 0.5.

check.prompt: Can output rise while MPN falls?
check.answer: Yes. Output rises more slowly as labor increases.

concepts.title: Capital and labor can raise each other’s productivity
concepts.explain: Cobb–Douglas capital and labor have positive cross partials. More equipment increases the productivity of a given worker; more workers increase the productivity of a given unit of capital.
concepts.formula: ∂MPN/∂K = ∂MPK/∂N = α(1−α)Y/(KN) > 0
steps: Differentiate MPN with respect to K.
Keep N and A fixed.
Distinguish this cross effect from diminishing own marginal product.
concepts.increase: At fixed N, higher K raises MPN. At fixed K, higher N raises MPK: each input improves the productivity of the other in Cobb–Douglas.
concepts.decrease: At fixed N, lower K reduces MPN. At fixed K, lower N reduces MPK. These are cross-input effects, distinct from diminishing own-input returns.
concepts.edge: Complementarity is a maintained property of this production technology, not a consequence of positive own marginal products alone. Simultaneous changes in K and N can offset; under constant returns, equal proportional changes leave both marginal products unchanged.
concepts.example: With Y = √(KN), doubling K at fixed N multiplies MPN by √2.

check.prompt: Why can MPK fall with K while MPN rises with K?
check.answer: One is an own derivative, the other a cross derivative.

concepts.title: Productivity shocks
concepts.explain: A changes output and marginal products at fixed input quantities. A supply shock affects what can be produced, which then changes firms’ willingness to hire.
concepts.formula: ∂Y/∂A = Y/A; ∂MPN/∂A = MPN/A; ∂MPK/∂A = MPK/A
steps: Start with A at unchanged K and N.
Trace the rise or fall in MPN.
Then allow firms to adjust hiring.
concepts.increase: Higher A raises Y, MPN and MPK proportionally at fixed positive inputs. The Y-versus-N curve becomes steeper and labor demand shifts up/right.
concepts.decrease: Lower A reduces Y, MPN and MPK proportionally at fixed positive inputs. The production curve becomes flatter and labor demand shifts down/left.
concepts.edge: Because Cobb–Douglas output remains zero with N = 0, a productivity change pivots the production graph around the origin rather than translating it in parallel. Equilibrium N can also change, so the total output response need not equal the percentage A shock.
concepts.example: A 10% increase in A increases Y and MPN by 10% at fixed inputs.

check.prompt: Does lower A move the economy along the original production function?
check.answer: No. The production function itself shifts down.

concepts.title: Returns to scale versus diminishing returns
concepts.explain: Returns to scale changes all inputs together. Diminishing marginal products changes one input while holding the other fixed. Constant returns and diminishing marginal products can therefore coexist.
concepts.formula: F(zK,zN) = z^(α+β)F(K,N)
steps: Add the exponents in a Cobb–Douglas specification.
Compare their sum with one.
Use own derivatives for marginal returns instead.
concepts.increase: Scaling both inputs up by z doubles output when z = 2 and the exponents sum to one.
concepts.decrease: For a common input multiplier 0 < z < 1 and degree d, output becomes z^dY. With increasing returns d > 1, output falls by a larger percentage than the common input reduction; with decreasing returns 0 < d < 1, it falls by a smaller percentage.
concepts.edge: Returns to scale vary all inputs together while holding A fixed. Diminishing marginal products vary one input alone. Y = K^0.6N^0.6 has diminishing own marginal products but increasing returns to scale; z = 1 means no change.
concepts.example: Y = K^0.6N^0.4 has constant returns. Y = K^0.6N^0.6 has increasing returns despite diminishing own marginal products.

check.prompt: What happens to Y = K^0.3N^0.7 when both inputs triple?
check.answer: Output triples.

concepts.title: Factor payments under Cobb–Douglas
concepts.explain: If each factor is paid its marginal product, multiplying marginal product by quantity gives its income. Under constant returns, these factor payments exhaust output.
concepts.formula: MPK·K/Y = α; MPN·N/Y = 1−α
steps: Compute each marginal product.
Multiply by its factor quantity.
Divide by Y to obtain a share.
concepts.increase: Higher Y with unchanged α raises both factor incomes proportionally.
concepts.decrease: Lower Y with unchanged α reduces both factor incomes proportionally.
concepts.edge: These shares rely on marginal-product pricing and the specified technology. Fixed capital is not free capital.
concepts.example: If α = 0.35 and Y = 200, capital receives 70 and labor receives 130.

check.prompt: Does a larger capital stock necessarily increase the capital income share in this specification?
check.answer: No. With unchanged α and marginal-product pricing, the share remains α.

concepts.title: Hiring equates real wage and marginal product
concepts.explain: A competitive firm with homogeneous labor takes w = W/P as given and chooses N while K and A are fixed. Real revenue is output Y, so the relevant objective is A F(K,N) − wN. A fixed capital charge can be subtracted without changing the hiring FOC; the residual before charging capital is not pure economic profit.
concepts.formula: max π = AF(K,N) − wN; AFN = w
steps: Compare MPN with w.
Hire more if MPN > w.
Hire less if MPN < w.
Stop at equality when feasible.
concepts.increase: A higher real wage lowers optimal hiring along the demand curve.
concepts.decrease: A lower real wage raises optimal hiring along the demand curve.
concepts.edge: At an interior optimum with diminishing MPN, MPN = w. If the right-hand marginal product at N = 0 is at most w, no hiring may be optimal. At an externally imposed hiring cap, MPN may exceed w because extra workers are infeasible. A wage change also changes output through hiring; output is not fixed along labor demand.
concepts.example: For Y = 10√N and w = 1, 5/√N = 1 gives N = 25.

check.prompt: Why does the firm not maximize total output?
check.answer: Additional output can cost more in wages than it is worth.

concepts.title: Deriving labor demand and its sensitivities
concepts.explain: Solve the marginal-product equation for N, then differentiate the demand function. This exposes how technology, capital and wages affect hiring.
concepts.formula: Nd = K[((1−α)A)/w]^(1/α); ∂Nd/∂w = −Nd/(αw); ∂Nd/∂A = Nd/(αA); ∂Nd/∂K = Nd/K
steps: Set (1−α)AK^αN^(−α) = w.
Rearrange N^α = (1−α)AK^α/w.
Raise both sides to 1/α.
concepts.increase: Higher A or K raises Nd at every w. A higher w reduces Nd.
concepts.decrease: Lower A or K reduces Nd at every w. A lower w raises Nd.
concepts.edge: These formulas require A,K,w > 0 and 0 < α < 1. Log differentiation gives dN/N = dK/K + (dA/A − dw/w)/α. It is a local approximation for general finite percentage changes; exact finite changes use ratios and powers.
concepts.example: With α = 0.5, K = 100, A = 1 and w = 1, Nd = 25. Doubling w reduces Nd to 6.25.

check.prompt: If α = 0.25, what is the labor-demand wage elasticity?

concepts.title: Comparative statics without a functional form
concepts.explain: The implicit-function rule derives response signs from the first-order condition. It does not require solving N explicitly. Local results require a nonzero derivative with respect to N.
concepts.formula: H(N,A,w) = A FN(K,N) − w = 0; FN dA + A FNN dN − dw = 0 at fixed K; ∂Nd/∂w = 1/(A FNN); ∂Nd/∂A = −FN/(A FNN)
steps: Start from the interior FOC and hold K fixed.
Take the total differential, including the direct A term and N’s effect on FN.
For the wage derivative set dA = 0; for the productivity derivative set dw = 0.
Solve for dN and use A > 0, FN > 0 and FNN < 0 to sign each response.
concepts.increase: Higher A increases Nd because −FN/(AFNN) > 0.
concepts.decrease: Lower A reduces Nd; a higher wage reduces Nd since 1/(AFNN) < 0.
concepts.edge: FNN ≠ 0 is needed for this local solution. If K also changes, add A FNK dK. A firm’s demand response at fixed w is not the market-equilibrium employment response when wages and supply also adjust.
concepts.example: For F = √N and A = 10, AFNN = −2.5N^(−3/2), so dN/dw is negative.

check.prompt: What assumption gives downward-sloping labor demand here?
check.answer: Diminishing marginal product of labor, FNN < 0.

concepts.title: The income–leisure budget
concepts.explain: Time is allocated to work or leisure. Each hour of leisure costs the real wage in forgone consumption. Nonlabor income shifts resources without changing this opportunity cost.
concepts.formula: n = h − l; c = w(h−l)+m; c+wl = wh+m
steps: Write total time h.
Subtract leisure to obtain work.
Multiply work by w and add m.
Impose 0 ≤ l ≤ h.
concepts.increase: Higher m shifts the budget line upward by the same amount at every l. Higher w rotates it around (h,m).
concepts.decrease: Lower m shifts the line down. Lower w flattens it around (h,m).
concepts.edge: With m > 0, the algebraic horizontal intercept h+m/w lies beyond feasible leisure h. Do not permit leisure above h.
concepts.example: With h = 16, w = 5 and m = 20, c = 100−5l and the no-work point is (16,20).

check.prompt: Why is the no-work point unchanged when w changes?
check.answer: At l = h there are no paid hours, so c = m.

concepts.title: Why MRS equals the real wage
concepts.explain: Choose c and leisure l to maximize u(c,l) subject to c = w(h−l)+m and 0 ≤ l ≤ h. Substitution leaves U(l) = u(w(h−l)+m,l). Both c and l are desirable; indifference curves slope downward, and convexity means a diminishing MRS. The highest attainable IC is tangent to the budget at a smooth interior optimum.
concepts.formula: U′(l) = −wuc + ul; interior ul/uc = w; IC slope = −ul/uc; budget slope = −w
steps: Substitute c = w(h−l)+m into utility.
Differentiate the direct leisure effect and indirect consumption effect.
Set their sum to zero.
concepts.increase: If ul/uc > w at a feasible interior point, more leisure gives greater benefit than cost.
concepts.decrease: If ul/uc < w, reducing leisure and working more raises utility locally.
concepts.edge: Under concavity along the feasible budget, l = h can be optimal when U′(h) ≥ 0, or MRS(h,m) ≥ w: the worker would prefer still more leisure but has no time left. At l = 0, U′(0) ≤ 0 can support maximum work. Use one-sided derivatives where needed; log utility makes zero consumption or leisure infeasible.
concepts.example: For u = ln c + ln l, ul/uc = c/l. At w = 5, an interior optimum has c = 5l.

check.prompt: Why is ul − wuc the derivative, rather than just ul?
check.answer: Changing leisure also changes the consumption financed by work.

concepts.title: Wealth effects on work
concepts.explain: With normal consumption and leisure, more nonlabor income raises both consumption and leisure. Labor supply falls because leisure uses some of the fixed time endowment.
concepts.formula: At an interior optimum with normal leisure: dn/dm = −dl/dm < 0; a binding no-work corner can make the local response zero.
steps: Shift the budget line without changing its slope.
Move to higher normal-good consumption and leisure.
Convert higher l into lower n.
concepts.increase: Higher m raises leisure and reduces labor supplied at each w.
concepts.decrease: Lower m reduces leisure and increases labor supplied at each w.
concepts.edge: At the no-work corner, additional income cannot reduce work below zero.
concepts.example: With u = ln c+ln l, h = 16 and w = 5, m = 0 gives l = 8. m = 20 gives l = 10 and work falls from 8 to 6.

check.prompt: Does higher nonlabor income cause a movement along a labor-supply curve?
check.answer: No. It shifts labor supply because w is unchanged.

concepts.title: A wage change has two opposing effects
concepts.explain: A higher wage makes leisure more expensive, encouraging work through substitution. It also expands purchasing power for a worker, encouraging normal leisure through income. The net effect is not fixed by normality alone.
concepts.formula: Δn = substitution effect + income effect
steps: Draw the original and new wage budget lines; both pass through (h,m).
Construct an intermediate line parallel to the new budget and tangent to the original IC.
The original optimum to the compensated tangency is the substitution effect at fixed utility.
The compensated tangency to the new optimum is the income effect at fixed new relative prices.
Sum the two signed leisure changes and reverse the sign for work because n = h−l.
concepts.increase: A wage rise raises work through substitution and reduces it through income. Work rises only if substitution dominates.
concepts.decrease: A wage fall reduces work through substitution and increases it through the adverse income effect. The net depends on magnitudes.
concepts.edge: Equal opposing effects leave hours unchanged, although consumption can change. Income dominance gives backward-bending individual supply. At a no-work corner a small wage change may leave hours at zero; strict interior arrows need not apply there. Compensated substitution is weak rather than necessarily strict if preferences contain flat regions.
concepts.example: If substitution adds 3 hours and income subtracts 3 hours, hours do not change even though the wage rises.

check.prompt: Does leisure being normal prove upward-sloping individual labor supply?
check.answer: No. Normality determines the income effect, not which effect dominates.

concepts.title: Individual and aggregate labor supply
concepts.explain: Aggregate labor supply sums individuals’ desired hours at each current real wage. A wage rise can increase hours of existing workers, the intensive margin, and attract nonparticipants, the extensive margin. Under the course’s substitution-dominance assumption this produces an upward-sloping aggregate curve; individual responses need not be identical.
concepts.formula: Ns(w) = sum of individual ni(w)
steps: Separate a wage movement from nonwage determinants.
Add labor supplied across workers.
State the aggregate slope assumption.
concepts.increase: More working-age people or greater participation shifts supply right at a given w. Higher current w moves along the curve. Higher wealth or expected future wage instead shifts current supply left under the course’s normal-leisure mechanism.
concepts.decrease: Fewer working-age people or reduced participation shifts supply left. Lower current w moves down the curve. Lower wealth or expected future wages shifts current supply right under the maintained mechanism.
concepts.edge: The reservation wage is the wage at which a person is just willing to start working. In the static model with positive m and smooth preferences it is MRS at (l,c) = (h,m). Below that wage, zero work can remain optimal; above it, entry is possible. A lower birth rate affects future workforce size, not today’s working-age population immediately.
concepts.example: If 100 workers each supply 8 hours, total labor is 800 hours. Adding 10 identical workers increases supply to 880 at that wage.

check.prompt: Can aggregate supply rise when one worker reduces hours?
check.answer: Yes. Other workers or participation changes can outweigh that response.

concepts.title: Full employment is a market-clearing outcome
concepts.explain: The competitive labor-market intersection determines the real wage and full-employment labor. Substituting this labor into production determines potential output. Full employment is not everyone working all the time.
concepts.formula: Nd(w*) = Ns(w*); Y* = AF(K,N*)
steps: Equate Nd(w;A,K) and Ns(w;wealth,population,expected wages).
If w is above clearing, desired labor supply exceeds demand and competitive wage pressure is downward.
If w is below clearing, desired labor demand exceeds supply and firms bid wages upward.
Substitute the clearing N* into Y* = A F(K,N*).
concepts.increase: A demand increase with upward supply raises w*, N* and Y*.
concepts.decrease: A demand decrease with upward supply lowers w*, N* and Y*.
concepts.edge: Full employment means the outcome after wages and prices fully adjust, not every adult working or zero measured unemployment. New Keynesian wage rigidity can delay this adjustment even with optimizing firms; the early competitive model assumes the adjustment has occurred.
concepts.example: If Nd = 100−5w and Ns = 10w, w* = 20/3 and N* = 200/3.

check.prompt: Is Y* determined by arbitrary desired spending in this labor-market calculation?
check.answer: No. It follows from technology, capital and equilibrium employment.

concepts.title: Supply shifts and adverse energy shocks
concepts.explain: Immigration can increase labor supply, while depleted energy reduces productivity. Trace the curve shift and then output, keeping the other determinants fixed.
concepts.formula: Y* = AF(K,N*); MPN = w*
steps: Identify whether the first effect is on labor supply or demand.
Solve the new intersection.
Combine changed employment and technology in production.
concepts.increase: Higher A at fixed K and an unchanged upward-sloping Ns raises demand, w*, N* and Y*. Increased immigration or participation at fixed A and K shifts Ns right, lowers w*, raises N* and raises aggregate output through positive MPN.
concepts.decrease: Lower A, such as an adverse energy shock, lowers demand, w*, N* and Y*: output falls directly through A and indirectly through N*. A workforce or participation decline shifts Ns left, raises w*, lowers N* and lowers aggregate output at fixed A and K.
concepts.edge: These arrows hold the other curve fixed. Simultaneous demand and supply shifts can leave the wage or employment unchanged or make one response ambiguous. More aggregate output after immigration does not establish higher output per person. A permanent productivity shock can also change future income and labor supply; the single-shock illustration holds that channel fixed.
concepts.example: Immigration and a productivity improvement can both raise employment, but their wage predictions differ.

check.prompt: What distinguishes an immigration shock from higher productivity in the labor diagram?
check.answer: The former initially shifts supply, the latter demand.

concepts.title: Employment, participation and unemployment
concepts.explain: The lecture’s US/BLS illustration counts adults aged 16 or above. Employed includes part-time workers and those temporarily absent from a job, such as on vacation or sick leave. Unemployed means not employed and actively searching in the preceding four weeks. Those neither employed nor searching are outside the labor force; discouraged workers belong there. These are the course illustration’s categories, not a universal definition for every country.
concepts.formula: LF = E + U; unemployment rate = U/LF; participation rate = LF/adult population; employment-population ratio = E/adult population
steps: Classify employed, unemployed and outside the labor force.
Construct L.
Use the correct denominator for each rate.
concepts.increase: At fixed adult population, a job finder moving U to E lowers unemployment and raises the employment ratio while participation is unchanged. A nonparticipant entering unemployment raises participation and usually raises the unemployment rate.
concepts.decrease: An unemployed person stopping search lowers both U and LF; measured unemployment and participation fall even though employment does not rise. A job loss from E to U leaves participation fixed, lowers the employment ratio and raises unemployment.
concepts.edge: u is undefined if LF = 0. A falling unemployment rate need not mean more jobs. The employment ratio equals participation × (1−u) when both rates are expressed as decimals.
concepts.example: E = 180, U = 20 and adult population = 250 give LF = 200, u = 10%, participation = 80% and employment ratio = 72%. If 10 unemployed people stop searching, E stays 180, LF falls to 190, u becomes about 5.26% and participation 76%; employment ratio stays 72%.

check.prompt: Is a full-time student who neither works nor seeks work unemployed?
check.answer: No. They are outside the labor force under this classification.

concepts.title: Natural unemployment and Okun’s law
concepts.explain: Frictional unemployment comes from the time needed to find a suitable match. Structural unemployment is persistent mismatch or lack of suitable opportunities, for example after an industry declines. The natural rate includes these components at full employment. Cyclical unemployment is actual minus natural unemployment and can be positive, zero or negative. Okun’s relation is an empirical association, not an exact identity or proof of a particular causal mechanism.
concepts.formula: Cyclical gap = u−u*; GDP growth (%) ≈ 3−2Δu when Δu is measured in percentage points
steps: Distinguish level u from change Δu.
Measure the change in percentage points.
Apply the stated coefficient and normal-growth intercept.
concepts.increase: If unemployment rises by 1 percentage point, predicted output growth falls by 2 points from its 3% normal-growth benchmark to 1%. Actual u above u* gives a positive cyclical gap.
concepts.decrease: If unemployment falls by 1 percentage point, predicted growth rises by 2 points to 5%. Actual u below u* gives a negative cyclical gap.
concepts.edge: Unchanged unemployment gives about 3% growth in this calibration, not zero growth. This is the growth-change version, not an output-gap formula. Coefficients depend on the empirical setting and must not be treated as universal constants.
concepts.example: If u rises from 4% to 6%, Δu = 2 percentage points and predicted GDP growth is −1%.

check.prompt: Can natural unemployment be positive at full employment?
check.answer: Yes. Frictional and structural unemployment can remain.

lessons.title: Consumption and saving across time
lessons.subtitle: Solve the lifetime trade-off, then distinguish income, wealth and interest-rate shocks.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 1.pdf
[EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3A - Rewriting Budget Constraints with Initial Wealth.pdf
[EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 2.pdf
[EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 3.pdf

concepts.title: Private, public and national saving
concepts.explain: Private saving is disposable income not consumed. Public saving is taxes less government purchases. Combining them cancels taxes directly, although taxes can still affect consumption behavior.
concepts.formula: Sp=Y−T−C; Sg=T−G; S=Y−C−G
steps: Calculate private and public saving separately.
Add them and cancel T.
Distinguish an accounting cancellation from a behavioral effect.
concepts.increase: Higher Y with C and G fixed increases S. Higher G with Y and C fixed reduces S.
concepts.decrease: Lower Y with C and G fixed reduces S. Lower G with Y and C fixed increases S.
concepts.edge: T > G gives public saving/a surplus; T < G gives public dissaving/a deficit; T = G gives zero public saving. Taxes cancel directly in national saving, but a tax-induced consumption response can still change national saving.

check.prompt: Why do taxes disappear from the national saving identity?
check.answer: They transfer resources between the private and public sectors, but may still change consumption decisions.

concepts.title: Goods equilibrium versus accounting
concepts.explain: In the closed-economy model, output is allocated to consumption C, investment I and government purchases G, with G taken as exogenous. Investment includes new business capital, new housing and inventory accumulation. Actual saving equals actual investment when unintended inventories are counted. Desired saving equals desired investment only at goods-market equilibrium; r is the price that reconciles the desired plans in the loanable-funds model.
concepts.formula: Y = Cd+Id+G ⇔ Sd = Id
steps: Define desired expenditure.
Compare it with actual production.
Use inventory surprises to reconcile actual accounting.
Adjust to equilibrium.
concepts.increase: If production exceeds desired spending, unintended inventories accumulate.
concepts.decrease: If desired spending exceeds production, inventories are run down unexpectedly.
concepts.edge: Zero unplanned inventory investment means production matches desired spending in this simple setup. An accounting identity does not prove everyone achieved desired choices. The illustrative US GDP table includes net exports, but the course model omits foreign trade. Consumption is a large GDP component and investment is especially volatile; those observations motivate modeling their separate decisions.
concepts.example: If Y=100, Cd=60, Id=15 and G=20, unintended inventory accumulation is 5.

check.prompt: Can desired saving exceed desired investment even though actual saving equals actual investment?
check.answer: Yes. Unintended inventory investment makes the accounting identity hold.

concepts.title: Why consumption is smoother than income
concepts.explain: A forward-looking household chooses a stream of consumption subject to lifetime resources, not just today’s income. Diminishing marginal utility makes it valuable to avoid very uneven consumption, subject to prices and patience. The life-cycle/permanent-income illustration has low earnings and possible borrowing when young, higher earnings and saving in middle age, and dissaving after retirement. Two periods are the minimum needed to model transferring resources across dates.
steps: Compare current income with desired consumption.
Borrow or save to transfer resources.
Repay debts or spend accumulated wealth by the terminal date.
concepts.increase: A temporary income increase is spread across current and future consumption under smoothing.
concepts.decrease: A temporary income loss can be cushioned by reducing saving or borrowing.
concepts.edge: Consumption smoothing does not require equal consumption or positive saving in every period. Young and retired households can dissave; a household with existing assets can dissave without borrowing. Borrowing constraints can prevent the planned smoothing.
concepts.example: A worker can save during high-income years and dissave in retirement even while choosing a smooth consumption path.

check.prompt: Does consumption smoothing mean c1 must equal c2?
check.answer: No. Equality additionally depends on the interest rate, patience and the utility structure.

concepts.title: Building the intertemporal budget
concepts.explain: Saving transfers current resources to the future. Combining both period budgets yields one lifetime constraint. The simple lecture model allows borrowing and lending at the same real interest rate.
steps: Write s1=y1−c1.
Write c2=y2+(1+r)s1.
Substitute and rearrange.
Check that debt is repaid at the terminal date.
concepts.increase: Higher y1 raises Ω one for one; higher y2 raises Ω by 1/R per unit. Both shift the lifetime budget outward in parallel when r is fixed.
concepts.decrease: Lower y1 reduces Ω one for one; lower y2 reduces Ω by 1/R per unit. Both shift the budget inward in parallel at unchanged r.
concepts.edge: The equality assumes positive marginal utility, no bequest motive and full terminal debt repayment, so no resources are optimally left unused. Nonnegative consumption requires 0 ≤ c1 ≤ Ω and c2 = R(Ω−c1) ≥ 0. If Ω < 0, this simple nonnegative-consumption allocation cannot repay all debts. Borrowing and lending at different rates produce a kink rather than one straight line.
concepts.example: With y1=100, y2=110 and r=10%, resources are 200. Choosing c1=120 leaves c2=88.

check.prompt: Why is c2 divided by 1+r in the present-value constraint?
check.answer: One unit saved today purchases 1+r future units.

concepts.title: Discounting goods is not discounting utility
concepts.explain: The market rate r converts dated goods into comparable resource units. The preference factor β converts future utility into present utility. They perform different tasks.
steps: Choose the date for valuation.
Discount later resources or compound earlier ones.
Use β only when aggregating utility.
concepts.increase: A higher r lowers the PV of a fixed positive future payment.
concepts.decrease: A lower r raises its PV.
concepts.edge: At r = 0, PV = face amount = FV for a fixed payment. For −1 < r < 0, a positive future payment has PV above its face amount. Real goods are discounted at the real rate; nominal money payments require a consistent nominal rate. β discounts utility, not goods.
concepts.example: At r=10%, 121 received in two periods has PV=100.

check.prompt: Should future income be discounted using ρ in the budget constraint?
check.answer: No. Use r for resources and ρ or β for preferences.

concepts.title: The endowment pivot
concepts.explain: On a graph with c1 horizontal and c2 vertical, the slope is −(1+r). The endowment bundle remains feasible at every interest rate in the model without initial assets.
concepts.formula: c2 = −Rc1+Ry1+y2; c1-axis intercept = y1+y2/R; c2-axis intercept = Ry1+y2, with R = 1+r
steps: Identify the endowment (y1,y2), where saving is zero.
Use the slope −R and the intercepts to draw the feasible boundary.
c1 < y1 means saving and c2 > y2; c1 > y1 means borrowing and c2 < y2.
Income increases move both intercepts outward at fixed slope; income decreases move both inward.
An interest change rotates the line through the endowment only when initial wealth is zero.
concepts.increase: Higher r steepens the line, expanding opportunities for savers and worsening terms for borrowers.
concepts.decrease: Lower r flattens the line, worsening returns to saving and improving borrowing terms.
concepts.edge: At zero saving the household can consume the endowment at any r. With initial wealth under Supplement 3A timing, the budget is c2 = −Rc1+R²a0+Ry1+y2; the resource effect of r includes the return on a0, so the old endowment is no longer the common pivot.
concepts.example: For endowment (100,100), r=0 gives c2=200−c1. r=0.1 gives c2=210−1.1c1; both pass through (100,100).

check.prompt: Which side of the endowment has positive saving?
check.answer: c1<y1, the left side.

concepts.title: Patience and diminishing marginal utility
concepts.explain: U = u(c1)+βu(c2) is lifetime utility; lowercase u is the same period-utility function at each date. Increasing u means more consumption is preferred; concavity means each extra unit adds less utility. Strictly convex indifference curves favor mixtures of two equally ranked uneven bundles. The lifetime marginal utility of c2 is βu′(c2), so the IC slope in a c1-horizontal graph is −u′(c1)/[βu′(c2)].
steps: Read β as a utility weight.
Read concavity as diminishing marginal utility.
Use both with prices to determine the consumption profile.
concepts.increase: Higher β shifts preferred consumption toward the future at fixed resources and r in the standard model.
concepts.decrease: Lower β shifts preferred consumption toward the present.
concepts.edge: The standard course case is 0 < β < 1. At the limit β = 1 (ρ = 0), future and present utility receive equal weights, but unequal goods prices can still make consumption unequal. At β = 0 the consumer ignores future utility and an interior Euler equality generally fails. Multiplying the whole U by a positive constant leaves choices unchanged; scaling only one period changes relative preferences.
concepts.example: ρ=0.25 implies β=0.8; ρ=0.1 implies β≈0.909. The second consumer is more patient.

check.prompt: Does a higher β mean a higher market return on saving?
check.answer: No. It changes preferences, not the market interest rate.

concepts.title: Deriving the Euler condition
concepts.explain: After substituting the budget constraint, more c1 directly raises current utility but lowers c2 by 1+r. The optimum balances these marginal utility effects.
concepts.formula: U′(c1) = u′(c1)−βR u′(c2); interior u′(c1) = βR u′(c2); equivalently MRS of c1 for c2 = R
steps: Write c2=(1+r)(y1−c1)+y2.
Apply the chain rule to u(c1)+βu(c2(c1)).
Combine with the budget constraint.
concepts.increase: If current marginal utility exceeds discounted marginal utility from saving, increase c1 locally.
concepts.decrease: If current marginal utility is smaller, reduce c1 and save more locally.
concepts.edge: With concave utility and a no-borrowing upper bound c1 ≤ y1, a constrained optimum at c1 = y1 can satisfy u′(c1)−βR u′(c2) ≥ 0: it would like more c1 but cannot borrow. Equality can hold exactly when the limit just touches the unconstrained optimum. Nonnegative-consumption corners require their own one-sided conditions.
concepts.example: With logarithmic utility, 1/c1=β(1+r)/c2, so c2=β(1+r)c1.

check.prompt: Why does the Euler equation include 1+r?
check.answer: Forgoing one current unit finances 1+r future units.

concepts.title: Interest versus impatience
concepts.explain: With the same strictly concave period utility in both periods and an interior optimum, comparing r with ρ determines whether consumption rises, stays constant or falls over time.
concepts.formula: r>ρ ⇒ c2>c1; r=ρ ⇒ c2=c1; r<ρ ⇒ c2<c1
steps: Rewrite β(1+r)=(1+r)/(1+ρ).
Compare marginal utilities.
Reverse the inequality when converting marginal utility into consumption.
concepts.increase: Raising r above ρ makes future consumption exceed current consumption at the optimum.
concepts.decrease: Lowering r below ρ makes current consumption exceed future consumption.
concepts.edge: This compares c1 with c2 at an optimum. It does not by itself establish how c1 changes when r changes.
concepts.example: If r=ρ=0.05 and y1=80, y2=122, constant consumption is (1.05×80+122)/2.05≈100.488.

check.prompt: Does r>ρ imply the person must save rather than borrow?
check.answer: No. Saving also depends on current income relative to c1.

concepts.title: Current and future income have different saving effects
concepts.explain: With normal consumption in both periods and unconstrained smoothing, both incomes raise current consumption. Current income also directly funds saving; future income does not.
concepts.formula: ds1/dy1=1−dc1/dy1>0; ds1/dy2=−dc1/dy2<0
steps: Track the change in lifetime resources.
Allocate the gain or loss across both periods.
Use s1=y1−c1 to obtain the saving effect.
concepts.increase: Higher y1 raises c1, c2 and s1. Higher y2 raises c1 and c2 but reduces s1.
concepts.decrease: Lower y1 lowers c1 and c2 and reduces s1. Lower y2 lowers consumption and raises s1.
concepts.edge: For unrestricted normal dated consumption, a current gain is partly saved. A permanent gain means income rises in both periods, not merely a larger current gain; it produces a larger lifetime-resource change than an equally sized temporary current gain. A timing change Δy1+Δy2/R = 0 leaves optimal consumption unchanged at fixed prices and preferences but changes saving by Δy1. Binding borrowing limits can break that timing neutrality.
concepts.example: If current income rises 10 and MPC=0.6, c1 rises 6 and saving rises 4. A future-income gain raising c1 by 6 reduces saving by 6.

check.prompt: Why do equal signs for current consumption coexist with opposite signs for saving?
check.answer: Only the current-income change directly changes y1 in s1=y1−c1.

concepts.title: Interest changes are not one universal arrow
concepts.explain: For a saver, higher r creates a favorable income effect and a substitution effect away from current consumption. These oppose for c1. For a borrower, higher r reduces purchasing power and makes c1 relatively expensive.
concepts.formula: Higher r raises the relative price of c1 to c2
steps: Identify the initial saving sign, with no initial wealth in the simple endowment diagram.
Draw an intermediate budget parallel to the new budget and tangent to the original IC.
Original optimum to compensated tangency is substitution; compensated tangency to new optimum is income at fixed new prices.
Combine the two signed effects separately for c1 and c2.
At fixed y1, the saving response is the negative of the c1 response.
concepts.increase: For a small rise in r, substitution lowers c1 and raises c2. For an initial saver the favorable income effect raises both: c1 is ambiguous and c2 rises. For an initial borrower the adverse income effect lowers both: c1 falls and c2 is ambiguous.
concepts.decrease: For a small fall in r, substitution raises c1 and lowers c2. For an initial saver the adverse income effect lowers both: c1 is ambiguous and c2 falls. For an initial borrower the favorable income effect raises both: c1 rises and c2 is ambiguous.
concepts.edge: These are local results with normal dated consumption and unchanged borrowing status. At initial zero saving, the first-order income effect of a rate change is zero: the local response is the compensated substitution effect. Finite changes may change saver/borrower status. The course maintains aggregate C_r < 0 and S_r > 0 as an additional assumption, not an identity.
concepts.example: A saver facing a higher return may save less to fund a target or save more because future consumption is cheaper. The net requires preferences.

check.prompt: Why is upward-sloping aggregate saving an extra maintained assumption?
check.answer: Individual saver income and substitution effects do not prove it for every household.

concepts.title: Initial wealth earns interest before period 1 consumption
concepts.explain: The supplement dates a0 at the beginning of period 1. It earns r before c1 is chosen. Saving is the change in wealth, not simply the level of assets carried forward.
steps: Compound a0 into period 1.
Add y1 and subtract c1 to obtain a1.
Subtract a0 to obtain saving.
Impose terminal a2=0.
concepts.increase: At fixed r, y1 and y2, a rise in a0 raises lifetime resources by R times the wealth gain and raises both normal consumption quantities. It also raises current interest income by r times the gain; current saving changes by rΔa0−Δc1.
concepts.decrease: At fixed r, y1 and y2, a fall in a0 reduces lifetime resources by R times the loss and reduces both normal consumption quantities. Current interest income changes too, so use Δs1 = rΔa0−Δc1 rather than mechanically reversing consumption alone.
concepts.edge: Positive end-period assets can coexist with dissaving: a1 > 0 but a1 < a0. Dissaving need not be borrowing when existing assets are available. At fixed total current income, higher wealth reduces saving through higher c1; at fixed endowment income under 3A, the extra interest-income term can alter that sign. For log utility, ds1/da0 = r−R/(1+β), which can be zero or positive at sufficiently high r. A zero terminal asset balance follows from no bequest motive and full repayment, not from two periods alone.
concepts.example: With a0=100, r=0.1, y1=50 and c1=80, a1=80 and s1=−20, although end-period wealth is positive.

check.prompt: Why is s1 not equal to a1 when initial wealth is positive?
check.answer: Saving measures the change from a0, so s1=a1−a0.

concepts.title: Solving logarithmic and square-root cases
concepts.explain: Tutorials 3 and 4 use square-root period utility. Its derivatives are u′(c) = 1/(2√c) > 0 and u″(c) = −1/(4c^(3/2)) < 0 for c > 0. Substituting these into Euler gives the consumption ratio. Logarithmic utility is an additional illustrative functional form used in this bank: u′ = 1/c and u″ = −1/c². A solution for one form must not be copied into the other.
concepts.formula: R = 1+r, Ω = Ra0+y1+y2/R. Square root: c2 = β²R²c1, c1 = Ω/(1+β²R). Log illustration: c2 = βRc1, c1 = Ω/(1+β).
steps: Differentiate the stated period utility, checking increasingness and curvature.
Insert its marginal utility into u′(c1) = βR u′(c2).
Solve for c2/c1, then insert that ratio into c1+c2/R = Ω.
Compute c2 and saving, including ra0 in saving under Supplement 3A timing.
Check positive consumption, resource equality and any borrowing restriction.
concepts.increase: For log utility at fixed r and β, higher Ω raises c1=Ω/(1+β).
concepts.decrease: Lower Ω reduces c1 and c2 in the same proportion for these homothetic examples.
concepts.edge: At r = ρ, βR = 1 and both forms imply equal dated consumption at an interior optimum. Positive resources, R > 0 and β > 0 give interior consumption for these unbounded-MU-at-zero forms without extra restrictions. Linear utility lacks diminishing MU and can yield a corner or indifference, so the same strict smoothing conclusions cannot be presumed.
concepts.example: For square-root utility, c1=Ω/[1+β²(1+r)]. With β=0.8, r=0.25 and Ω=180, c1=100 and c2=100.

check.prompt: What is the square-root c2/c1 ratio when β=0.9 and r=0.2?

concepts.title: Check feasibility before declaring an optimum
concepts.explain: An unconstrained solution assumes borrowing and lending are available and all dated resources can be traded at r. A borrowing limit may prevent the desired transfer, making current income especially important.
concepts.formula: No borrowing with a0=0 implies s1≥0 and c1≤y1
steps: Solve the unconstrained problem.
Check c1 against the borrowing limit.
If it violates the limit, consider the boundary.
Recheck future consumption and utility.
concepts.increase: A current income increase can relax a binding borrowing limit and permit higher c1.
concepts.decrease: A current income fall can tighten the limit and force a larger consumption drop.
concepts.edge: If the strictly concave unconstrained optimum has c1 > y1 and borrowing is prohibited with a0 = 0, the constrained optimum is c1 = y1, s1 = 0 and c2 = y2. If desired c1 = y1 exactly, the limit just touches the unconstrained optimum and Euler equality can still hold. If desired c1 < y1, the no-borrowing limit is slack.
concepts.example: If desired c1=120 but y1=80 and borrowing is forbidden, c1 cannot exceed 80 in the simple endowment model.

check.prompt: Should the Euler equality be used to justify c1=120 here?
check.answer: No. The candidate violates the constraint.

concepts.title: Current and future MPCs use different dates
concepts.explain: Assume an unconstrained interior consumer with U = √c1 + β√c2, β > 0 and R = 1+r > 0. An MPC must name both the consumption date and the income date. Tutorial 3 asks for c1’s and c2’s responses to current income. A future consumption response can exceed one because the part saved earns interest; the present values of the two responses, rather than their raw sum, exhaust the income gain.
concepts.formula: For square-root utility, R = 1+r > 0, D = 1+β²R: ∂c1/∂y1 = 1/D; ∂c2/∂y1 = β²R²/D; ∂c1/∂y2 = 1/(RD); ∂c2/∂y2 = β²R/D.
steps: Hold β and r fixed when differentiating the closed-form consumption choices.
Differentiate Ω with respect to y1 (one) or y2 (1/R).
Multiply by the c1 resource coefficient 1/D and the c2 ratio β²R².
Check ∂c1/∂y1 + (∂c2/∂y1)/R = 1; current saving’s response is 1−∂c1/∂y1.
concepts.increase: A rise in y1 raises both consumption levels and current saving. A rise in y2 also raises both consumption levels but reduces current saving. The same number of real goods arriving later has a smaller PV when r > 0.
concepts.decrease: A fall in y1 reduces both consumption levels and current saving. A fall in y2 reduces both consumption levels but raises current saving. Differentiate with the negative income change rather than treating future income as today’s cash.
concepts.edge: 0 < ∂c1/∂y1 < 1, but ∂c2/∂y1 need not be below one. At r = 0 the two current-income MPCs sum to one. A binding no-borrowing limit can instead give ∂c1/∂y1 = 1 locally and no current response to future income.
concepts.example: With β = 0.9 and R = 2, D = 2.62. A 131-unit current-income gain raises c1 by 50 and c2 by 162; saving rises by 81, which grows to 162. The PV check is 50+162/2 = 131.

check.prompt: Why is a future MPC of 162/131 above one not a resource violation?
check.answer: The future increment includes interest earned on saving. Discounting it by R = 2 makes its current cost 81, leaving 50 for current consumption.

lessons.title: Working and saving over a lifetime
lessons.subtitle: Combine consumption timing with the choice of when to work.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 1.pdf

concepts.title: Labor income becomes endogenous
concepts.explain: Replacing endowment income with wage times chosen hours links consumption to work. Wages and time endowments are inputs, while hours and earnings are outcomes of the household problem.
concepts.formula: yt=wt(h−lt); nt=h−lt
steps: Choose leisure in each period.
Convert leisure into work.
Calculate labor income.
Finance consumption and saving from that income.
concepts.increase: More current work raises current income at fixed w1.
concepts.decrease: Less current work lowers current income at fixed w1.
concepts.edge: An increase in w1 need not increase hours because income and substitution effects oppose.
concepts.example: With h=16, l1=10 and w1=4, n1=6 and y1=24.

check.prompt: Is y1 still exogenous after this substitution?
check.answer: No. It depends on the chosen leisure l1.

concepts.title: One lifetime budget for four goods
concepts.explain: Current consumption, future consumption and leisure in both periods compete for lifetime resources. Leisure has an opportunity cost equal to the wage earned by working instead.
concepts.formula: c1+c2/R = w1(h−l1)+w2(h−l2)/R; equivalently c1+w1l1+(c2+w2l2)/R = w1h+w2h/R, R = 1+r > 0
steps: Write s1=w1(h−l1)−c1.
Write c2=w2(h−l2)+(1+r)s1.
Eliminate s1.
Keep the time bounds in both periods.
concepts.increase: Higher w1 or w2 expands earning opportunities at fixed leisure.
concepts.decrease: Lower w1 or w2 contracts earning opportunities at fixed leisure.
concepts.edge: Full income values the time endowment as if every hour were worked; it is not actual labor earnings unless leisure is zero. Feasibility requires 0 ≤ lt ≤ h and ct ≥ 0, with terminal debts repaid. Labor earnings are endogenous, but the household still takes wages and r as given.
concepts.example: With h=10, l1=l2=5, w1=2, w2=3 and r=0, lifetime consumption totals 25.

check.prompt: Does the model allow c1 to exceed current labor income?
check.answer: Yes, if borrowing is allowed and future resources repay the debt.

concepts.title: Three independent choices after substitution
concepts.explain: Start from U = u(c1,l1)+βu(c2,l2). The lifetime budget eliminates c2, leaving c1, l1 and l2 as independent choices, with the resulting feasible bounds still in force. Differentiating with respect to one choice holds the other two independent choices fixed. Subscripts c and l denote marginal utilities; a positional u1(c2,l2) means consumption marginal utility evaluated in period 2.
concepts.formula: c2 = R[w1(h−l1)−c1]+w2(h−l2). FOCs: uc(c1,l1)−βRuc(c2,l2) = 0; ul(c1,l1)−βRw1uc(c2,l2) = 0; β[ul(c2,l2)−w2uc(c2,l2)] = 0.
steps: Solve the budget for c2.
Substitute it into lifetime utility.
Differentiate with respect to c1, l1 and l2.
Recover c2 from the budget.
concepts.increase: Increasing c1 by one reduces c2 by 1+r. Increasing l1 by one reduces c2 by (1+r)w1.
concepts.decrease: Reducing l2 by one frees w2 future consumption units. Reducing l1 frees (1+r)w1 future units.
concepts.edge: Eliminating the equality constraint does not remove time bounds or nonnegative-consumption restrictions. The displayed equalities describe an interior optimum. At a leisure boundary, use feasible one-sided changes instead. c2 remains an economically chosen outcome, although it is no longer independently selectable after substitution.
concepts.example: If w1=4, w2=6 and r=0.25, the three derivatives are −1.25, −5 and −6.

check.prompt: Why would independently choosing c2 as well overcount freedom?
check.answer: The lifetime budget has already determined c2 from the other three choices.

concepts.title: Consumption Euler condition with leisure
concepts.explain: The intertemporal condition still compares marginal consumption utility across dates. Here each marginal utility is evaluated at both consumption and leisure in its period.
concepts.formula: uc(c1,l1) = βRuc(c2,l2); MRS of c1 for c2 = uc(c1,l1)/[βuc(c2,l2)] = R
steps: Differentiate current consumption utility.
Include c1’s effect on c2.
Balance the marginal utilities at an interior optimum.
concepts.increase: If the current marginal utility exceeds β(1+r) times future marginal utility, raise c1 locally.
concepts.decrease: If it is lower, reduce c1 and transfer resources forward.
concepts.edge: For nonseparable u(c,l), r = ρ equates uc across dates but need not equate c when leisure differs. Equality of consumption follows for identical separable strictly concave consumption utility. The endowment-model response of c1 to an income shock cannot be mechanically reused for an endogenous wage shock that also changes leisure prices.
concepts.example: With u=ln c+ln l, uc=1/c and c2=β(1+r)c1. Leisure does not enter uc in this separable example.

check.prompt: What changes relative to the endowment Euler condition?
check.answer: The marginal utilities may now depend on leisure as well as consumption.

concepts.title: Two within-period leisure conditions
concepts.explain: Each period has its own consumption–leisure trade-off. Combining the c1 and l1 FOCs cancels the future marginal-utility term and gives the familiar MRS condition.
concepts.formula: ul(c1,l1)/uc(c1,l1)=w1; ul(c2,l2)/uc(c2,l2)=w2
steps: For l1, differentiate direct leisure and indirect future consumption.
Use the Euler condition to simplify.
For l2, both effects occur in period 2, so β cancels.
concepts.increase: If a period’s leisure MRS exceeds its wage, increase leisure locally.
concepts.decrease: If its leisure MRS is below its wage, work more locally.
concepts.edge: The future within-period condition is MRS=w2, not βw2 or (1+r)w2.
concepts.example: For u=ln c+ln l, c1=w1l1 and c2=w2l2 at an interior optimum.

check.prompt: Why is there no β in the future within-period MRS condition?
check.answer: Both future marginal utilities receive the same β weight.

concepts.title: The price of leisure across time
concepts.explain: An hour of leisure today sacrifices w1 current goods, which could grow to (1+r)w1 future goods. An hour of future leisure sacrifices w2 future goods. Their ratio governs substitution between dates.
concepts.formula: Price of l1 in units of l2 = Rw1/w2; at an interior optimum ul(c1,l1)/[βul(c2,l2)] = Rw1/w2
steps: Value both forgone earnings at the same date.
Divide current leisure’s future-valued cost by future leisure’s cost.
Use the ratio to interpret the substitution effect.
concepts.increase: Higher w1 raises Rw1/w2 and makes current leisure relatively expensive, encouraging current work through substitution. Holding r fixed, a fall in w2 also raises this ratio.
concepts.decrease: Lower w1 reduces Rw1/w2 and makes current leisure relatively cheap. A rise in w2 also reduces the ratio and encourages shifting work toward period 2 through the tutorial’s substitution mechanism.
concepts.edge: Equal proportional wage changes leave this relative-leisure price unchanged but still change earning capacity and consumption prices relative to leisure. The ratio alone cannot determine hours. The recording explicitly omits comparative statics of r on labor supply; do not use this ratio to assert a taught interest-sensitive FE curve.
concepts.example: With w1=10, w2=15 and r=0.2, the ratio is 0.8. An hour of current leisure costs 0.8 hours of future leisure.

check.prompt: Why is w1/w2 insufficient when r is nonzero?
check.answer: Current forgone earnings could earn interest before period 2.

concepts.title: A current wage shock has opposing effects
concepts.explain: A higher current wage makes current leisure expensive relative to consumption and future leisure. It also makes the worker wealthier. With normal leisure, these substitution and income effects conflict.
concepts.formula: Higher w1 → substitution raises n1; income lowers n1
steps: Hold w2 and r fixed.
Trace the relative-price substitution effect.
Trace the lifetime-income effect.
Compare magnitudes.
concepts.increase: A rise in w1 increases n1 if substitution dominates, reduces n1 if income dominates, and leaves it unchanged under cancellation.
concepts.decrease: A fall in w1 reduces n1 through substitution but raises it through the negative income effect. The net remains conditional.
concepts.edge: The opposing income/substitution argument describes an initially working household with normal leisure. At a no-work corner a small wage change may leave work at zero. Upward-sloping current labor supply additionally assumes substitution dominance; normal leisure alone is insufficient.
concepts.example: For the illustrative one-period log case u = ln c+ln l with no nonlabor income, l = h/2 at every positive w: the effects cancel exactly and hours are unchanged. In the two-period model, earnings opportunities at both dates matter, so do not assume that special cancellation without solving it.

check.prompt: Is the response to w1 a shift of the current labor-supply curve?
check.answer: No. w1 is the axis variable, so this is movement along the curve.

concepts.title: A future wage shock changes current work
concepts.explain: The tutorial maintains that making future leisure relatively more expensive shifts leisure toward today, alongside normal current leisure. A higher future wage then raises lifetime earning opportunities and makes future leisure dearer relative to current leisure. Both maintained effects raise current leisure and reduce current work.
concepts.formula: Higher w2 → lower n1; lower w2 → higher n1
steps: Hold current w1 fixed.
Compare the intertemporal relative wage.
Add the current leisure income effect.
Classify the current labor-supply shift.
concepts.increase: Higher w2 encourages shifting work toward the future and consuming more leisure today. Current labor supply shifts left.
concepts.decrease: Lower w2 encourages work today relative to tomorrow and reduces lifetime wealth. Both effects increase current work, shifting supply right.
concepts.edge: Normal leisure alone does not mathematically sign every cross-price substitution effect in an arbitrary four-good utility function; the direction here uses the tutorial’s stated intertemporal-substitution mechanism. A binding borrowing limit, unavailable future work or a current no-work corner can prevent a strict response. Keep w1 fixed when calling this a current supply shift.
concepts.example: A credible expected rise in future earning power can reduce current part-time work even though today’s wage is unchanged.

check.prompt: Why is the current work response clearer for w2 than for w1?
check.answer: For w2 the two effects on current leisure reinforce; for w1 they oppose.

lessons.title: Government spending and tax timing
lessons.subtitle: Follow the resources across both periods before predicting consumption.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 2.pdf
[EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 1.pdf

concepts.title: The government must finance its purchases
concepts.explain: Fiscal policy comprises purchases and taxation. G is exogenous: its path is given rather than chosen inside this model. All amounts are real. Borrowing transfers tax collection across dates. With no inherited public assets or debt and no terminal public assets or debt, spending and taxes have equal present values.
concepts.formula: B₁=G₁−T₁; G₁=T₁+B₁; G₂=T₂−(1+r)B₁; G₁+G₂/(1+r)=T₁+T₂/(1+r), with 1+r>0
steps: Write B₁=G₁−T₁; a positive B₁ is borrowing and a negative B₁ is government saving.
Substitute into G₂=T₂−(1+r)B₁, including principal and interest.
Rearrange to (1+r)G₁+G₂=(1+r)T₁+T₂ and divide by 1+r.
For a policy comparison identify which spending or tax dates adjust. A deficit alone does not describe a complete policy.
concepts.increase: With T₁,G₂ fixed, increasing G₁ by x raises B₁ by x and required T₂ by (1+r)x. Increasing G₂ alone by x with current purchases and taxes fixed raises T₂ by x without changing B₁.
concepts.decrease: With T₁,G₂ fixed, reducing G₁ by x lowers B₁ by x and T₂ by (1+r)x. Reducing G₂ alone by x lowers required T₂ by x without changing current borrowing.
concepts.edge: B₁<0 is an asset earning interest, so T₂ can be below G₂. The equality uses the stated terminal-wealth condition; allowing unspent positive terminal wealth adds a term. An unfunded permanent tax cut is not a feasible fixed-G tax-timing experiment.
concepts.example: G₁=100,T₁=80,G₂=50,r=.10 gives B₁=20,T₂=72. If G₁ instead is 70 while T₁ remains 80, the surplus is 10 and T₂=50−11=39.

check.prompt: Can unchanged future spending and taxes finance an extra current purchase forever?
check.answer: No. The terminal budget condition rules out unpaid debt in this two-period model.

concepts.title: Lump-sum taxes change wealth, not relative prices
concepts.explain: A lump-sum tax is independent of the individual’s behavior. A head tax is an example; an earnings tax is not. The lecture’s lump-sum cut reduces each taxpayer’s liability by the same absolute amount. A fixed liability changes lifetime resources without directly changing the marginal reward to work or the price of dated consumption.
concepts.formula: s₁=y₁−t₁−c₁; c₂=y₂−t₂+(1+r)s₁; c₁+c₂/(1+r)=y₁+y₂/(1+r)−[t₁+t₂/(1+r)]
steps: Start with zero initial assets in this illustration and allocate current disposable income to c₁ and s₁.
Carry saving or borrowing into period 2 at gross return 1+r.
Eliminate s₁; the right side is after-tax lifetime resources W.
At fixed r the c₁,c₂ budget slope is −(1+r). A lump-sum liability shifts its intercept; an earnings-tax change can also change the net wage and leisure price.
concepts.increase: An additional current tax x reduces W by x; an additional future tax x reduces W by x/(1+r). At fixed income and interest rate, normal consumption at both dates falls.
concepts.decrease: Current relief x increases W by x, whereas future relief x increases W by x/(1+r). With no offsetting tax increase, normal consumption at both dates rises.
concepts.edge: No direct substitution effect does not mean no behavior change: the wealth effect can affect consumption, saving and labor. A compensated tax-timing change can preserve W. If initial assets are present, add them using their specified timing convention.
concepts.example: At r=.10, incomes 100 and 132 and taxes 10 and 22 give W=90+110/1.10=190. An extra future tax of 11 lowers W by 10; an extra current tax of 11 lowers W by 11.

check.prompt: Does a lump-sum tax have no effects at all?
check.answer: No. It has a wealth or income effect even though it has no direct substitution effect.

concepts.title: Which date of government purchases changes?
concepts.explain: Temporary G in the lecture means G₁ changes while G₂ stays fixed. Hold incomes and r fixed and assume G has no direct utility or productivity benefit. Extra present-value purchases require extra present-value taxes, lowering private lifetime resources. When Ricardian financing conditions hold, collecting those taxes now or later does not change that wealth loss. The purchase date still matters for current saving, which subtracts G₁ rather than G₂.
concepts.formula: ΔW=−ΔG₁−ΔG₂/(1+r); ΔC₁=mΔW; ΔS₁=−ΔC₁−ΔG₁=−(1−m)ΔG₁+[m/(1+r)]ΔG₂, with 0<m<1
steps: Specify each date’s spending change and the fixed income/r assumptions.
Use the government budget to calculate the PV tax burden; the representative household bears it.
Apply consumption smoothing: m is the response of current consumption to PV wealth.
Calculate current national saving using Y₁−C₁−G₁.
Future-only and persistent cases are deductions from these budgets, not a claim that the temporary-current-G slide describes all paths.
concepts.increase: A current-only rise x reduces C₁ by mx and S₁ by (1−m)x. A future-only rise x reduces C₁ by mx/(1+r), but raises S₁ by that amount because current G₁ is unchanged. An increase at both dates requires both terms in the formula.
concepts.decrease: A current-only cut x raises C₁ by mx and S₁ by (1−m)x. A future-only cut x raises C₁ by mx/(1+r) and lowers current saving by that amount. Cutting both dates is a different spending path.
concepts.edge: For spending changes at both dates, the saving response depends on preferences and timing. At r=0 with equal-consumption smoothing, equal increases at both dates leave S₁ unchanged. Binding credit limits, changing output/r, or productive or utility-providing G require another comparison.
concepts.example: With U=ln c₁+ln c₂, c₁=W/2. At r=.10 a current-only G increase of 100 gives ΔC₁=−50,ΔS₁=−50. A future-only increase of 110 gives the same ΔC₁=−50 but ΔS₁=+50. Reversing these changes gives ΔC₁=+50 and, respectively, ΔS₁=+50 or −50.

check.prompt: Why can higher future purchases raise saving today even though higher temporary current purchases lower it?
check.answer: Both reduce wealth and current consumption. Only current purchases directly absorb current output; future G is not subtracted from current national saving.

concepts.title: Ricardian equivalence is a tax-timing result
concepts.explain: For a fixed spending path, feasible lump-sum tax timing preserves aggregate PV taxes. Consumption neutrality additionally needs forward-looking households to internalize their own future liability, face the relevant borrowing/lending rate and be able to shift resources across dates. The classical benchmark accepts these conditions; the Keynesian discussion examines failures.
concepts.formula: ΔT₂ = −(1+r)ΔT₁ when ΔG₁=ΔG₂=0
steps: Hold G₁,G₂ fixed and calculate the interest-adjusted future tax offset.
Check that the same household or an operative family transfer system internalizes it.
Confirm the household’s feasible lifetime budget and preferences remain unchanged, with no newly binding financing restriction.
Then both dates’ consumption stay fixed and extra private saving offsets government dissaving.
concepts.increase: A current tax cut increases disposable income, but the matching future liability induces equal extra private saving.
concepts.decrease: A current tax increase reduces disposable income, but the matching future tax cut induces lower private saving.
concepts.edge: Bonds are private assets but their aggregate value is offset by future taxes under these conditions. Each particular bondholder need not personally pay exactly the tax on its own bond. Redistribution, differing horizons/rates, myopia or distortionary taxes can break neutrality.
concepts.example: At r=5%, a current cut of 200 requires a future increase of 210. Its present value is 200.

check.prompt: Why must the future tax offset exceed the current tax cut when r>0?
check.answer: The government must repay interest as well as principal.

concepts.title: Private and public saving move separately
concepts.explain: National saving combines private saving and government saving. Under Ricardian equivalence, a tax-timing change moves the two components in opposite directions without changing their sum.
concepts.formula: Sprivate = Y − T − C; Sgovernment = T − G; Snational = Y − C − G
steps: Calculate private saving after taxes.
Calculate the government surplus.
Add them and cancel taxes.
concepts.increase: A tax increase with unchanged C and G raises government saving and lowers private saving equally.
concepts.decrease: A tax cut with unchanged C and G lowers government saving and raises private saving equally.
concepts.edge: Taxes disappear from the accounting formula but can still affect national saving indirectly if they change consumption.
concepts.example: Y=1000,C=600,G=200,T=150 gives private saving 250, government saving−50, national saving 200.

check.prompt: If T falls by 50 and C rises by 20 at fixed Y and G, what happens to national saving?
check.answer: It falls by 20. Private saving rises 30 while government saving falls 50.

concepts.title: A borrowing limit can make timing matter
concepts.explain: A forward-looking household may wish to borrow against future income but be unable to do so. A tax cut can then raise current consumption despite unchanged lifetime wealth.
