Myopia is different: the household overlooks the later tax liability and perceives a wealth gain, even if borrowing is available. Neither failure removes the government budget.
concepts.formula: c₁ ≤ y₁ − t₁ when borrowing is prohibited and initial wealth is zero
steps: Find unconstrained desired c₁ from lifetime resources.
With no initial assets and no borrowing, compare it with c₁≤y₁−t₁.
Apply the tax shift and test the new ceiling against the unchanged target.
Separately ask whether future taxes were recognized; neglecting them is myopia, not proof of a credit limit.
concepts.increase: A current tax cut raises the ceiling and can increase c₁ until the limit stops binding. A myopic consumer can also raise c₁ by wrongly treating temporary relief as lifetime wealth.
concepts.decrease: A current tax increase lowers the ceiling and can force c₁ down despite later relief. A myopic consumer can cut c₁ because it overlooks that future tax reduction.
concepts.edge: A saver can absorb a small current tax rise by saving less; a larger rise can make the same borrowing prohibition bind. Low income, a legal borrowing limit and a binding limit are distinct facts.
concepts.example: A household at c₁=y₁−t₁=80 can consume 100 after a current tax cut 20 if its desired consumption remains above 100.

check.prompt: Does every household with low income violate Ricardian equivalence?
check.answer: No. What matters is whether the financing constraint binds, together with the other assumptions.

concepts.title: Taxpayer incidence, horizons and bequests
concepts.explain: A balanced aggregate tax shift need not preserve each household’s lifetime taxes. Identify who receives relief and who pays later. Parents can internalize descendants’ future taxes by increasing bequests, but this requires an operative transfer margin and sufficient concern. Finite lives alone do not rule out neutrality.
concepts.formula: ΔW_h=−Δt₁,h−Δt₂,h/(1+r); ΣΔW_h=0 need not imply Σm_hΔW_h=0
steps: Allocate current and future tax changes to households or families.
Compute each household’s PV wealth change.
If family transfers offset the future liability, trace extra saving into the bequest.
If wealth is redistributed among households with different current-consumption responses, add those responses. This is an explicitly derived incidence illustration.
concepts.increase: An operative increase in bequests can offset a descendant’s future tax burden and preserve current family consumption. A redistribution toward a household with a higher current-consumption response can instead increase aggregate current consumption.
concepts.decrease: Existing bequests can fall to offset a current tax increase paired with future relief for descendants. A redistribution toward a lower-current-spending household can reduce aggregate consumption despite unchanged aggregate PV taxes.
concepts.edge: Zero intended bequests cannot be reduced below zero. Caring about descendants does not ensure positive bequests if they are expected to be rich. Equal linear consumption responses can make a zero-total-wealth redistribution cancel; different responses remove that guarantee.
concepts.example: At r=.10, a current cut of 100 for A funded by a future tax of 110 on unrelated B gives ΔW_A=100,ΔW_B=−100. Current-consumption responses .75 and .25 imply ΔC₁=75−25=50, so national saving falls 50 at fixed Y₁,G₁.

check.prompt: Does unchanged aggregate PV taxes prove every household’s consumption is unchanged?
check.answer: No. Check whose lifetime taxes changed and whether transfers offset the incidence; the aggregate constraint alone does not preserve each household’s budget.

concepts.title: Evidence tests conditions, not an identity
concepts.explain: The lecture’s 1992 US withholding reduction delayed tax payment until April 1993 rather than granting lasting relief. In the survey, 43% intended to spend the extra cash and 57% intended to save, repay debt or adjust withholding. These intentions challenge universal zero response, but do not measure every household’s actual spending or identify the reason for a response.
concepts.formula: Tax timing unchanged in present value does not imply observed ΔC must equal zero when assumptions fail
steps: Distinguish permanent relief from delayed payment.
Compare observed plans with the neutrality prediction.
Separate evidence of a response from evidence about its cause.
concepts.increase: A larger current spending response to a temporary withholding reduction is harder to reconcile with universal strict equivalence.
concepts.decrease: A smaller spending response and larger saving or debt repayment response is more consistent with consumption smoothing, without proving all assumptions.
concepts.edge: A majority planning saving does not establish aggregate neutrality; a minority’s spending can matter. Saving/debt repayment is consistent with smoothing without proving every assumption. Intentions alone distinguish neither myopia nor liquidity constraints.
concepts.example: A group matching those reported shares has 43 of 100 planning extra spending. This does not establish aggregate consumption rises by 43% of the cash: respondent counts do not give amounts or actual behavior.

check.prompt: Can spending after a tax delay prove every spender is myopic?
check.answer: No. A binding borrowing constraint can also produce that response.

lessons.title: Capital, investment and the goods market
lessons.subtitle: Separate the desired stock from the flow needed to reach it.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 3.pdf

concepts.title: What counts as investment?
concepts.explain: A capital good is produced, used to produce other goods and not entirely used up in its production period. Business fixed investment includes structures, equipment and intellectual property such as software and R&D. Residential investment includes new housing acquired by households or landlords. Inventories include finished goods, work in progress and production materials. Fixed means staying in use for a while, not a fixed spending amount.
concepts.formula: I = business fixed investment + residential investment + inventory investment
steps: Identify new business capital, new housing or inventory additions.
Distinguish new production from ownership transfers of existing financial or physical assets.
Inventory investment is production minus sales; it can be intended or unintended.
Distinguish the stock K from the flow I. The lecture’s chart shows I more volatile than C or GDP; this motivates the model but does not identify causation.
concepts.increase: Higher production relative to sales raises inventory investment.
concepts.decrease: Lower production relative to sales reduces inventories and can make inventory investment negative.
concepts.edge: Existing-house or share sales mainly transfer ownership; newly produced accompanying services can still count in output. The lecture’s approximately three-quarter business-fixed share is historical context, not a universal identity.
concepts.example: A firm produces 100 units and sells 92. Inventory investment is 8 units.

check.prompt: Does purchasing a company share automatically add to GDP investment?
check.answer: No. The financial transaction itself is not production of a new capital good.

concepts.title: Capital moves through accumulation and depreciation
concepts.explain: K₁ is inherited. Current investment is chosen and becomes productive K₂ next period, after inherited capital depreciates. In the lecture’s pₖ=1 normalization, physical capital additions and real investment spending have the same numerical value. Choosing I₁ or K₂ is equivalent, not two independent controls.
concepts.formula: K₂=(1−d)K₁+I₁ when pₖ=1; generally K₂=(1−d)K₁+J₁ and real investment expenditure=pₖJ₁
steps: Start with inherited capital.
Subtract depreciation.
Add current gross investment to obtain next-period capital.
concepts.increase: More current investment raises next-period capital one for one in this specification.
concepts.decrease: Less current investment lowers next-period capital relative to its former path.
concepts.edge: Zero I shrinks capital if d>0; I=dK maintains it. At d=0 all investment is net; at d=1 no inherited stock survives. With general pₖ, distinguish physical additions J from expenditure pₖJ. A single period without subsequent production or resale payoff offers no reason for lagged investment.

check.prompt: What investment holds K constant at 80 with depreciation 5%?

concepts.title: Why the firm values future profits
concepts.explain: The representative competitive firm maximizes current profit plus discounted future profit. It pays for investment now, produces with K₂ next period, sells the surviving (1−d)K₂ after final production/depreciation, and shuts down. This sale is a positive future receipt, also interpretable as terminal disinvestment. Aggregate investment sums firm investments.
concepts.formula: Π = A₁F(K₁,N₁)−w₁N₁−[K₂−(1−d)K₁] + [A₂F(K₂,N₂)−w₂N₂+(1−d)K₂]/(1+r)
steps: Start with Π=π₁+π₂/(1+r), real output Y_t=A_tF(K_t,N_t), real wages and pₖ=1.
Substitute I₁=K₂−(1−d)K₁ into current profit.
Include future production, subtract future wages, add salvage, and discount the entire future bracket.
Differentiate K₂: −1+[MPK₂+(1−d)]/(1+r)=0. Multiply by 1+r and subtract salvage to get MPK₂=r+d.
At optimized N₂, its own FOC removes any additional first-order labor-response term in the optimized profit derivative.
concepts.increase: Higher expected future productivity raises the marginal benefit of current investment.
concepts.decrease: Lower expected future productivity lowers that benefit.
concepts.edge: Current investment cost is not discounted; future output, wages and resale all are. Omitting salvage gives MPK₂=1+r, a different terminal assumption; d=1 also removes salvage. The FOCs require an interior candidate; curvature and feasible boundaries determine whether it is a finite maximum.
concepts.example: With r=.05,d=.10, capital yielding MPK₂=.15 also leaves .90 of salvage. Total payoff 1.05 matches its opportunity cost.

check.prompt: Why is the relevant marginal product future MPK?
check.answer: Current investment becomes capital only in the next period.

concepts.title: The firm has three choice conditions
concepts.explain: The two-period firm chooses N₁, N₂ and K₂. Within each period, labor is hired until its real marginal product equals the real wage. Discounting the future condition multiplies both benefit and wage cost equally.
steps: The independent choices are N₁,N₂,K₂; K₁,d,r and real wages are given.
MPN₁=A₁F_N includes productivity A₁.
Future production and wages share the discount factor, which cancels from MPN₂=w₂.
Capital affects current cost, future output and salvage, so all three enter its derivative.
Solve jointly when inputs interact and check nonnegative feasibility and concavity; equality alone does not prove uniqueness.
concepts.increase: At a fixed capital stock and technology, a higher current wage lowers current labor demand along diminishing MPN. A higher future wage lowers future labor demand conditional on K₂; joint capital adjustment can add another response.
concepts.decrease: A lower current wage raises current labor demand at fixed capital and technology. A lower future wage raises future labor demand conditional on K₂. Discounting alone does not insert (1+r) into the within-period wage condition.
concepts.edge: A higher interest rate does not insert an extra (1+r) into MPN₂=w₂. Both future revenues and wages are discounted.
concepts.example: For Π=8√N₁−2N₁−(K₂−40)+[8√K₂+6√N₂−3N₂+.8K₂]/1.2, FOCs give 4/√N₁=2, 3/√N₂=3 and 4/√K₂=.4. Thus N₁=4,N₂=1,K₂=100; concavity and positivity validate this interior solution.

check.prompt: Must MPN₂ equal (1+r)w₂?
check.answer: No. At an interior optimum MPN₂=w₂.

concepts.title: The user cost is an opportunity cost
concepts.explain: With the same real purchase and resale price pₖ, owning a unit ties up pₖ goods and loses fraction d physically. Foregone interest rpₖ plus depreciation dpₖ give (r+d)pₖ. User cost and MPK are both output goods per capital unit per period.
concepts.formula: uc = (r+d)pₖ
steps: Use r,d as decimals and pₖ as output per capital unit.
Write pₖ=[MPK₂+(1−d)pₖ]/(1+r).
Rearrange to MPK₂=(r+d)pₖ; principal cancels against surviving resale value.
Change the horizontal cost line for r,d or common pₖ changes, not the technological MPK schedule.
concepts.increase: Higher r or d raises cost by pₖ times the change. A higher common pₖ raises cost if r+d>0. Each lowers desired K along diminishing MPK.
concepts.decrease: Lower r or d reduces cost. A lower common pₖ reduces it when r+d>0. Each raises desired K in the interior comparison.
concepts.edge: Depreciation also affects replacement, so its total effect on gross I is ambiguous. Changing only future resale price requires the next concept’s extension. With nonpositive cost and strictly positive MPK at every finite stock, a finite interior optimum need not exist.
concepts.example: r=.04,d=.08,pₖ=50 gives uc=6 goods per unit per period.

check.prompt: Is pₖ itself the entire one-period cost?
check.answer: No. The remaining capital can be sold, so the cost includes interest and depreciation rather than the full purchase price.

concepts.title: Changing future resale price: a derived extension
concepts.explain: The lecture uses a common purchase/resale price. To expose that assumption, allow purchase price q₁ now and deterministic expected resale price q₂ next period. This extension is derived from its profit function, not asserted as a separate slide formula. A higher future resale price can encourage investment without changing physical productivity.
concepts.formula: uc=(1+r)q₁−(1−d)q₂=(r+d)q₁−(1−d)(q₂−q₁); MPK₂=uc; with output-revenue tax τ, (1−τ)MPK₂=uc
steps: Pay q₁ for an extra physical unit now.
Receive marginal output plus (1−d)q₂ from resale next period.
Set −q₁+[MPK₂+(1−d)q₂]/(1+r)=0 and rearrange.
Check q₂=q₁ gives (r+d)q₁. If only output is taxed, multiply MPK by 1−τ; do not tax salvage unless specified.
concepts.increase: Increasing q₂ at fixed q₁ lowers cost by (1−d)Δq₂ and raises desired K when d<1. Increasing q₁ alone raises cost by (1+r)Δq₁ and lowers desired K.
concepts.decrease: Reducing q₂ raises cost and lowers desired K. Reducing q₁ alone lowers cost and raises desired K. An expected resale loss is distinct from physical depreciation.
concepts.edge: At d=1 no capital survives to resell, so q₂ has no effect. Nonpositive user cost with positive MPK may leave no finite unconstrained optimum. A genuinely uncertain resale payoff may need risk adjustment; this illustration is deterministic.
concepts.example: r=.10,d=.20,q₁=10. For q₂=10, cost=11−8=3. For q₂=12, cost=11−9.6=1.4; for q₂=8, cost=11−6.4=4.6. With an output-only revenue tax .30 and q₂=12, pre-tax MPK=1.4/.7=2.

check.prompt: Why do a common capital-price rise and a future-only resale-price rise have different effects?
check.answer: The common-price rise increases purchase cost as well as resale proceeds; a future-only rise increases resale proceeds without increasing today’s cost.

concepts.title: Read the MPK and user-cost intersection
concepts.explain: With diminishing future MPK and constant user cost, the interior optimal stock equates the marginal return and marginal cost. Stocks on either side leave a profitable adjustment.
concepts.formula: MPKᶠ(K*) = uc
steps: Draw a downward-sloping MPK curve.
Draw horizontal user cost.
Compare the marginal benefit and cost on each side.
concepts.increase: If MPK exceeds uc at the current stock, increasing capital raises profit until the gap closes.
concepts.decrease: If MPK is below uc, reducing capital raises profit until equality is restored.
concepts.edge: Equality is necessary for an interior optimum and sufficient with appropriate concavity; boundaries can replace it. A downward MPK schedule holds relevant other inputs or optimized conditions fixed. Three FOCs alone do not establish a unique finite joint K,N solution for every production function. No adjustment cost permits reaching K* next period, not immediate productive use today.
concepts.example: MPK=12/√K and uc=3 imply √K=4 and K*=16.

check.prompt: Why does a horizontal user-cost line not imply a horizontal investment demand curve?
check.answer: User cost is horizontal against K for a given r. Changing r moves that line and changes K*.

concepts.title: Distinguish a shift from a movement
concepts.explain: Future technology changes the MPK schedule. A real interest-rate change alters user cost and therefore moves the optimum along a given MPK schedule.
concepts.formula: For MPK=A K^(−α), K*=(A/uc)^(1/α), α>0
steps: Identify whether benefit or cost changes.
Find the new intersection.
Translate the desired stock into investment.
concepts.increase: Higher future productivity shifts MPK up and raises K* and I at a given r, inherited K and d. Higher r raises cost and reduces K*, a movement along investment demand against r.
concepts.decrease: Lower future productivity shifts MPK down and lowers K* and I. A lower effective tax shifts investment right; a higher tax shifts it left. A fall in r moves along the unchanged investment curve toward higher I.
concepts.edge: Current productivity alone need not change future MPK. Specify persistence and future wage/price responses. Higher K* implies higher I only holding inherited K,d fixed; simultaneous changes require the accumulation equation.
concepts.example: With MPK=A/√K and uc=2, raising A from 8 to 10 raises K* from 16 to 25.

check.prompt: Does higher r shift the technological MPK curve?
check.answer: No. It raises user cost.

concepts.title: Taxes alter the required pre-tax return
concepts.explain: The lecture’s τ taxes output revenue, not a lump sum and not automatically pure economic profit. With untaxed investment costs and salvage in this simplified wedge, the firm equates retained marginal output to user cost. An effective tax rate is the hypothetical revenue-tax rate producing the same K* as the actual code; it need not equal a statutory rate.
concepts.formula: −pₖ+[(1−τ)MPK₂+(1−d)pₖ]/(1+r)=0 ⇒ MPK₂=(r+d)pₖ/(1−τ); d[uc/(1−τ)]/dτ=uc/(1−τ)²
steps: Write retained output (1−τ)MPK₂.
Specify purchase, wage and salvage tax treatment separately.
Equate retained output plus salvage to gross financing cost, then divide by 1−τ.
For MPK=A K^(−α), solve K*=[(1−τ)A/uc]^(1/α).
As a derived consistency check, a revenue tax on output in each period with no wage deduction gives (1−τ)MPN_t=w_t. Other tax rules require a newly specified objective.
concepts.increase: A higher revenue or effective tax rate raises the tax-adjusted user cost and lowers K*.
concepts.decrease: A lower rate reduces the required pre-tax MPK and raises K*.
concepts.edge: Use τ<1. With positive cost, the required pre-tax return diverges as τ approaches 1; a positive interior K can disappear. A fully symmetric tax on economic profits need not create the same marginal wedge. Deductions, credits and salvage treatment matter.
concepts.example: MPK=12/√K,uc=3. At τ=.25, √K=.75×12/3=3 and K*=9. Cutting τ to 0 raises K* to 16; raising it to .50 lowers K* to 4.

check.prompt: Is a tax rate increase from 20% to 40% a 20% increase in the required return?
check.answer: No. uc/.6 divided by uc/.8 is 4/3, a 33.3% rise.

concepts.title: Allowances and credits act differently
concepts.explain: Depreciation allowances deduct part of the capital purchase price from taxable profit in the purchase year or later years. An investment credit deducts a specified share of expenditure directly from tax due. Both can lower the effective revenue-tax wedge, but identical nominal deduction/credit amounts do not imply identical tax savings.
concepts.formula: Tax saving from a deduction = tax rate × deduction; tax credit reduces tax due directly
steps: Determine whether the provision changes taxable income or tax due.
Compute the monetary tax saving.
Interpret the resulting investment incentive.
concepts.increase: A more generous allowance or credit normally increases the incentive to invest, holding other provisions fixed.
concepts.decrease: A smaller allowance or credit normally reduces that incentive.
concepts.edge: A deduction of 100 at a 25% rate saves 25; a usable credit of 100 saves 100. The same deduction later has lower PV if r>0. Limited taxable profits or unusable credits can prevent an immediate saving, so actual tax rules must be specified.
concepts.example: With a 25% tax rate, a 100 deduction saves 25 in tax. A 100 usable credit saves 100.

check.prompt: Why use an effective tax rate?
check.answer: It summarizes the combined investment incentives from the actual tax provisions as an equivalent revenue-tax wedge.

concepts.title: Gross investment is not net investment
concepts.explain: With no adjustment cost, next period’s capital reaches K*. Gross investment combines expansion and replacement. Net investment is the stock change; their gap is dK, an amount rather than the rate d. These quantities use pₖ=1 normalization.
steps: Calculate the desired net change.
Calculate replacement dK.
Add them, keeping their meanings separate.
concepts.increase: A higher desired stock raises gross investment one for one with inherited K and d fixed.
concepts.decrease: A lower desired stock reduces gross investment, which may remain positive.
concepts.edge: Higher d increases replacement but reduces K*, so total gross I can rise or fall. At d=1 inherited K does not reduce required new capital. Negative I requires sale/disinvestment; imposing irreversible I≥0 can prevent reaching the unconstrained target.
concepts.example: K=100,d=.10,K*=96 gives net investment−4 but gross investment 6.

check.prompt: Does I>0 prove the capital stock rises?
check.answer: No. I must exceed dK.

concepts.title: Desired spending versus the accounting identity
concepts.explain: Actual Y=C+I+G includes unintended inventories. Desired equilibrium additionally requires Y=Cᵈ+Iᵈ+G, equivalently Sᵈ=Iᵈ. Saving supplies loanable funds and investment demands them, through direct bond finance or banks. At fixed output the real rate adjusts. Upward aggregate saving is the lecture’s maintained substitution-dominant case, not a theorem about every saver.
concepts.formula: Y=Cᵈ+Iᵈ+G ⇔ Sᵈ=Iᵈ, where Sᵈ=Y−Cᵈ−G
steps: Calculate Sᵈ=Y−Cᵈ−G and compare with Iᵈ.
S<I means desired goods demand exceeds output: r rises, C falls, S rises along its curve and I falls.
S>I means desired demand is below output: r falls, C rises, S falls along its curve and I rises.
Current Y rising shifts S right when 0<MPC<1; falling Y shifts it left. Higher future income or wealth shifts S left through higher current C; lower future income or wealth shifts it right.
Temporary current G rising shifts S left; a cut shifts it right. A current tax rise shifts S right only if C falls; Ricardian timing leaves it fixed. A consumption-raising tax cut shifts it left.
Higher future MPK or lower effective tax shifts I right; lower future MPK or higher tax shifts it left. Changing r moves along the plotted schedules.
concepts.increase: If desired investment exceeds desired saving, r rises, raising desired saving and reducing desired investment in the maintained model.
concepts.decrease: If desired saving exceeds desired investment, r falls, reducing saving and increasing investment.
concepts.edge: Fixed-output loanable funds adjusts r. An inventory-driven output-adjustment story is another adjustment assumption, not to be silently combined with it. Actual S=I does not prove desired investment matches: unwanted inventories preserve the accounting identity.

check.prompt: Does observing actual S=I prove firms wanted their inventory accumulation?
check.answer: No. Actual investment includes unintended inventories.

concepts.title: Crowding out works through the interest rate
concepts.explain: At fixed output, higher government purchases reduce desired national saving, given the consumption response. The real interest rate rises to clear the goods market and discourages investment.
concepts.formula: G↑ → Sᵈ schedule left → r↑ → Iᵈ↓
steps: Hold the output level and other schedules fixed.
Shift desired saving for the fiscal change.
Move along the investment curve to the new equilibrium.
concepts.increase: A temporary current G rise shifts desired saving left. Equilibrium r rises and I falls; equilibrium S also falls because S=I, despite the upward movement along the new saving curve.
concepts.decrease: A temporary current G cut shifts saving right, lowering r and raising equilibrium S and I. A pure Ricardian tax cut does not shift national saving.
concepts.edge: The lecture’s crowding-out channel is G↑→r↑→I↓. Fixed-price IS–LM can also change Y, so magnitudes differ. Reagan-era higher defense spending/tax cuts need not satisfy Ricardian conditions. Decade averages fit lower S,higher r,lower I but do not uniquely identify causation. Foreign borrowing can explain S≠I in real-world data, unlike the closed-economy diagram.
concepts.example: At fixed Y, a G rise of 30 paired with C falling 10 requires I to fall 20. Equilibrium national S also falls 20. Reading only higher r and concluding S rises ignores the prior schedule shift.

check.prompt: Does a tax cut necessarily crowd out investment under Ricardian equivalence?
check.answer: No. A pure Ricardian tax-timing change leaves national saving unchanged.

lessons.title: Money, asset markets and inflation
lessons.subtitle: Keep real balances, nominal returns and expectations distinct.

concepts.title: Money solves an exchange problem
concepts.explain: Money is widely accepted as payment. Its medium-of-exchange role avoids the double coincidence of wants, its unit-of-account role denominates values, and its store-of-value role transfers purchasing power through time.
concepts.formula: Real purchasing power of nominal money = M/P
steps: Barter requires each party to want what the other offers. Widely accepted money removes this double-coincidence requirement.
Lower search/exchange costs allow specialization in productive tasks and trade for other goods.
Quoting prices/contracts uses the unit of account; making payment uses the medium of exchange.
Holding money for later purchases uses its store-of-value function. Calculate purchasing power as M/P.
concepts.increase: A higher P reduces the purchasing power of a fixed nominal balance and weakens its store-of-value performance.
concepts.decrease: A lower P raises its purchasing power.
concepts.edge: An asset can store value without being money. Money may be a poor store of value yet useful in exchange. Zero nominal yield need not imply zero real return. Severe inflation can also damage its use for quoting contracts and accepting payment.
concepts.example: A price tag of 10 dollars uses money as a unit of account. Paying those 10 dollars uses it as a medium of exchange.

check.prompt: Does money have to earn interest to store value?
check.answer: No. It can transfer purchasing power even at zero nominal interest, although inflation can erode it.

concepts.title: Liquidity differs from return and intrinsic value
concepts.explain: Liquidity describes ease and speed of converting an asset into payment. Fiat money has no intrinsic commodity value, while commodity money does. Neither definition ranks every asset by expected return.
concepts.formula: Portfolio choice compares expected return, risk and liquidity
steps: Ask how readily the asset pays for purchases.
Separately assess its expected return and uncertainty.
Avoid equating physical value with monetary usefulness.
concepts.increase: Higher liquidity makes an asset more attractive when return and risk are unchanged.
concepts.decrease: Lower liquidity makes it less attractive under the same comparison.
concepts.edge: An asset may be liquid yet risky. A stable-valued asset may still be costly to sell quickly.
concepts.example: A banknote is fiat money. A cigarette used in a camp has both monetary and consumption uses.

check.prompt: Is the highest-return asset necessarily the most liquid?
check.answer: No. These are separate portfolio characteristics.

concepts.title: Monetary definitions can change measured money
concepts.explain: Use the lecture’s December 2021 US table: M1 is currency plus liquid deposits, including checking/transaction and savings deposits. M2 is M1 plus small time deposits below $100,000 and retail, noninstitutional money-market mutual funds. These are dated course definitions, not all wealth or all mutual funds.
concepts.formula: M1=currency+liquid deposits; M2=M1+small time deposits+retail MMMFs (lecture table)
steps: Classify each component and avoid adding M1 components twice when computing M2.
Time deposits have fixed terms and usually early-withdrawal penalties; this reduces liquidity relative to checking/savings deposits.
MMMFs pool shareholders’ funds into short-term government/corporate debt, generally original maturity below a year. They pay market-based returns with limited transaction services.
The lecture describes removal of savings-account transfer limits in 2020 and revised M1 presentation in early 2021. Moving existing savings balances inside M1 did not add them a second time to M2.
concepts.increase: A new balance increases an aggregate only if it is included and not offset by a fall elsewhere within it. Reclassifying existing M2-only balances into M1 raises M1 but leaves M2 unchanged.
concepts.decrease: Moving 10 from a liquid deposit into an M2-only time deposit lowers M1 but leaves M2 unchanged. A deposit withdrawal into currency need not reduce either aggregate when both forms are included. Removing a category by definition does not destroy the underlying assets.
concepts.edge: Definitions are date-dependent. The older reading on PDF p53 explains money versus wealth but uses an older narrow-money description; use the revised table for component membership. Rounding can make displayed components differ slightly from the displayed total.
concepts.example: Currency 20,liquid deposits 180,qualifying time deposits 15 and retail MMMFs 25 imply M1=200,M2=240. Moving 10 from liquid to time deposits gives M1=190,M2=240.

check.prompt: Does a definitional jump in M1 by itself establish a monetary stimulus?
check.answer: No. First separate classification effects from changes in actual assets and policy.

concepts.title: Open-market operations change nominal money
concepts.explain: In the course model the central bank sets nominal M exogenously. Buying existing assets from the public pays out money. Selling assets withdraws money from the public.
concepts.formula: Real supply = M/P
steps: Track what the central bank gives to the public.
Determine the change in nominal money.
Divide by P to obtain real balances.
concepts.increase: An open-market purchase increases M and, at fixed P, increases real money supply.
concepts.decrease: An open-market sale reduces M and real balances at fixed P.
concepts.edge: Directly purchasing new government debt is fiscal financing, distinct from an open-market purchase of existing securities.
concepts.example: M rises from 200 to 220 at P=2, so real supply rises from 100 to 110.

check.prompt: If M and P both rise 10%, do real balances rise?
check.answer: No. Their ratio is unchanged.

concepts.title: Money demand is a desired stock
concepts.explain: Money demand is a desired stock at a date, not income earned per period. Wealth is assets minus liabilities; rich or high-income people need not hold much money. In the two-asset abstraction, money plus net nonmonetary holdings exhausts wealth. Allocation compares expected total return, risk and liquidity. Payouts such as dividends, interest or rent and price changes both contribute to total returns.
concepts.formula: W=assets−liabilities; money+net nonmonetary assets=W; holding-period return=(payout+sale price−purchase price)/purchase price
steps: Measure money and wealth as stocks and income/saving as flows over a specified period.
Subtract liabilities when calculating net wealth; do not confuse gross asset values with net positions.
Compare expected returns before choosing. Realized returns can differ because of prices, payouts, inflation or default.

At fixed risk/liquidity, higher expected return makes an asset more attractive. At fixed return/liquidity, greater risk makes it less attractive to a risk-averse holder. At fixed return/risk, more liquidity is desirable.
When one attribute improves and another worsens, preferences and magnitudes determine the result. At a fixed portfolio share, more wealth increases desired money.
concepts.increase: Greater wealth increases money holdings at an unchanged share. At fixed wealth, a higher bond return relative to money encourages bonds; greater bond risk or a greater need for liquidity can instead increase money’s share.
concepts.decrease: Lower wealth reduces money holdings at an unchanged share. A lower relative bond return can raise money’s share, while lower bond risk or greater bond liquidity can reduce it. Simultaneous changes need not have a determinate net effect.
concepts.edge: Cash has inflation risk even if its nominal amount is safe. Expected return is not guaranteed realized return. Buying bonds transfers money to sellers; trades alone do not eliminate aggregate M. The portfolio constraint must include liabilities or assume them absent.
concepts.example: Money 25 plus other assets 150 less debt 30 gives net wealth 145. Annual income 40 is a different flow. An asset bought for 100,paying 3 and sold for 102 earns a 5% holding-period return, not merely its 3% payout rate.

check.prompt: Can high income and high wealth coexist with little money?
check.answer: Yes. Income is a flow and wealth includes nonmonetary assets net of liabilities. Only monetary asset holdings are money.

concepts.title: The nominal return is money’s opportunity cost
concepts.explain: In the baseline model money pays zero nominal interest and bonds pay i. Higher output raises transactions demand, while higher i makes holding money more costly.
concepts.formula: Mᵈ=P L(Y,i−iₘ); baseline iₘ=0 and i≈r+πᵉ; L_Y>0,L_i<0; ∂Mᵈ/∂Y=P L_Y and ∂Mᵈ/∂i=P L_i at fixed P
steps: More Y means more transactions and a larger desired real liquidity stock.
Identify nominal return forgone relative to money. With iₘ=0 it is i, not r alone.
A graph against r holds πᵉ fixed. Higher πᵉ shifts demand left/down because i rises at every r; lower πᵉ shifts it right/up.
Multiply L by P for nominal demand. A price-level rise alone increases nominal demand proportionately without changing L.
The lecture summary additionally assumes a less-than-proportional income response. This is stronger than the sign L_Y>0 and cannot be deduced from that sign alone.
concepts.increase: Higher Y raises L. Higher r or πᵉ at a fixed value of the other raises i and lowers L. Greater wealth can raise L at unchanged Y,i. Equal increases in i and iₘ leave the return-gap channel unchanged.
concepts.decrease: Lower Y reduces L. Lower r or πᵉ at a fixed value of the other lowers i and raises L. Lower wealth can reduce monetary holdings. A lower P alone reduces nominal demand PL, not L.
concepts.edge: If monetary assets earn interest, i alone is insufficient without iₘ. Do not extrapolate linear demand into negative balances or presume its ordinary slope describes unlimited substitution at the nominal lower bound. Money also supplies transaction services.
concepts.example: L=20+0.5Y−100i gives L=65 at Y=100 and i=.05.

check.prompt: At fixed r, why can higher expected inflation reduce money demand?
check.answer: It raises i≈r+πᵉ and the opportunity cost of holding zero-interest money.

concepts.title: Exact Fisher arithmetic
concepts.explain: Nominal returns measure money growth, while real returns measure purchasing-power growth. Divide the gross nominal payoff by gross inflation to find the real payoff.
steps: A dollar invested now forgoes 1/P_t goods; its future payoff buys (1+i)/P_(t+1) goods.
Divide future goods by goods forgone: 1+r=(1+i)/(1+π).
Expand to i=r+π+rπ, or r=(i−π)/(1+π).
Drop rπ only as a small-rate approximation. Actual π determines the realized return; stated forecasts determine conditional forecast benchmarks.
concepts.increase: At fixed i, higher realized inflation lowers the lender’s real payoff and the fixed-nominal borrower’s real repayment burden. At fixed π, higher i raises the real return.
concepts.decrease: At fixed i, lower inflation raises the lender’s real payoff and borrower’s real burden. Deflation can give zero-interest money a positive real return. At fixed π, lower i reduces the real return.
concepts.edge: Require positive price levels, hence π>−1. Large rates make subtraction materially inaccurate. Fixed nominal contracts do not automatically adjust to inflation surprises; indexed or renegotiated contracts need different assumptions.

check.prompt: If nominal interest is zero and prices fall 2%, is the real return zero?

concepts.title: Expected inflation: state what stays fixed
concepts.explain: The Fisher effect holds the expected real rate fixed: i≈r+πᵉ then rises approximately one for one with expected inflation. A different comparison holds M,P,Y and a stable downward money-demand function fixed. M/P=L(Y,i) then pins down i; an expected-inflation increase reduces r instead. The results are consistent because the fixed variables differ.
concepts.formula: Fixed r: Δi≈Δπᵉ. Fixed M,P,Y with invertible L: Δi=0, Δr≈−Δπᵉ. Deterministic forecast: i=(1+r)(1+πᵉ)−1.
steps: Separate expected inflation used in decisions from realized inflation measuring the eventual payoff.
For the Fisher comparison, hold r fixed. The approximate nominal-rate response equals the expected-inflation change.
For fixed real balances and Y, solve money demand for i before recovering r≈i−πᵉ.
On the graph against r, higher πᵉ shifts demand down/left and lowers the clearing r; lower πᵉ shifts demand up/right and raises it.
Under the exact deterministic gross relation at fixed r, di/dπᵉ=1+r rather than exactly 1. Historical π need not equal πᵉ and r can also move.
concepts.increase: A 2-point increase in πᵉ raises i approximately 2 points if r is fixed. With M,P,Y fixed, it instead leaves i fixed and lowers r approximately 2 points.
concepts.decrease: A 2-point fall in πᵉ lowers i approximately 2 points at fixed r. With M,P,Y fixed, i remains fixed and r rises approximately 2 points.
concepts.edge: The exact gross formula with a single forecast is deterministic or conditional. Under genuine uncertainty E[(1+i)/(1+π)] need not equal (1+i)/(1+Eπ); do not call a ratio of means an unrestricted exact expected return. In full IS–LM Y may change, so the fixed-Y result cannot be imposed mechanically.
concepts.example: L=200+Y−1000i,Y=100,M/P=250 imply i=.05. When πᵉ rises from .02 to .04, approximate r falls from .03 to .01. If r had instead been fixed at .03, i would rise from .05 to .07 and another variable would have to adjust.

check.prompt: Does higher expected inflation always raise equilibrium nominal interest one for one?
check.answer: No. That Fisher comparison fixes r. Fixed M,P,Y with stable demand pins down i, so approximate r falls instead.

concepts.title: One asset-market condition can be enough
concepts.explain: With wealth held in only money and nonmonetary assets, consistent portfolio budgets link excess demands. If money demand equals supply, nonmonetary asset demand must also equal its supply.
concepts.formula: E_money+E_nonmoney=0 in consistent value units; general Walras law: Σp_j z_j=0
steps: Value desired and supplied assets at the same prices.
Subtract total supplied values from desired portfolio values, both constrained by the same wealth.
An excess money demand equals an excess nonmoney supply; clearing one asset group clears the residual group.
More generally, if N−1 markets clear, a positive price in the remaining market and the value identity imply that final market clears.
concepts.increase: Excess money demand implies an offsetting excess supply of nonmonetary assets in this setup.
concepts.decrease: Excess money supply implies an offsetting excess demand for nonmonetary assets.
concepts.edge: Consistent budgets and valuations are essential. Walras law does not make arbitrary prices clear all markets. Clearing money in a two-asset abstraction alone does not prove goods equilibrium or full employment in the larger model. Revaluing assets can also change valued wealth.
concepts.example: If total wealth is 100, supplied money 40 and bonds 60, desired money 50 implies desired bonds 50.

check.prompt: If the money market clears, can the bond market have independent excess demand in this two-asset system?
check.answer: No, not when the portfolio budget identity holds.

concepts.title: Bond trades transmit money-market pressure
concepts.explain: At fixed Y,P and expected inflation, exogenous M gives a vertical real-supply curve. Demand slopes down against r because i≈r+πᵉ. Excess supplied money induces bond purchases, higher bond prices and lower yields until desired money absorbs supply. Excess money demand induces bond sales, lower prices and higher yields.
concepts.formula: For one-period fixed total payoff F, i=F/p_B−1; di/dp_B=−F/p_B²<0
steps: Compare M/P with desired L.
Identify which asset people try to buy.
Follow bond prices and yields to the new equilibrium.
concepts.increase: More M at fixed P creates excess real balances, raising bond demand and lowering r in the baseline short-run comparison.
concepts.decrease: Less M creates excess money demand, causing bond sales and higher r.
concepts.edge: The yield formula assumes holding the fixed payoff to its stated maturity. With coupons or earlier resale, include all relevant payouts in total holding-period return; coupon rate alone is not total return. Trades redistribute money without destroying M. In general equilibrium the same real r clears goods and assets; actual financial rates vary by maturity,risk and liquidity though often comove.
concepts.example: A one-period bond paying 110 yields 10% at price 100, but only 4.7619% at price 105.

check.prompt: Why do bond prices and yields move in opposite directions?
check.answer: The fixed future payoff is divided by a changing purchase price.

concepts.title: Long-run money equilibrium determines P
concepts.explain: In the classical long run, the labor market determines Y*, the goods market determines r, and the asset market determines P. Holding Y, r and expected inflation fixed makes P proportional to M.
concepts.formula: P=M/L(Y,r+πᵉ)
steps: Solve the real side first.
Evaluate the real money demand.
Choose the price level that makes real supply equal demand.
concepts.increase: With L fixed, a larger M raises P proportionately. At fixed M, greater demand from higher Y or wealth lowers P. At fixed r,Y, higher πᵉ lowers L and raises P.
concepts.decrease: With L fixed, lower M lowers P proportionately. At fixed M, lower L raises P. Lower πᵉ at fixed r,Y raises L and lowers P.
concepts.edge: The classical sequence solves labor for Y*,goods for r,then assets for P. A permanent higher M level can produce a one-time price jump; persistent money growth is a different experiment. Expected-inflation/demand changes require rechecking proportionality. Historical comovement does not mean money growth equals inflation in every episode.
concepts.example: M=300 and L=150 imply P=2. M=450 with the same L implies P=3.

check.prompt: Does doubling M necessarily double real balances in this long-run case?
check.answer: No. P doubles, so M/P remains equal to unchanged L.

concepts.title: Exact growth and small-change approximations
concepts.explain: For positive quantities, log differentiation gives exact proportional relationships among infinitesimal changes. Replacing differentials by finite simple growth rates generally produces a first-order approximation. General elasticities are signed weights, which need not sum to one: the result is a weighted sum, not necessarily an average.
concepts.formula: z=xy: dz/z=dx/x+dy/y; g_z=g_x+g_y+g_xg_y. z=x/y: dz/z=dx/x−dy/y; g_z=(1+g_x)/(1+g_y)−1. z=f(x,y): dz/z=(f_x x/z)dx/x+(f_y y/z)dy/y.
steps: For a product take ln z=ln x+ln y, then differentiate.
For finite growth expand (x+Δx)(y+Δy); the cross term g_xg_y explains the error in simply adding rates.
For a ratio take ln z=ln x−ln y. Alternatively write x=zy and rearrange the product rule. Exact finite growth divides gross factors.
For a general f, first write dz=f_x dx+f_y dy and divide by z, then multiply terms by x/x or y/y to expose point elasticities.
Use the actual function or gross-growth identity for larger changes.
concepts.increase: When both factors grow, product growth exceeds the sum by their positive cross term. Equal proportional increases in a ratio’s numerator and denominator cancel; faster numerator growth raises the ratio.
concepts.decrease: When both factors fall while remaining positive, the product decline is smaller in magnitude than the sum of their declines. Equal proportional declines in a ratio cancel; a larger denominator decline raises the ratio.
concepts.edge: Log differentiation requires positive quantities; growth from a zero baseline is undefined. A rate going from 4% to 5% changes by 1 percentage point and 25%. Opposite-sign product changes have a negative cross term. Exact log changes add, but are not identical to finite simple growth rates.
concepts.example: Growth of 10% and 20% produces 32%, not exactly 30%. Declines of 10% and 20% produce .9×.8=.72, a 28% decline. A ratio with numerator growth 10% and denominator growth 5% grows 1.10/1.05−1=4.7619%, approximately 5%.

check.prompt: Can a 10% rise followed by a 10% fall restore the starting level?
check.answer: No. 1.10×0.90=0.99, so the final level is 1% lower.

concepts.title: Elasticities convert causes into demand growth
concepts.explain: An elasticity is a proportional response, not the coefficient of a linear demand function. The growth approximation weights each argument’s growth by its elasticity.
concepts.formula: dL/L=(L_Y/L)dY+(L_i/L)di=ηLY dY/Y+ηLi di/i; ηLY=L_Y Y/L,ηLi=L_i i/L; dP/P=dM/M−dL/L; π≈gM−ηLYgY−ηLi g_i
steps: Differentiate stable positive L: dL=L_YdY+L_idi. In L=a+bY+ci, level derivatives are b,c.
Normalize to point elasticities bY/L and ci/L; these vary across points in a linear function.
Rewrite equilibrium P=M/L and combine the quotient rule with demand growth. Apply the minus sign to BOTH demand terms.
For i>0, ηLi<0 makes a rate rise lower L and add to implied inflation at given money growth. This accounting comparison is not alone a causal policy rule.
At i=0 use (L_i/L)Δi directly because Δi/i is undefined.
For a finite change recalculate L and set M_new=P_target L_new. To keep P,i fixed as Y changes, accommodate the resulting L.
concepts.increase: Higher Y raises L and offsets inflation at fixed money growth. Higher i lowers L and increases implied inflation. To hold P,i fixed while Y rises, M must rise with real demand.
concepts.decrease: Lower Y reduces L and raises implied inflation at fixed money growth. Lower i raises L and reduces implied inflation. To hold P,i fixed as Y falls, M must fall with demand.
concepts.edge: The finite formula is approximate unless the particular functional form makes a step exact. At i=0 the point elasticity is zero but a level change in i can still affect L; zero times undefined growth is invalid. A shifting demand function adds another term. Keep L positive and distinguish percent change from percentage points.
concepts.example: L=300+.8Y−1000i at Y=1000,i=.10 gives L=1000,ηLY=.8,ηLi=−.1. A 5% Y rise at unchanged i gives L=1040 exactly; at P=2,M must rise from 2000 to 2080. At i=0,Y=1000,L=1100; i rising to .01 lowers L by 10 despite the initial zero interest elasticity.

check.prompt: Why is −1000 not an interest elasticity, and what replaces percentage rate growth at zero i?
check.answer: −1000 is a level derivative; elasticity is −1000i/L. At i=0 percentage growth of i is undefined, so use (L_i/L)Δi or direct evaluation.

concepts.title: Monetary financing and the fiscal constraint
concepts.explain: Hyperinflation in the lecture means at least 50% per month. Rapid erosion harms store of value and can also make money unreliable for price/contract quotation and exchange. People may substitute stable foreign currency or costly barter. Monetary financing often reflects inability to tax or borrow enough; sustained stabilization must close that fiscal gap.
concepts.formula: π≈gM−gL; fiscal financing pressure can drive gM
steps: Trace the government financing need.
Connect money creation to nominal demand and prices.
Check whether the fiscal gap remains after monetary restraint.
concepts.increase: Faster money growth tends to raise inflation when real money-demand growth does not offset it.
concepts.decrease: Slower money growth reduces inflation pressure, but sustainable stabilization may require replacing the lost financing.
concepts.edge: Disinflation is a lower positive inflation rate: P still rises. Deflation means P falls. Falling real money demand can amplify monetary inflation. Historical annual figures are not the monthly definition, and a large annual rate alone does not establish that every month crossed the threshold.
concepts.example: At 50% monthly inflation, the annual price factor is 1.5¹²≈129.75, or about 12,874.6% annual inflation. A fixed nominal balance retains about .771% of its initial purchasing power. Removing money creation without replacing its financing leaves a fiscal gap.

check.prompt: Is stopping money printing costless if the government still has an unfunded deficit?
check.answer: No. Another financing source or a fiscal adjustment is needed.

concepts.title: Match the policy instrument to the institution
concepts.explain: These are descriptions in the supplied lecture, not a current policy update. The Fed is the US central bank and the Treasury handles fiscal policy. The Fed’s dual objectives are price stability and full employment; the federal funds target concerns overnight interbank reserve lending. The lecture describes eight FOMC meetings annually,twelve regional districts and a central Board in Washington. MAS is Singapore’s central bank and manages the Singapore dollar against a trade-weighted currency basket.
concepts.formula: A model’s policy variable is an assumption, not a complete institutional description
steps: Distinguish monetary and fiscal authorities before attributing an operation.
The federal funds rate is a nominal overnight interbank rate, not automatically real r.
Connect the Fed comparison to price stability and full employment.
Connect Singapore’s high import exposure to exchange-rate effects on domestic-currency import costs; larger trading partners receive greater basket weights.
Use an assigned exogenous-M model when specified. Detailed modern operating tools,independence and the open-economy trilemma are not formal models supplied by these official slides.
concepts.increase: In the model, increasing M raises real balances at fixed P. In the Singapore intuition, a stronger domestic currency can reduce import costs when foreign-currency prices stay fixed.
concepts.decrease: Reducing M lowers real balances at fixed P. A weaker domestic currency can raise import costs at fixed foreign prices; actual pass-through and policy require more information.
concepts.edge: Meeting counts and the above-300% gross-trade/GDP figure are lecture context, not universal model parameters. Gross trade can exceed GDP because gross flows differ from domestic value added. Do not infer a current rate,officeholder,exact pass-through or complete open-economy causal model from this overview.
concepts.example: A textbook problem specifying M exogenously should be solved with that assumption even if the institution uses an interest-rate target in practice.

check.prompt: Why might the exchange rate matter strongly for Singapore inflation?
check.answer: Imports have a large role in expenditure, so exchange rates affect domestic-currency import prices.

concepts.title: Expected future money can affect today
concepts.explain: Anticipating a future cigarette shipment can raise expected inflation before the shipment arrives. At a given real rate, the higher nominal opportunity cost reduces demand for cigarette balances, raising today’s price level if M is unchanged.
concepts.formula: πᵉ↑ → i↑ → L↓ → P=M/L↑, holding r,Y,M fixed
steps: An unanticipated current shipment increases cigarette M. With Y,r,πᵉ and L unchanged, flexible P rises proportionately.
An announcement of a future shipment does not itself add current cigarettes, but can change expected inflation.
At fixed r,Y, higher πᵉ raises i approximately, lowers L and raises current P=M/L before arrival.
Cancellation can work through lower expected inflation and higher L without mechanically changing current M.
concepts.increase: A more credible larger future shipment can increase expected depreciation of cigarette money and raise current prices through lower L.
concepts.decrease: Cancellation of an expected shipment can reduce expected inflation, increase L and lower current prices under the same assumptions.
concepts.edge: This is a conditional flexible-price comparison, not a full dynamic solution for all future prices. Specify the expectations response rather than infer it mechanically from any news. With current P,M,Y fixed, asset clearing would instead adjust r. Unanticipated events cannot change behavior before the information arrives.
concepts.example: With current M=200, a fall in desired real balances from 100 to 80 raises P from 2 to 2.5 before M changes.

check.prompt: Must the current nominal money stock rise for current prices to rise?
check.answer: No. A fall in real money demand can raise P at unchanged M.

lessons.title: Reading business cycles
lessons.subtitle: Classify direction and timing without confusing either with causation.

concepts.title: Peaks, troughs and phases
concepts.explain: In the lecture’s activity-direction convention, expansion/boom means rising aggregate activity and contraction/recession means falling activity. A particularly severe recession is a depression. A peak or trough is a turning point, not an entire phase. A complete peak-to-peak or trough-to-trough cycle contains an expansion and a contraction.
concepts.formula: Expansion = rising activity; contraction = declining activity
steps: Observe the direction of activity over time.
Locate reversals.
Label the intervals between turning points.
concepts.increase: Rising activity after a trough is expansion even if the level remains low.
concepts.decrease: Falling activity after a peak is contraction even if the level remains high.
concepts.edge: These are local cyclical extrema, not necessarily all-time maximum/minimum output in a growing economy. One noisy point need not establish a reversal; revisions,persistence and wider evidence matter. Other textbook uses of boom/recession are discussed separately.
concepts.example: Output 100,104,108,105,101,103 has a local peak at 108 and trough at 101.

check.prompt: Is the trough itself the entire recession?
check.answer: No. It is a turning point at the end of the contraction.

concepts.title: Growth and position relative to trend are different
concepts.explain: Growth and position relative to trend differ. Abel–Bernanke–Croushore’s activity-direction convention used here treats rising/falling activity as expansion/boom and contraction/recession. Williamson’s quoted boom/recession concern sequences of positive/negative trend deviations leading toward peaks/troughs. The quoted Blanchard convention uses negative GDP growth, usually two consecutive quarters. State the convention rather than treat these terms as universally identical.
concepts.formula: Gap=(Y−Ytrend)/Ytrend; growth=(Y_t−Y_(t−1))/Y_(t−1); log gap=ln Y−ln Ytrend≈proportional gap for small deviations
steps: Read whether the vertical axis is a level,log level,growth rate or percentage deviation.
Compute actual growth from consecutive observations.
Compute the gap from the stated trend; another trend estimate can change it.
Apply the specified textbook convention consistently.
concepts.increase: Output can increase from 90 to 94 while trend rises from 100 to 102, giving expansion but still a negative gap.
concepts.decrease: Output can decrease from 110 to 108 while trend is 100, giving contraction with a positive gap.
concepts.edge: Two negative quarters is the lecture’s quoted Blanchard convention, not a universal mechanical institutional rule. A price-level fall is deflation, not by itself recession. Y can grow while Y/trend falls if trend grows faster; Y can fall while Y/trend rises if trend falls faster.
concepts.example: Y=102 with trend 100 gives a 2% positive gap regardless of whether Y was rising or falling.

check.prompt: Does a negative output gap necessarily imply negative current growth?
check.answer: No. Level relative to trend and change over time are different measurements.

concepts.title: Recurrent does not mean clockwork
concepts.explain: Expansions and contractions recur, but their durations and sizes are irregular. Persistence means recent increases or decreases tend to be followed by further movement in the same direction.
concepts.formula: Recurrent ≠ periodic; persistent ≠ permanent
steps: Distinguish repeating patterns from fixed intervals.
Inspect how changes continue across periods.
Recognize that persistence does not identify the next turning point exactly.
concepts.increase: Several consecutive increases can indicate persistence without establishing a fixed expansion duration.
concepts.decrease: Several decreases can indicate persistence without implying activity falls forever.
concepts.edge: Historical phase lengths vary, so recurrence does not establish a fixed calendar cycle. Persistence is a tendency, not a guaranteed remaining duration. Official dating can come after the turning point while revisions and sustained evidence are assessed.
concepts.example: Cycles lasting 4,7 and 3 years recur but are not periodic.

check.prompt: Can a persistent series still turn at a trough?
check.answer: Yes. Persistence is a tendency, not a prohibition on reversals.

concepts.title: Direction compares comovement
concepts.explain: Procyclical variables move with aggregate activity, countercyclical variables move against it, and acyclical variables show no clear systematic pattern. Classification concerns a pattern across observations.
concepts.formula: Procyclical positive comovement; countercyclical negative comovement
steps: Compare the variable with aggregate activity.
Use both expansion and contraction observations.
Avoid inferring a stable pattern from one episode.
concepts.increase: A procyclical variable tends to rise in expansion. A countercyclical variable tends to fall.
concepts.decrease: A procyclical variable tends to fall in contraction. A countercyclical variable tends to rise.
concepts.edge: Acyclical does not mean constant. It can fluctuate strongly without systematic cycle-related comovement.
concepts.example: If output rises while a variable regularly falls, and output falls while it rises, the variable is countercyclical.

check.prompt: Does a strongly varying series have to be procyclical?
check.answer: No. Volatility and cyclicality are separate properties.

concepts.title: Timing compares turning points
concepts.explain: Leading variables turn before aggregate activity, lagging variables after it, and coincident variables at approximately the same time. Timing and direction are independent classifications.
concepts.formula: A variable can be countercyclical and leading at the same time
steps: Align dates for the variable and output.
Locate corresponding turning points.
Report timing separately from direction.
concepts.increase: A variable beginning to rise before output rises may lead, but whether it is procyclical depends on the direction pattern.
concepts.decrease: A countercyclical leading variable may begin to rise before output begins to fall.
concepts.edge: Leading association does not prove causation or ensure perfect forecasting. False signals can occur.
concepts.example: A countercyclical indicator peaks in March before output reaches a trough in May. It leads by two months.

check.prompt: Can a lagging variable move in the same direction as output?
check.answer: Yes. It is then procyclical and lagging.

concepts.title: Facts constrain theories without proving them
concepts.explain: The lecture explicitly requires knowing the definitions rather than memorizing each variable’s classification. Its emphasized examples are procyclical average labor productivity,slightly procyclical real wages,and procyclical leading nominal money growth. The displayed productivity and money series are less variable than output in those figures. These are patterns theories should explain,not identities or unique causal evidence.
concepts.formula: Shared movement can arise from causation, reverse causation or common shocks
steps: Identify direction,timing and relative variability separately.
Interpret the stated examples: productivity moves with activity,the real-wage relation is weak,and money growth can turn first.
Compare theories against several facts rather than one successful chart.
Read historical output,unemployment and price plots with their different units and episode context.
Distinguish the activity turning date from the later official announcement: revisions and persistence explain delays.
concepts.increase: Stronger comovement may make a pattern more informative but does not by itself identify a causal channel.
concepts.decrease: Weaker or unstable comovement can challenge a theory that predicts a tight relation.
concepts.edge: Leading money may reflect policy responding to expected activity or common shocks. A weakly procyclical real wage can fall in some expansions. Historical examples are not guarantees of identical correlations across dates or countries.
concepts.example: Money growth can lead output because policy causes output changes or because policy responds to an anticipated downturn.

check.prompt: Why are revised data relevant to cycle dating?
check.answer: Initial releases can misidentify a temporary fluctuation as a lasting turning point.

concepts.title: Cycles can be shared across economies
concepts.explain: The country industrial-production panels and Euro-area/Germany illustration show related cycles. Common shocks and cross-border transmission can both explain synchronization; the pattern alone identifies neither causal direction nor a required common currency.
concepts.formula: Comovement across countries is an empirical pattern, not a unique structural equation
steps: Compare direction and turning dates across countries.
Identify potential shared or transmitted shocks.
Distinguish correlation from a causal claim.
concepts.increase: An expansion in several countries at once is international comovement.
concepts.decrease: A contraction in several countries at once is also international comovement.
concepts.edge: Related cycles can have different levels,turning dates and amplitudes. Selected historical figures do not establish perfect worldwide synchronization. The closed-economy course model does not itself supply a complete cross-border mechanism.
concepts.example: If countries A and B both contract after a global oil disruption, a common shock is plausible but must be tested against alternatives.

check.prompt: Does synchronized recession prove one country caused the other’s recession?
check.answer: No. Both may be responding to a common disturbance.

lessons.title: IS, LM, FE and aggregate demand
lessons.subtitle: Trace every curve back to the market it clears.

concepts.title: Three markets, three conditions
concepts.explain: A competitive equilibrium combines optimization with mutual consistency. A representative household takes real wages, interest and prices as given when choosing labor, consumption, saving and a portfolio to maximize lifetime utility subject to its intertemporal budget. Firms maximize the present value of profits when choosing labor and investment. Government satisfies its budget constraint. Desired labor supply equals demand, desired saving equals investment, and desired real money equals supplied real balances. In the two-asset setup, clearing money also clears the other asset market by the aggregate budget constraint. An IS–LM intersection alone clears goods and assets; it is full equilibrium only on FE.
concepts.formula: Nˢ = Nᵈ; Sᵈ = Iᵈ; M/P = L(Y,r+πᵉ)
steps: Solve labor for N* and Y*.
Use goods equilibrium to determine r at Y*.
Use money equilibrium to determine P.
concepts.increase: If demand pushes the IS–LM intersection above FE, goods and assets clear at excessive demand for full-employment output. Prices subsequently rise in the adjustment model.
concepts.decrease: If the intersection is below FE, deficient demand depresses output in the sticky-price short run. Falling prices raise real balances and help restore output.
concepts.edge: This is a closed-economy, price-taking benchmark with a consistent aggregate budget. Actual saving equals actual investment by accounting even away from desired goods-market equilibrium; desired equality is the extra equilibrium condition. Full employment can include frictional and structural unemployment.
concepts.example: Given FE at Y = 100, IS at r = 10 − 0.05Y implies r = 5. If L = 2Y − 10r = 150 and M = 300, equilibrium P = 2.

check.prompt: Does an IS–LM intersection always clear the labor market?
check.answer: No. It must also be on the FE line for all three markets to clear.

concepts.title: The FE line
concepts.explain: FE records combinations of output and real interest consistent with labor-market equilibrium. In the course model, r does not enter that labor equilibrium, so FE is vertical.
concepts.formula: Y = Y* = AF(K,N*)
steps: Find the labor-market equilibrium.
Insert N* into production.
Draw a vertical line at the resulting Y*.
concepts.increase: With fixed capital and a standard upward-sloping labor supply, higher productivity raises output directly and, when it raises MPN, shifts labor demand right, raising N* and the real wage. More capital raises output directly and, with labor–capital complementarity, raises MPN and employment. More labor supply instead lowers the clearing real wage while raising N* and output. Each can shift FE and LRAS right through a different mechanism.
concepts.decrease: Lower productivity reduces direct output and, if MPN falls, labor demand, employment and the real wage. Capital destruction lowers direct output and, with complementarity, MPN and employment. A smaller labor supply raises the clearing real wage but lowers N* and output. These mechanisms shift FE and LRAS left.
concepts.edge: The wage directions differ across shocks: a labor-supply increase lowers w, whereas a favorable MPN shock raises w. Capital or productivity only has the stated employment channel when its effect on MPN has the assumed sign. A pure change in r or P leaves FE unchanged in this closure. In the efficiency-wage model, labor-supply changes leave FE fixed while supply remains above hiring demand.
concepts.example: If Y* changes from 100 to 110, FE moves right by 10 at every r. The line does not rotate.

check.prompt: Why is FE vertical rather than upward sloping?
check.answer: The model pins down potential output in the labor market independently of the real interest rate.

concepts.title: Deriving IS from saving and investment
concepts.explain: IS is the set of output–real-interest pairs where desired saving equals desired investment, equivalently desired expenditure equals output. The lecture fixes Y and finds the clearing r in the loanable-funds market. The alternative Keynesian-cross construction fixes r and finds the clearing Y. They describe the same locus. With 0<MPC<1 and no direct current-Y effect on investment, higher Y raises saving; lower r then reduces saving and raises investment until equality returns.
concepts.formula: Sᵈ = Y − Cᵈ − G = Iᵈ
steps: Raise Y in the loanable-funds diagram.
Saving shifts right because consumption rises less than income.
The clearing r falls, giving another point on IS.
concepts.increase: Higher Y moves down along an unchanged IS curve, provided other determinants stay fixed.
concepts.decrease: Lower Y shifts saving left in the underlying loanable-funds diagram, raises the clearing r and moves up along IS.
concepts.edge: A change in current Y shifts saving in the underlying loanable-funds graph but traces an unchanged IS curve. A single saving–investment intersection is only one point on IS. The standard downward slope requires positive interest sensitivity and positive spending leakage; it is not implied by the letters IS alone.

check.prompt: Why does saving shift while IS itself does not when deriving IS?
check.answer: Y varies to trace the locus. Exogenous spending determinants remain fixed.

concepts.title: IS algebra and tax rules
concepts.explain: Substitute consumption, investment and the stated tax rule into goods equilibrium. Keep income-induced taxes separate from lump-sum taxes. The slope reflects spending leakage and interest sensitivity.
concepts.formula: Let D=1−c(1−t), H=a+b and A₀=c₀−cT₀+i₀+G. Goods equilibrium is DY=A₀−Hr. For H>0, r=A₀/H−(D/H)Y.
steps: Substitute T=T₀+tY into C=c₀+c(Y−T)−ar and I=i₀−br.
Collect terms: [1−c(1−t)]Y=c₀−cT₀+i₀+G−(a+b)r.
With H>0 and D>0, IS has intercept A₀/H and negative slope −D/H in an r-versus-Y graph. Tutorial 7 uses t=0 and a fixed lump-sum T.
concepts.increase: A higher marginal tax rate t increases spending leakage and makes IS steeper in an r-versus-Y graph, holding a+b fixed.
concepts.decrease: A lower t reduces leakage and flattens IS when 0<c<1.
concepts.edge: The usual case assumes 0<c<1, 0≤t<1 and H>0. If H=0 and D>0, IS is vertical at Y=A₀/D, so changing autonomous spending still changes output. If D=0 and H>0, IS is horizontal at r=A₀/H; dividing by D to write Y(r) is invalid. If both are zero, either every pair meets goods equilibrium when A₀=0 or none does when A₀≠0. These limiting results are algebraic extensions of the lecture equation, not additional empirical claims.
concepts.example: For c = 0.8 and t = 0.25, the output coefficient is 1−0.8×0.75 = 0.4, not 0.2.

check.prompt: With c = 0.75 and t = 0.2, what is 1−c(1−t)?

concepts.title: What shifts IS
concepts.explain: An exogenous rise in desired spending at a given Y and r creates excess goods demand. A higher r is required to reduce spending and restore equilibrium at that Y. IS shifts up and right.
concepts.formula: At fixed Y, ΔIᵈ > ΔSᵈ implies a higher clearing r
steps: Identify the direct change at fixed Y and r.
Translate it into saving or investment.
Determine the interest change that restores equality.
concepts.increase: Higher autonomous consumption, household wealth or expected future output/income raises C at a given Y and r, lowering national saving and shifting IS up/right. Higher G directly lowers national saving. Higher expected future MPK raises desired investment. A lower effective tax rate on capital raises the after-tax investment return and desired investment. A current tax cut shifts IS right only to the extent that it raises desired C.
concepts.decrease: Lower autonomous consumption, household wealth or expected future income reduces current C and raises national saving, shifting IS down/left. Lower G releases saving. Lower expected future MPK reduces investment demand. A higher effective capital tax lowers the after-tax investment return and investment. A current tax increase shifts IS left if households reduce desired C.
concepts.edge: A tax-timing change with the same government-spending path leaves IS unchanged under Ricardian equivalence. Effective capital taxation concerns investment incentives; lump-sum household tax timing is a separate experiment. Changing current Y or r moves along IS. A permanent productivity shock may affect both current FE and future-income/MPK determinants of IS; a deliberately temporary current shock need not.
concepts.example: With r = 12 − 0.1Y, a rise of 2 in the intercept gives r = 14 − 0.1Y. At r = 4, desired equilibrium Y rises from 80 to 100.

check.prompt: Does a lower r shift IS right?
check.answer: No. It causes movement along IS unless an exogenous determinant also changes.

concepts.title: Bonds transmit money-market adjustment
concepts.explain: When people collectively want less money than supplied, they try to buy nonmonetary assets. Bond prices rise and yields fall, making money relatively more attractive until people willingly hold the existing supply.
concepts.formula: For a one-period bond with fixed total payoff F: i=(F−P_b)/P_b and P_b=F/(1+i). At fixed expected inflation, i≈r+πᵉ links the yield change to r.
steps: Compare money supplied with money demanded.
Infer whether people buy or sell bonds.
Use the inverse relation between bond price and yield.
concepts.increase: Excess money supply induces bond purchases, higher bond prices and lower nominal yields. With expected inflation fixed, r falls too.
concepts.decrease: Excess money demand induces bond sales, lower bond prices and higher yields. With expected inflation fixed, r rises too.
concepts.edge: The inverse price–yield relation holds for a fixed promised payoff; changing risk or payoff is a different experiment. Private purchases transfer existing money and cannot change aggregate M. A central-bank open-market purchase creates money as it buys existing government bonds; an open-market sale withdraws money. The portfolio response then reconciles desired holdings with the new supply.
concepts.example: A bond paying 110 next year costs 100 at i = 10%. If its price rises to 104.76, its yield is approximately 5%.

check.prompt: If everyone wants to obtain more money by selling bonds, what happens to bond yields?
check.answer: Bond prices fall and yields rise until money demand is brought into line with supply.

concepts.title: Deriving LM from the money market
concepts.explain: At a given price level and nominal money supply, real balances are fixed. Higher output raises transactions demand, so interest must rise to discourage money holding and clear the asset market.
concepts.formula: M/P = L(Y,r+πᵉ)
steps: Hold M, P and expected inflation fixed.
Raise Y and shift real money demand right.
Find the higher clearing r and plot the new point on LM.
concepts.increase: Higher Y moves up along a given LM curve because transactions demand rises.
concepts.decrease: Lower Y reduces transactions demand, allowing a lower r and a move down along LM.
concepts.edge: The usual upward slope requires money demand to rise with Y and fall with nominal interest. A change in Y shifts the money-demand curve in its own graph but traces movement along LM. With no interest sensitivity, solve a vertical LM directly; on the liquidity-trap branch, extra balances can be held without a rate change.
concepts.example: For L = 2Y − 10r and M/P = 100, LM is r = 0.2Y − 10. Raising Y from 80 to 90 raises r from 6 to 8.

check.prompt: What is held fixed when deriving an LM curve?
check.answer: Nominal money supply, price level, expected inflation and other money-demand determinants.

concepts.title: LM algebra and expected inflation
concepts.explain: Money demand depends on nominal interest because that is the opportunity cost of holding non-interest-bearing money. In an r-versus-Y diagram, substitute i ≈ r + πᵉ before solving.
concepts.formula: L = l₀ + kY − h(r+πᵉ); r = (l₀−M/P)/h + (k/h)Y − πᵉ
steps: Write real money supply equal to real demand.
Substitute nominal interest with real interest plus expected inflation.
Collect r to reveal the slope and intercept.
concepts.increase: Higher expected inflation shifts LM down in real-interest space. At a fixed r it raises i and lowers money demand.
concepts.decrease: Lower expected inflation shifts LM up. At a fixed r it lowers i and raises money demand.
concepts.edge: This linear expression assumes k>0 and h>0 and uses the course Fisher approximation i≈r+πᵉ. At a fixed Y and M/P, a one-point increase in πᵉ lowers the clearing r one point while i stays fixed. At the new IS–LM intersection Y also changes, so that one-for-one real-rate change need not hold. The unconstrained line cannot be extended below the maintained nominal-rate floor.
concepts.example: If M/P = 100, l₀ = 20, k = 2, h = 10 and πᵉ = 1 in consistent rate units, LM is r = 0.2Y − 9.

check.prompt: Does expected inflation mechanically change current M/P?
check.answer: No. It changes money demand through nominal interest, unless current P or M also changes.

concepts.title: Real balances and LM shifts
concepts.explain: LM shifts when real money supply changes relative to money demand at a given output. More real balances require a lower rate to make people hold them.
concepts.formula: Real balances = M/P
steps: Compute whether M/P rises or falls.
At fixed Y, compare money supply with demand.
Adjust r to clear the market.
concepts.increase: Higher M or lower P raises M/P and shifts LM down/right. Higher expected inflation lowers money demand at a given real r by raising nominal opportunity cost, also shifting LM down. Lower household wealth lowers desired money holdings in the lecture and shifts LM down, with other determinants fixed.
concepts.decrease: Lower M or higher P reduces M/P and shifts LM up/left. Lower expected inflation raises money demand at a given real r, shifting LM up. Higher wealth or an autonomous increase in the preference for liquid balances raises money demand and shifts LM up.
concepts.edge: If M and P change in the same proportion, M/P and LM stay unchanged. A compensating money-supply increase can offset an autonomous money-demand increase exactly. Wealth also shifts IS through consumption, so an LM-only wealth experiment must explicitly hold the other channel aside. Income Y and r changes move along an existing LM rather than shift it.
concepts.example: M rises from 200 to 220 while P rises from 2 to 2.2. M/P remains 100, so there is no net LM shift.

check.prompt: A rise in autonomous money demand with M/P fixed shifts LM in which direction?
check.answer: Up and left because a higher r is needed to reduce money demand at any Y.

concepts.title: Solving short-run and long-run equilibria
concepts.explain: At fixed prices, solve IS and LM for Y and r. In full equilibrium, impose FE first, use IS for r and solve money equilibrium for P. The unknown price level makes the distinction essential.
concepts.formula: IS: r=a−bY. LM: r=c+dY. At fixed P, Y_SR=(a−c)/(b+d), r_SR=(ad+bc)/(b+d). With L=l₀+kY−h(r+πᵉ), full equilibrium has Y=Y*, r*=a−bY*, P*=M/[l₀+kY*−h(r*+πᵉ)].
steps: For the short run, use the given P in LM.
Equate IS and LM to solve Y and r.
For the long run, replace Y with Y* and solve P.
concepts.increase: A higher IS intercept raises short-run Y and r. With fixed Y*, long-run r rises and P adjusts.
concepts.decrease: A lower IS intercept reduces short-run Y and r. With fixed Y*, long-run r falls and P adjusts.
concepts.edge: Require b+d>0 for the stated unique short-run solution and positive real money demand for P*>0 when M>0. Tutorial 9 explicitly assumes perfectly flexible prices: its strict Classical version has no sustained sticky-price short-run output boom. A temporary boom after doubling M belongs to a separately stated sticky-price or surprise-information comparison.
concepts.example: Tutorial 9 integration: MPN=15−N and Nˢ=−5+3w give N*=10 and w=5. Then Y*=15(10)−0.5(10²)=100, C=10+0.7(100)=80 and I=20. From I=30−200r, r=0.05.
