The original PDF gives L=10+Y−200r, not 10Y−200r; hence L=100 and M=200 implies P=2. IS is r=0.2−0.0015Y, and substitution into money demand gives AD: Y=(30+200/P)/1.3. Doubling M changes this to Y=(30+400/P)/1.3; fully flexible prices immediately give P=4 and unchanged real outcomes.

check.prompt: Must the short-run intersection equal Y*?
check.answer: No. Price rigidity can keep the economy away from full employment.

concepts.title: Deriving aggregate demand
concepts.explain: AD is the set of IS–LM output equilibria generated by different price levels. A higher P reduces real balances, raises r and crowds out interest-sensitive spending.
concepts.formula: With IS r=a−bY and money demand L=l₀+kY−h(r+πᵉ), AD is Y=[M/P−l₀+h(a+πᵉ)]/(k+hb), with k+hb>0.
steps: Choose a price level and solve IS–LM.
Change only P and solve again.
Plot the resulting pairs of P and Y.
concepts.increase: An increase in P moves upward and left along a fixed AD curve. It shifts LM, not AD itself.
concepts.decrease: A decrease in P moves downward and right along AD because real balances rise and spending recovers.
concepts.edge: The slope is ∂Y/∂P=−M/[P²(k+hb)]<0 for M>0 and P>0 in this unconstrained model. Price changes move along AD while shifting LM. A liquidity-trap branch or a different money-demand specification can alter the usual transmission; an AD curve is an equilibrium locus, not an individual demand curve.
concepts.example: For IS r = 10−0.1Y and L = 2Y−10r, M/P = 3Y−100. Thus Y = (100+M/P)/3.

check.prompt: Does a price increase shift AD left?
check.answer: No. With other determinants fixed it generates movement along AD.

concepts.title: AD shifts from either market
concepts.explain: An exogenous change that raises IS–LM equilibrium output at every fixed P shifts AD right. Both goods-market and money-market changes can do this.
concepts.formula: AD shift = change in equilibrium Y at a fixed P
steps: Freeze the price level.
Work out the IS or LM shift.
Read the change in intersection output.
concepts.increase: At each fixed P, more M or less autonomous money demand shifts LM right and raises Y. Higher expected inflation does the same in the unconstrained real-rate diagram. Higher future income/output, autonomous C, G or future MPK, and lower effective capital tax, shift IS right and raise AD. A household tax cut raises AD only if it raises consumption. Higher wealth raises AD through consumption when its money-demand effect is held fixed.
concepts.decrease: At each fixed P, less M, more autonomous money demand or lower expected inflation shifts LM left and reduces AD. Lower future income, autonomous C, G or future MPK, and higher effective capital tax, shift IS left and reduce AD. A household tax rise reduces AD if it lowers C. Lower wealth lowers AD through consumption when its money-demand channel is held fixed.
concepts.edge: Wealth is listed in both the IS and LM shifters: higher wealth increases C, pushing IS right, but can increase money demand, pushing LM left. If both channels operate, r rises while the net AD/output shift can be right, left or zero depending on magnitudes. A pure capacity change shifts FE/LRAS without AD if no demand determinant changes. Tax timing with Ricardian equivalence does not shift AD.
concepts.example: From Y=[R−l₀+h(a+πᵉ)]/(k+hb), a wealth shock that raises the IS intercept by Δa and autonomous money demand by Δl₀ changes Y by [hΔa−Δl₀]/(k+hb). If hΔa exceeds Δl₀, AD shifts right; if smaller, left; if equal, it does not shift.

check.prompt: If higher expected inflation shifts LM down, what happens to AD under the standard fixed-P setup?
check.answer: It shifts right as lower r raises desired spending and output.

concepts.title: Two supply curves, two horizons
concepts.explain: Lecture 6 assumes prices fixed in the short run, so firms meet demand at the preset price and SRAS is horizontal. With full price adjustment, output returns to the supply-determined Y*, giving vertical LRAS.
concepts.formula: SRAS P = preset P; LRAS Y = Y*
steps: Identify whether prices can adjust.
Use AD with the appropriate supply curve.
Track the output gap and subsequent price adjustment.
concepts.increase: An AD increase raises Y at a fixed P initially. With fixed Y*, prices later rise until Y returns to Y*.
concepts.decrease: An AD decrease lowers Y at a fixed P initially. Prices later fall until real balances support Y*.
concepts.edge: Short run and long run denote whether adjustment has occurred, not a fixed number of calendar months. At Y=Y* there is no output-gap pressure to change P. Firms must have the ability and incentive to meet extra orders temporarily; later Keynesian markup and spare-labor assumptions explain this. The horizontal fixed-price SRAS differs from the upward-sloping misperceptions SRAS and from immediate Classical adjustment. IS–LM–FE and AD–AS describe the same aggregate equilibrium but highlight r–Y and P–Y respectively.
concepts.example: AD rises while Y* stays 100 and P is initially 2. Short-run Y can be 110. Long-run Y is 100 at a higher P.

check.prompt: Does vertical LRAS mean output can never change?
check.answer: No. Supply-side changes shift LRAS by changing Y*.

concepts.title: Monetary expansion and contraction
concepts.explain: With initially sticky prices, changing nominal money changes real balances, interest and demand. Once prices fully adjust and real determinants stay fixed, real balances and real outcomes return to their initial levels.
concepts.formula: Long-run ΔP/P = ΔM/M when Y*, r and money-demand determinants stay fixed
steps: For expansion the central bank buys existing government bonds and raises M; for contraction it sells bonds and withdraws M.
With P initially fixed, compare M/P with desired balances. Expansion induces bond purchases, raises their price and lowers i and r at fixed πᵉ; contraction induces sales and higher rates.
Lower r raises desired C and I, so expansion raises Y and employment; higher r reduces spending and output after contraction.
If output is above fixed Y*, P rises, M/P falls and LM shifts back. Below Y*, P falls, M/P rises and LM shifts back. At Y*, gap-induced price adjustment stops.
With unchanged real determinants and πᵉ, final Y, N, w, r, C and I return to their initial values, while P and nominal W scale with M.
concepts.increase: More M lowers r and raises Y and interest-sensitive spending initially. Later P rises, LM shifts back and real outcomes return.
concepts.decrease: Less M raises r and lowers Y and interest-sensitive spending initially. Later P falls, LM shifts back and real outcomes return.
concepts.edge: The proportional final P result requires fixed real determinants, expected inflation and money-demand behavior; it is a one-off money-level experiment. Changing money growth or expected inflation is different. In the fully flexible Classical benchmark the final allocation is reached immediately. A liquidity trap can interrupt the fixed-price transmission, and hysteresis is a distinct challenge to an unchanged long-run real benchmark.
concepts.example: A permanent 20% rise in M ultimately raises P by 20% in this setup. A 20% fall in M ultimately lowers P by 20%, rather than undoing a prior 20% rise.

check.prompt: After a long-run monetary expansion, must nominal wages remain unchanged?
check.answer: No. With unchanged real wages and a higher P, nominal wages rise proportionately.

concepts.title: Fiscal policy with fixed FE
concepts.explain: With fixed FE, higher G raises desired goods spending and shifts IS right. At the original P, output and r rise; the rate increase restrains interest-sensitive private spending relative to what it would otherwise be. As P adjusts upward, real balances fall and LM shifts up until Y returns to fixed Y*. During this comparative-static adjustment the specified higher-G policy remains in place; its later expiry would be another shock.
concepts.formula: At fixed Y*, ΔC + ΔI = −ΔG
steps: Increase G and shift IS.
Solve the short-run intersection.
Raise P and shift LM until Y returns to fixed Y*.
concepts.increase: Higher G raises short-run Y, N and r. Investment falls if it decreases with r. Consumption has opposing current-income and rate effects, so its short-run total change is not fixed without coefficients. At fixed Y* in the long run, r and P are higher and C+I falls exactly by ΔG.
concepts.decrease: Lower G lowers short-run Y, N and r. Investment rises as r falls. Consumption has a negative income effect and positive rate effect, so its short-run net change is conditional. At fixed Y* in the long run, lower r raises money demand, P falls and C+I rises by the released purchases.
concepts.edge: Full crowding out concerns C+I together, not necessarily I alone. Finite upward-sloping LM usually gives partial short-run crowding out; vertical LM gives complete short-run crowding out and a liquidity-trap segment removes rate crowding out. This fixed-FE conclusion differs from the Classical labor-supply wealth effect. A permanent or temporary tax-financing rule must be stated; a pure tax-timing change need not stimulate under Ricardian equivalence.
concepts.example: If G rises 12 and long-run C falls 5 at unchanged Y, I must fall 7.

check.prompt: Why is it incorrect to claim I always falls one-for-one with G?
check.answer: Consumption can also change, so the resource identity constrains total private spending.

concepts.title: Money-demand sensitivity and policy
concepts.explain: The slope of LM is the income sensitivity of money demand divided by its interest sensitivity. A flat LM allows fiscal demand changes with little rate crowding out. A money-supply change has a smaller interest effect when money demand is very interest-sensitive.
concepts.formula: LM slope = k/h; for Y = A−Br and M/P = kY−hr, ∂Y/∂A = h/(h+kB), ∂Y/∂(M/P) = B/(h+kB)
steps: Hold the other behavioral coefficients fixed.
Change h and observe the LM slope.
Compare the resulting output response to the same policy change.
concepts.increase: Higher h flattens LM, strengthens fiscal effects and weakens the output effect of a fixed increase in real balances.
concepts.decrease: Lower h steepens LM, weakens fiscal effects and strengthens the output effect of a fixed increase in real balances.
concepts.edge: These derivatives compare fixed-price equilibria with B,k,h>0 and all other coefficients held fixed. A is the intercept of the solved goods equation Y=A−Br, not necessarily G itself: if Y=[a₀+G−Hr]/D, then ∂Y/∂G=(1/D)h/(h+kB). Reducing k also flattens LM but increases the money multiplier, whereas raising h reduces it. A slope comparison without naming the parameter change is incomplete.
concepts.example: With k = 1 and B = 2, raising h from 2 to 6 raises ∂Y/∂A from 1/2 to 3/4 and lowers ∂Y/∂(M/P) from 1/2 to 1/4.

check.prompt: Why is fiscal policy stronger with more interest-sensitive money demand?
check.answer: A smaller rise in r is sufficient to absorb the extra transactions demand, so less private spending is crowded out.

concepts.title: The vertical LM limit
concepts.explain: If money demand depends only on income, money-market equilibrium pins output independently of r. LM is vertical. A fiscal shift changes r at that fixed output, while a change in real balances shifts the output level itself.
concepts.formula: With L=l₀+kY, k>0, money equilibrium gives Y=(M/P−l₀)/k independently of r.
steps: Set the interest coefficient to zero in money demand.
Solve directly for Y, without dividing by that coefficient.
Intersect the resulting vertical LM with IS.
concepts.increase: Higher G raises r but leaves Y unchanged at fixed P and M. Higher M raises the output level allowed by the money market.
concepts.decrease: Lower G reduces r without changing Y. Lower M reduces the output consistent with money-market clearing.
concepts.edge: Solve directly when h=0; do not divide by h in the usual LM expression. The vertical LM conclusion assumes the intersecting rate is feasible, spending has a rate response and the calculated output is in the model domain. If IS is also vertical at a different Y there is no joint fixed-price equilibrium; if at the same Y, these equations do not uniquely determine r.
concepts.example: If k = 2 and M/P = 200, Y = 100. An IS shift from r = 20−0.1Y to r = 24−0.1Y raises r from 10 to 14.

check.prompt: Can fiscal expansion raise Y with vertical LM and fixed real balances?
check.answer: No. It raises the clearing interest rate and crowds out the added spending.

concepts.title: The nominal-rate bound and liquidity trap
concepts.explain: At zero nominal interest, money and short bonds have the same financial return in the simplified model. Additional money can be willingly held without a further interest fall. The relevant lower bound is on i, not r.
concepts.formula: i ≈ r + πᵉ; i ≥ 0 implies r ≥ −πᵉ
steps: Use the Fisher relation to find the real-rate floor.
Identify whether the flat segment is binding.
Separate cash injections from policies that move spending or expected inflation.
concepts.increase: While trapped, more M alone need not raise Y. Higher G can raise Y without interest crowding out until the flat segment ends. Higher expected inflation lowers the real-rate floor.
concepts.decrease: A G reduction lowers Y along the flat segment. Lower expected inflation raises the real-rate floor and can deepen weak demand. A money contraction has no effect only while balances remain sufficient to stay in the trap.
concepts.edge: Tutorial 8 sets i=0 and πᵉ=0, making the trap branch horizontal at r=0. The extension to πᵉ≠0 follows from the lecture Fisher approximation: its real-rate floor is r≈−πᵉ. The flat branch is conditional on supplied balances being sufficient; it is not a globally horizontal LM for every M and Y. Below that threshold a contraction can leave the trap. A nominal zero bound is an assumption of this simplified exercise, not a universal empirical prohibition on negative nominal rates.
concepts.example: At i = 0 and expected inflation 3%, approximate r = −3%. With expected deflation of 3%, r = +3%, which can restrain spending.

check.prompt: At zero nominal interest, does expected deflation make borrowing cheaper in real terms?
check.answer: No. It raises the real interest rate because r ≈ i − πᵉ.

lessons.title: New Classical and RBC models
lessons.subtitle: Separate flexible prices, real shocks and imperfect information.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 7- The New Classical and RBC Models.pdf

concepts.title: Real shocks and business cycles
concepts.explain: A business-cycle theory needs both a source of disturbances and a model of propagation. RBC emphasizes real shocks, especially productivity, within a competitive flexible-wage/flexible-price equilibrium. Technology, management, input quality, usable energy and materials, weather and regulation can change productive efficiency. Labor-force changes, government purchases, and changes in household spending or saving preferences are also real disturbances affecting FE or IS; money supply and money-demand disturbances are nominal/asset-market shocks in the lecture classification. A real shock need not be beneficial or exclusively a technology invention.
concepts.formula: Y* = AF(K,N*); MPN = w
steps: Identify the real shock.
Solve the labor-market and production response.
Use IS and money equilibrium for r and P.
concepts.increase: A beneficial temporary productivity shock raises labor demand, real wages, employment and Y* under the standard upward-sloping labor supply.
concepts.decrease: An adverse temporary shock lowers labor demand, real wages, employment and Y*.
concepts.edge: An RBC contraction can be a fall in equilibrium potential output rather than a negative demand gap. The stated productivity directions assume higher A raises MPN and labor supply slopes upward. When future productivity or household wealth changes, labor supply and IS responses must also be considered; the simple temporary-current-A exercise deliberately holds them aside.
concepts.example: A temporary energy disruption lowers effective productivity. A lower Y is consistent with market clearing rather than proof of deficient AD.

check.prompt: Does a fall in actual output necessarily mean Y is below Y* in RBC?
check.answer: No. Potential output itself may fall with the real shock.

concepts.title: Following productivity through all markets
concepts.explain: In the lecture experiment, a temporary productivity shock shifts FE while IS is unchanged. The full-employment output change alters saving, which changes r. Money demand then determines P.
concepts.formula: Negative A → FE left → lower Y on IS → higher r → lower L → higher P
steps: With capital fixed, temporary lower A and MPN shift labor demand left: competitive real w and N* fall, and lower A plus employment reduce Y*. FE and LRAS move left.
With future determinants held fixed, IS does not shift. At the new lower Y*, goods equilibrium moves upward along IS: r rises, reducing desired C and I through interest; lower income also reduces C.
At fixed M and πᵉ, lower Y and higher r both reduce L. Therefore P=M/L rises and LM shifts up until it meets IS on the new FE.
For a beneficial temporary shock, MPN, w, N* and Y* rise; r falls along IS, C and I rise, money demand rises and P falls.
concepts.increase: Higher temporary A raises Y*, lowers r along IS and raises money demand through both Y and r, so P falls with M fixed.
concepts.decrease: Lower temporary A reduces Y*, raises r and lowers money demand through both channels, so P rises.
concepts.edge: The exercise keeps expected future income, future MPK and nominal money fixed. If those change, IS or LM may also shift. The negative productivity shock produces a higher price level during transition; a one-time level jump is not by itself permanently higher inflation. With full flexibility the economy is at each new equilibrium, not necessarily below its new potential.
concepts.example: With IS r = 15−0.1Y, Y* falling from 100 to 90 raises r from 5 to 6. L = 2Y−10r falls from 150 to 120, so fixed M = 300 raises P from 2 to 2.5.

check.prompt: Why does an adverse temporary productivity shock raise P in this lecture case?
check.answer: Both lower Y and higher r reduce real money demand. Fixed nominal M then requires a higher P.

concepts.title: Fiscal policy can shift FE
concepts.explain: Higher government purchases require current or future taxes. With leisure normal, households feel poorer and supply more labor. Thus Classical fiscal policy can affect output even with flexible prices.
concepts.formula: G↑ → lifetime private resources↓ → leisure↓ → Nˢ↑ → N*↑ → Y*↑
steps: Raise temporary G financed by present or future lump-sum taxes; lifetime private resources fall.
With normal leisure, desired leisure falls and labor supply shifts right. Against unchanged downward-sloping labor demand, the competitive real wage falls and N* rises.
Higher employment raises Y*, shifting FE/LRAS right. Separately, G lowers national saving at a given Y and r and shifts IS up/right.
Locate the new IS intersection with the original LM relative to the new FE. The lecture assumes that intersection lies to the right of the new FE.

Under that condition there is excess demand at the old P. P rises, M/P falls and LM shifts up until all three curves meet. Final Y and N rise, real w falls, and r and P rise in the pictured configuration.
concepts.increase: Higher G gives lower private wealth, less leisure, greater labor supply, lower competitive real wage, more employment and higher Y*. IS also shifts right. If the new IS–old LM intersection is right of the new FE, P and r rise. More output means total C+I need not fall one-for-one with G; Δ(C+I)=ΔY−ΔG.
concepts.decrease: Lower G reduces current/future taxes and raises private wealth. Normal leisure rises, labor supply shifts left, the competitive real wage rises and N* and Y* fall, shifting FE left. IS shifts down/left as national saving rises. If its old-LM intersection lies left of the new FE, P falls and LM shifts down to restore equilibrium, with r also lower in that configuration.
concepts.edge: Shift directions alone do not determine r or P: with IS r=a−bY*, Δr=Δa−bΔY*. Money demand changes by kΔY*−hΔr at fixed πᵉ, and P moves oppositely. Expansion raises r only if Δa>bΔY*. Even then P rises only if hΔr>kΔY*. Equality leaves P unchanged. A sufficiently strong FE shift can lower r and P. These comparisons hold b,k,h fixed and are derived from the lecture equations.
concepts.example: Take b=0.1,k=2,h=10. A fiscal expansion raises the IS intercept by 2 and Y* by 4: Δr=2−0.4=1.6 and ΔL=2(4)−10(1.6)=−8, so P rises at fixed M. If the same intercept change accompanies ΔY*=10, Δr=1 but ΔL=10, so P falls. The labor-supply and IS shifts have the same directions in both examples.

check.prompt: Why is fixed-output fiscal crowding out not universal across the course?
check.answer: The Classical labor-supply wealth effect can raise Y*, whereas the stated Keynesian fiscal case holds FE fixed.

concepts.title: Flexible prices and monetary neutrality
concepts.explain: With fully flexible prices and no information friction, nominal money does not change the labor and goods-market equations that determine real outcomes. P adjusts to keep desired real balances unchanged.
concepts.formula: P = M/L(Y*,r+πᵉ)
steps: Solve real variables from real markets.
Hold their determinants and expected inflation fixed.
Scale P with nominal M.
concepts.increase: A one-off rise in M raises P and nominal wages proportionately, leaving Y, N, w and r unchanged.
concepts.decrease: A one-off fall in M lowers P and nominal wages proportionately, leaving those real variables unchanged.
concepts.edge: A money-growth change can alter expected inflation and nominal interest. Do not confuse a money-level change with a permanent change in its growth rate.
concepts.example: If M and P both double, M/P and W/P are unchanged when W doubles too.

check.prompt: Does neutrality imply nominal interest must rise after every one-off increase in M?
check.answer: No. With expected inflation unchanged, i need not change.

concepts.title: Rational expectations are informed expectations
concepts.explain: Agents use available relevant information and the economic structure when forming expectations. Forecast errors remain possible because new information and genuine surprises occur.
concepts.formula: Rational expectations: forecast uses the available information set; unpredictable errors may remain, but a known systematic policy component should be incorporated.
steps: Specify what was known when the expectation was formed.
Identify the genuinely new information.
Separate a predictable policy rule from its surprise component.
concepts.increase: More credible information about a forthcoming expansion raises expected prices before implementation.
concepts.decrease: Credible information about a forthcoming contraction lowers expected prices.
concepts.edge: This does not mean perfect foresight, identical information for everyone or zero errors in every realization. The misperceptions explanation requires aggregate-price information to be imperfect when decisions are made. The lecture questions how long this friction lasts when economic information is rapidly available. Rational expectations by itself is not enough for anticipated-policy neutrality without the flexible-price information-model assumptions.
concepts.example: A weather forecast using all available information can still be wrong because tomorrow’s realization is uncertain. That is compatible with rational expectations.

check.prompt: Can rational agents be surprised by an unforeseeable shock?
check.answer: Yes. Rational expectations rules out systematically ignoring available information, not uncertainty.

concepts.title: Own prices versus the general price level
concepts.explain: A producer sees the price of their own product more clearly than the overall price level. They want to expand when their relative price rises, but not when every price rises equally. Imperfect information can confuse the two.
concepts.formula: Relative price = own price / aggregate price level
steps: Observe the own-price change.
Form a belief about the aggregate price change.
Adjust output according to the inferred relative-price change.
concepts.increase: An unexpected aggregate price increase can be partly mistaken for a relative-price improvement, inducing additional production.
concepts.decrease: An unexpected aggregate price decrease can be partly mistaken for a relative-price deterioration, inducing less production.
concepts.edge: With complete immediate information that all prices move proportionately, there is no mistaken relative-price incentive.
concepts.example: For a worker, the own price is the nominal wage W and the true relative price is W/P. If W rises 6% while P is unchanged, the real reward rises 6%. If W and P both rise 6%, W/P is unchanged; a fully informed worker has no new relative-price incentive. If the P rise is initially missed, the worker may mistake the nominal increase for a real improvement. A wage decrease mistakenly viewed as relative can similarly reduce labor supplied.

check.prompt: Why does an anticipated general price rise have no relative-price signal?
check.answer: Producers already expect the common price movement and do not mistake it for a change in their own relative price.

concepts.title: The surprise-output equation
concepts.explain: The misperceptions model permits output above or below potential even with flexible prices because imperfect information changes perceived relative prices. Expected price is held fixed when moving along SRAS.
concepts.formula: Y = Y* + b(P−Pᵉ), b > 0
steps: Calculate the price surprise.
Multiply it by responsiveness b.
Add the result to potential output.
concepts.increase: If P exceeds Pᵉ, output exceeds Y*.
concepts.decrease: If P falls below Pᵉ, output falls below Y*.
concepts.edge: At P=Pᵉ output equals Y*. Raising Pᵉ shifts SRAS up by the same price units at fixed Y; lowering Pᵉ shifts it down. Raising Y* shifts it right; lowering Y* shifts it left. Changing P alone moves along the curve. Larger b flattens its P-versus-Y slope 1/b; b approaching zero approaches a vertical output response. With perfect aggregate-price information the surprise mechanism disappears. For the later inflation derivation P must be interpreted consistently as a log price, with the coefficient calibrated to those units.
concepts.example: For Y* = 100, b = 4 and Pᵉ = 10, P = 11 gives Y = 104 and P = 9 gives Y = 96.

check.prompt: What does larger b mean?
check.answer: A larger output response to a given unexpected price-level change, or a flatter SRAS in a P-versus-Y diagram.

concepts.title: Anticipated monetary changes
concepts.explain: If a policy is fully anticipated and credible in the misperceptions model, expected prices adjust with actual prices. AD and SRAS shift together and output stays at potential.
concepts.formula: P−Pᵉ = 0 implies Y = Y*
steps: Let agents incorporate the announced policy into Pᵉ.
Shift AD and SRAS consistently.
Check that the equilibrium price surprise is zero.
concepts.increase: A fully anticipated expansion raises P and Pᵉ together, leaving Y at Y*.
concepts.decrease: A fully anticipated contraction lowers P and Pᵉ together, leaving Y at Y*.
concepts.edge: The result assumes an initially full-equilibrium economy, fully credible and correctly anticipated policy, flexible prices and unchanged real determinants. Anticipated does not mean AD fails to shift: SRAS shifts consistently with Pᵉ. A one-off permanent money-level change need not change ongoing expected inflation; a money-growth regime change is a different experiment. Sticky-price Keynesian models need separate analysis.
concepts.example: If both actual and expected prices rise from 100 to 110, b(P−Pᵉ) remains zero.

check.prompt: Can you assess an announcement by shifting AD while forcing Pᵉ unchanged?
check.answer: Not if the announcement is fully credible and anticipated in the model.

concepts.title: Unexpected monetary changes
concepts.explain: When money changes unexpectedly, expected prices do not fully adjust immediately. The price surprise changes output temporarily. Once information catches up, output returns to potential.
concepts.formula: Short run P ≠ Pᵉ; long run P = Pᵉ
steps: Shift AD with initial Pᵉ held fixed.
Find the short-run intersection on the original SRAS.
Update expectations and shift SRAS until Y returns to Y*.
concepts.increase: An unexpected expansion raises P and Y initially. Later Pᵉ rises, SRAS shifts up and Y returns to Y*.
concepts.decrease: An unexpected contraction lowers P and Y initially. Later Pᵉ falls, SRAS shifts down and Y returns to Y*.
concepts.edge: Start at P=Pᵉ and Y=Y* when describing an expansion as producing a positive gap or a contraction as producing a negative gap; from a pre-existing gap, a shock may instead reduce that gap. The lecture money-level experiment compares price levels across equilibria. For changes in money growth, a lower price than the baseline path need not mean the actual price level falls over time. Repeated predictable attempted surprises cease to be surprises under rational expectations.
concepts.example: An unannounced monetary increase creates a positive price surprise today. Next period agents may fully anticipate the resulting price level, eliminating the output gap.

check.prompt: Why cannot the central bank permanently keep Y above Y* by repeating the same surprise?
check.answer: People learn the systematic policy pattern and incorporate it into expectations.

concepts.title: The Lucas critique and policy evaluation
concepts.explain: Historical behavioral relationships may change when the policy rule changes because agents change their expectations and decisions. A fit to past data is not automatically a reliable policy counterfactual.
concepts.formula: Policy rule change → expectations change → behavioral relationship changes
steps: Identify a historical relationship estimated under the old policy rule, such as inflation and unemployment.
Ask which expectations and incentives depend on that rule and therefore change when the rule changes.
Use a model of decisions and expectations under the proposed rule rather than holding the historical coefficient or curve fixed automatically.
Retain useful data but distinguish descriptive fit from a policy-invariant structural relationship.
concepts.increase: A systematic attempt to raise inflation to exploit an old Phillips tradeoff can raise expected inflation and shift that curve.
concepts.decrease: A credible disinflation rule can reduce expected inflation, altering the relationship observed under the previous regime.
concepts.edge: The critique is not that all data or all forecasting is useless, nor that every policy has zero effect. It warns that policy-dependent reduced-form relationships may be unstable. A credible disinflation can lower expected inflation and shift the short-run curve down; an attempted permanent employment gain from predictable inflation can shift it up.
concepts.example: A government cannot assume a past correlation between surprise money and output remains unchanged after it announces that money will always rise when output falls.

check.prompt: What is wrong with treating expectations as fixed after changing a predictable policy rule?
check.answer: The public can respond to the new rule, so the estimated old relationship may no longer describe behavior.

concepts.title: RBC assumptions, welfare and the debate
concepts.explain: The lecture RBC benchmark combines competitive optimization, flexible wages and prices, rational expectations, Ricardian fiscal behavior and neutral money. Under its efficiency assumptions, fluctuations can be optimal adaptations to changed resources or incentives. That is a conditional model interpretation, not proof that recessions are harmless or all observed unemployment is voluntary. The debate concerns whether the assumed shocks and adjustment mechanisms adequately describe actual cycles.
concepts.formula: Efficient equilibrium conditional on a shock does not imply that the shock improves welfare.
steps: Separate the adverse shock from the response to it: a loss of productive capacity can reduce welfare even if agents adapt efficiently.
Check whether competitive efficiency, information and market-clearing assumptions are appropriate before carrying over the welfare conclusion.

Evaluate the empirical objections: are productivity shocks large and exogenous enough, are employment changes voluntary, is money neutral in the short run, and do wages/prices actually adjust quickly?
For fiscal stabilization, weigh the benchmark efficiency argument plus distortionary taxes, imperfect information and policy lags. Those reasons depend on the model and policy design.
concepts.increase: A better productive opportunity can raise feasible output and welfare; a larger estimated real shock can explain more cyclical output within RBC. Stronger evidence of fast market clearing supports that propagation mechanism.
concepts.decrease: A destructive supply shock can reduce attainable welfare even if the resulting lower employment is privately optimal. Evidence of involuntary unemployment, slow price adjustment or real effects of monetary shocks weakens a strict RBC explanation.
concepts.edge: The fact that a fiscal change can raise Y and N does not prove it improves welfare. Conversely, a policy with little measured GDP effect may have other welfare consequences. Rational expectations alone neither proves competitive efficiency nor establishes monetary neutrality in every sticky-price model.
concepts.example: An energy shortage lowers production opportunities. Firms and households may choose the best feasible allocation in the RBC model while still being worse off than before the shortage; efficient response and beneficial shock are distinct claims.

check.prompt: Does RBC equilibrium efficiency prove that an adverse productivity shock leaves welfare unchanged?
check.answer: No. The optimal response is conditional on a worsened constraint. Welfare can fall, and the efficiency claim itself relies on the benchmark assumptions.

lessons.title: New Keynesian foundations
lessons.subtitle: Understand why rational firms may keep wages and prices sticky.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 8 - the New Keynesian Model.pdf

concepts.title: Demand-driven output gaps
concepts.explain: Keynesian models emphasize shifts in aggregate demand when wages and prices adjust slowly. Firms produce less and hire fewer workers because fewer goods are demanded at existing prices.
concepts.formula: Sticky P → IS–LM determines Y, which may differ from Y*
steps: Identify the demand shock.
Hold prices fixed in the immediate response.
Trace production and employment rather than assuming markets clear instantly.
concepts.increase: Higher demand raises production and employment in the short run when firms can meet it at preset prices.
concepts.decrease: Lower demand reduces production and employment, creating a negative output gap.
concepts.edge: A demand recession differs from an efficient response to a lower productive capacity in the RBC interpretation.
concepts.example: Consumer pessimism shifts IS left. At fixed P, Y falls even though machines, technology and potential output need not change.

check.prompt: Why can unemployment rise without a fall in workers’ desire to work?
check.answer: Firms require fewer workers when demand for their output falls.

concepts.title: Why wages may not clear the labor market
concepts.explain: The lecture considers legal minimum wages and union influence, the costs of replacing/training workers when turnover is high, and efficiency wages that elicit effort. Each can make a firm unwilling or unable to cut pay to the competitive clearing wage. Wage rigidity can coexist with optimizing firms and workers who want jobs at the going wage. Skill mismatch is another source of unemployment, but its ability to explain demand recessions must be assessed using vacancies and quits rather than asserted.
concepts.formula: Involuntary unemployment arises when Nˢ(w) > Nᵈ(w)
steps: Identify why wages resist adjustment.
Compare supply and demand at that wage.
Measure the excess labor supply.
concepts.increase: A fall in labor demand at an unchanged high wage lowers employment and increases unemployment.
concepts.decrease: A rise in labor demand at that wage increases employment and reduces excess labor supply.
concepts.edge: A wage above competitive clearing is not necessarily irrational for an individual firm when effort or turnover depends on pay. It produces excess supply only when desired labor supply at that wage exceeds jobs demanded. The lecture efficiency wage is a real wage chosen for incentives; nominal price rigidity is a separate ingredient of the demand model.
concepts.example: At wage 10, 100 workers wish to work and firms hire 70. Thirty workers are willing to work at the going wage but cannot obtain a job.

check.prompt: Does excess labor supply guarantee an immediate wage cut in this model?
check.answer: No. Firms may lose effort or incur higher turnover if they cut wages.

concepts.title: Effort responds to pay
concepts.explain: Real pay w can affect effort e(w) through reciprocity or gift exchange (the carrot) and the threat of losing an unusually valuable job if shirking is detected (the stick). The illustrated effort curve is increasing and S-shaped: low effort at very low wages, a steep middle region, and smaller marginal effort gains at high wages. Firms therefore care about effective labor e(w)N rather than headcount alone.
concepts.formula: Y=A F(e(w)N), abstracting from capital in this lecture; e′(w)>0 over the depicted range.
steps: Separate the number of workers from effort per worker.
Compare how effort responds to different wage levels.
Translate effective labor into production.
concepts.increase: A wage rise can increase effort and reduce turnover. The proportional effort increase may be large at intermediate wages.
concepts.decrease: A wage cut can reduce effort or increase shirking, so a lower wage per worker need not mean a lower cost per effective unit.
concepts.edge: An increasing effort curve alone does not guarantee an interior efficiency wage. Its proportional response must fall through one so the cost ratio changes from decreasing to increasing. If the ratio keeps improving to a boundary, the optimum is at that feasible boundary. If effort is unchanged by a wage cut, the cut lowers effective-unit cost in this stripped-down calculation.
concepts.example: At w = 8 and e = 2, cost per effective unit is 4. At w = 10 and e = 3, it is 3.33, despite higher pay.

check.prompt: Why compare effective labor rather than worker counts alone?
check.answer: Different wages can buy different amounts of effort per worker.

concepts.title: Minimizing cost per effective worker
concepts.explain: The firm chooses the wage that minimizes w/e(w), equivalently maximizes e(w)/w. Graphically it is the point where a ray from the origin is tangent to the effort curve.
concepts.formula: q(w)=w/e(w); q′(w)=[e(w)−w e′(w)]/e(w)². At an interior optimum w e′(w)=e(w), or ε_e,w=we′/e=1. With w fixed at w*, MPN=A F′(e(w*)N)e(w*)=w*.
steps: For a required amount E of effective labor, hire N=E/e(w), so total wage cost is wN=[w/e(w)]E. Minimize w/e, equivalently maximize e/w.
On the graph with e vertical and w horizontal, a ray from the origin has slope e(w)/w. The steepest attainable ray maximizes effort per dollar; its reciprocal is effective-unit cost.
At an interior tangency the ray slope e/w equals the curve slope e′, yielding we′=e. Check that the ratio is a maximum for e/w, not just any stationary point.
Choose headcount after the wage: differentiating A F(eN) with respect to actual N gives A F′(eN)e, so the hiring condition is actual-worker MPN=w.
If that efficiency wage exceeds the competitive clearing wage, Ns(w*)>Nd(w*) and involuntary unemployment remains. Wage underbidding need not attract firms when it lowers effort per dollar.
concepts.increase: If ε_e,w>1, a small wage rise increases effort by a larger percentage than pay, so w/e falls. If ε_e,w<1, a small wage rise instead raises cost per effective unit. At ε=1 the first-order change is zero.
concepts.decrease: If ε_e,w<1, a small wage cut lowers pay proportionately more than effort, so w/e falls. If ε_e,w>1, a small cut harms effort disproportionately and raises effective-unit cost. Around a true cost minimum, moving either side away from w* raises cost.
concepts.edge: Need w>0 and e(w)>0, an interior solution and the appropriate global ratio comparison. A tangency can be a local extremum without being the best feasible wage. The lecture expression MPN=w uses the marginal product of an actual worker; F′ alone is per effective unit, so omitting the effort multiplier changes the units.
concepts.example: If e/w at wages 8,10,12 is 0.25,0.30,0.28, the best listed wage is 10 even though pay per head is higher than 8. If ε=1.4, a 1% local wage rise lowers w/e by approximately 0.4%. If ε=0.6, a 1% local wage cut lowers w/e by approximately 0.4%.

check.prompt: At the interior efficiency wage, what is the elasticity of effort with respect to wages?
check.answer: One. The marginal percentage gain in effort equals the percentage increase in wage cost.

concepts.title: Efficiency wages and potential output
concepts.explain: In the lecture Keynesian setup, the efficiency wage and labor demand determine full-employment employment. A labor-supply shift by itself does not change that employment if supply remains sufficient.
concepts.formula: N*=Nd(w_eff), where A F′(e(w_eff)N*)e(w_eff)=w_eff; Y*=A F(e(w_eff)N*). Capital is suppressed in this lecture.
steps: Hold the effort relationship and efficiency wage fixed.
Read employment from labor demand.
Use production to determine potential output.
concepts.increase: More labor supply can increase unemployment without increasing Y* in this setup. Higher productivity can shift labor demand and raise Y*.
concepts.decrease: Less labor supply can reduce excess supply without changing Y*, until labor supply becomes a binding limit. Lower productivity can reduce Y*.
concepts.edge: Keynesian full-employment N* here is hiring where labor demand crosses the efficiency-wage line, not the competitive Ns=Nd intersection. Structural/involuntary unemployment can remain at this model-specific potential. A fiscal tax-financing wealth effect can shift Ns without shifting FE while available workers still exceed desired hiring. If labor supply becomes insufficient, the assumed fixed-wage unconstrained-hiring closure must be reconsidered.
concepts.example: If firms want 80 workers at the efficiency wage, labor supply increasing from 100 to 110 leaves employment 80 and raises excess supply from 20 to 30.

check.prompt: Why can immigration leave FE unchanged in this particular model?
check.answer: When the efficiency wage and labor demand determine hiring, additional labor supply only enlarges the pool of available workers.

concepts.title: Monopolistic competition and markups
concepts.explain: A differentiated producer has downward-sloping demand, so uniform-price marginal revenue is below price. Without adjustment costs it chooses output at MR=MC and reads the corresponding price from demand, producing a markup P>MC. A menu cost may keep that nominal price preset after a demand change. Meeting extra orders at that unchanged posted price is a different margin from cutting price along a fixed demand curve: extra sales yield the posted P each, and are profitable while their marginal cost is below P.
concepts.formula: MR = MC; P = (1+κ)MC for markup κ
steps: Find the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
Read the selling price on demand.
Distinguish the chosen price from marginal revenue.
concepts.increase: A demand increase at a fixed price can lead the firm to supply more while P remains above MC.
concepts.decrease: A demand decrease can lead the firm to sell less at that fixed price.
concepts.edge: A competitive price taker has P=MR. The equation P=(1+κ)MC describes the markup representation at the reference pricing optimum; after demand or cost changes with price preset, the actual markup need not stay κ. At MC=P the next sale has zero marginal operating profit; at MC>P it loses money, so arbitrary extra production is not justified. Spare labor and physical capacity are also needed.
concepts.example: If MC = 8 and markup κ = 0.25, P = 10. A small extra sale may remain profitable while its marginal cost stays below 10.

check.prompt: Why does MR lie below P for a downward-sloping demand curve?
check.answer: Selling an additional unit requires a price reduction that affects revenue on other units under uniform pricing.

concepts.title: Small adjustment costs can keep prices fixed
concepts.explain: Changing prices has administrative and customer-related costs. A profit-maximizing firm keeps its old price when the profit gain from resetting is smaller than the adjustment cost.
concepts.formula: Reset price if gain from adjustment > menu cost
steps: Find the optimal new price absent costs.
Compare the profit gain with the actual adjustment cost.
Choose whether to reset now.
concepts.increase: A larger upward demand or cost disturbance can make the gain from a higher new price exceed the menu cost, triggering repricing. Higher menu cost for the same gain makes retaining the existing price more attractive.
concepts.decrease: A sufficiently large downward demand or cost disturbance can make cutting the price worth the menu cost. A smaller gain or higher menu cost favors keeping the old price; lower menu cost can trigger adjustment even for the same shock.
concepts.edge: Compare the gain before paying the menu cost over a consistent decision horizon. Gain>cost implies reset; gain<cost implies retain; equality gives indifference in the simple rule. Small menu costs can matter when the profit gain from a small reset is even smaller. Nominal price stickiness does not mean firms never reset or always raise prices.
concepts.example: Resetting would raise profit by 30 but costs 50. Keeping the current price is privately optimal even though it is not the frictionless optimum.

check.prompt: Must firms reset prices after every change in demand?
check.answer: No. They compare the benefit of resetting with its cost.

concepts.title: Monetary and fiscal policy with rigid prices
concepts.explain: Monetary expansion increases real balances and lowers r. Fiscal expansion raises goods demand and r. Both can raise short-run output, but their composition effects differ. With fixed FE, prices later restore potential output.
concepts.formula: Fiscal multiplier over a specified horizon = ΔY/ΔG. Standard fixed-price expansion: M↑ gives r↓; G↑ gives r↑. Fixed-FE full adjustment: Δ(C+I)=−ΔG.
steps: Specify which curve shifts.
Trace interest-sensitive private spending.
Distinguish the short-run output effect from the long-run price response.
concepts.increase: With ordinary downward IS and finite upward LM, higher M at fixed P lowers r, raises Y and N, and supports C through both income and interest and I through interest. Higher G raises Y, N and r; I falls while C faces opposing higher-income and higher-rate effects. A household tax cut raises consumption and shifts IS right only under the stated non-Ricardian behavior.
concepts.decrease: Lower M at fixed P raises r and reduces Y, N, C and I in these functions. Lower G reduces Y, N and r; I rises while C has a negative income effect and positive interest effect. A tax increase that reduces C shifts IS left.
concepts.edge: Holding FE fixed, long-run monetary expansion raises P and nominal wages proportionately and leaves real Y,N,w,r,C,I unchanged. Long-run higher G raises r and P with Y,N fixed; C+I falls by ΔG. Potential does not shift merely because labor supply changes at a fixed efficiency wage with excess workers. Flat/vertical LM are special cases and require their own policy comparison.
concepts.example: If G rises 10 and Y rises 6 initially, private spending changes by −4. When Y returns to its original fixed potential, private spending is lower by 10.

check.prompt: Can two policies raise Y but move investment in opposite directions?
check.answer: Yes. A money expansion lowers r and supports I, while a G expansion raises r and crowds out some I.

concepts.title: Why stabilization is difficult
concepts.explain: Policy can offset demand fluctuations, but the current output gap, multiplier and future conditions are uncertain. Decisions and transmission take time. A policy suited to yesterday’s economy can destabilize tomorrow’s.
concepts.formula: Policy effect today depends on earlier decisions and variable transmission lags
steps: Estimate the current state and the output gap; both potential output and current data are imperfectly observed.
Estimate the size and timing of monetary/fiscal effects; the lecture gives an illustrative 6–12-month transmission lag, not a guaranteed timetable.
Allow for political, decision and implementation delays and forecast the economy when the effects will arrive.
Compare the risks of inaction and overshooting. The lecture cautions against fine tuning while allowing a role for policy in major recessions.
concepts.increase: An expansion arriving after recovery can push demand above capacity and increase inflation.
concepts.decrease: A contraction arriving during weakening demand can deepen a recession.
concepts.edge: The lecture argues against fine tuning while allowing intervention in major recessions. This is a conditional recommendation, not guaranteed success.
concepts.example: If stimulus takes nine months to affect demand but the economy recovers in three, the timing may be excessive even if the initial diagnosis was correct.

check.prompt: Why is knowing the sign of a multiplier insufficient for successful stabilization?
check.answer: The size, timing and future state of the economy also matter.

concepts.title: Supply shocks and stagflation
concepts.explain: An adverse oil shock reduces productive capacity and can prompt affected firms to raise prices quickly. FE shifts left and the higher P reduces real balances, shifting LM up. Lower output and higher prices can occur together.
concepts.formula: Oil cost↑ → effective productivity↓ → FE left; P↑ → M/P↓ → LM up
steps: An oil-price rise lowers usable energy/productivity at a given capital and labor input, reducing Y* and shifting FE left.
Oil-dependent firms raise prices promptly; the aggregate P rise lowers M/P and shifts LM up even though IS is unchanged in this exercise.
In the lecture diagram, the initial LM shift takes actual output Y₃ below the new potential Y₂. This is a larger fall than the capacity decline alone.
That remaining excess supply creates downward price pressure: P partly falls, M/P partly recovers and LM shifts down from its initial post-shock position to meet IS on the new FE.
The final output remains below old potential and the final price can remain above the old price even though prices fall during the later adjustment.
concepts.increase: Higher oil costs can lower potential output and raise prices, producing stagflation during the shock. If actual Y lies below the new Y*, demand expansion may help close that residual gap but can intensify inflation pressure.
concepts.decrease: Cheaper oil can improve productive capacity and reduce cost pressure. The initial price decline and output response need not be the exact mirror of an adverse shock: preset-price decisions, menu-cost thresholds and the starting demand gap can differ. Recalculate actual Y against the new higher Y* before deciding whether the economy has excess demand or supply.
concepts.edge: The source explicitly says Y₃<Y₂ is not logically necessary. A small initial price rise could leave Y above the new potential, and an exactly offsetting response could put it on FE. A fall from old actual output is not evidence of a negative new gap. Demand policy changes spending relative to capacity but does not directly restore the productive capacity lost to the oil shock.
concepts.example: Before a shock Y* = 100. Afterwards Y* = 90 and actual Y = 92. Output fell, but the economy is 2 above its new potential, not in a negative output gap.

check.prompt: Can demand stimulus restore the productive capacity directly lost in the oil shock?
check.answer: No. It can affect demand relative to the new capacity, while the supply constraint remains.

concepts.title: What the wage evidence does and does not establish
concepts.explain: The lecture uses two empirical arguments. A pure mismatch account of recessions suggests unfilled jobs and quits as workers search for better matches; the cited recession pattern does not show the increase in vacancies and quits that this account would suggest. Ford’s 1914 pay increase illustrates how higher pay might improve retention and effort. Neither argument by itself identifies a single causal mechanism or proves every wage increase pays for itself.
concepts.formula: Illustrative annual turnover count: monthly separation rate ×12 is not the fraction of distinct people who leave in a year.
steps: State the prediction of the mechanism before inspecting the evidence: mismatch, demand weakness and incentive wages imply different patterns.
For Ford, distinguish the simultaneous changes: daily pay rose from $2.30 for nine hours to $5 for eight hours; work hours and other business conditions also changed.

The lecture reports lower turnover and absenteeism and higher productivity, but profits and wider changes need not be caused solely by wages. Consider Model T production, union concerns and publicity as alternative or additional influences.
concepts.increase: Better pay can raise the value of retaining the job, reduce quits/absences and raise effective labor. More vacancies and quits during a downturn would be more consistent with the particular mismatch prediction discussed.
concepts.decrease: Lower pay can weaken effort or retention, but not every small pay cut has a large effect. Falling vacancies and hiring when spending weakens supports a labor-demand account of unemployment rather than simply unwillingness to work.
concepts.edge: The historical episode is an illustration, not a randomized experiment or a universal causal estimate. A reported 31% monthly turnover multiplied by 12 gives roughly 372% annual separations per reference workforce, not 372% of unique workers. Replacements may themselves leave.
concepts.example: Pay per hour changed from about 2.30/9=$0.256 to 5/8=$0.625. Even that large increase is not alone proof of a net profit gain: effort, productivity, hours, turnover costs and other contemporaneous changes all matter.

check.prompt: Why is the Ford episode compatible with efficiency wages without proving the theory causally?
check.answer: Pay, hours and other business conditions changed together, so improved performance is consistent with the mechanism but cannot isolate its causal contribution.

concepts.title: Other foundations named in the lecture
concepts.explain: Lecture 8 also names coordination failure and staggered wage/price setting. They are alternative ways to explain why decentralized optimization need not generate immediate aggregate adjustment. The slide names these approaches but does not derive a formal model; the mechanisms here are intuition, not extra examinable equations.
concepts.formula: No additional formal equation is supplied for these alternatives in Lecture 8.
steps: Coordination intuition: an individual firm’s desired production or pricing can depend on demand generated by other firms and households; individually reasonable caution can be mutually reinforcing.
Staggering intuition: different wages or prices are reset at different dates, so some remain preset while others adjust.
Keep these alternatives distinct from the effort-dependent wage and menu-cost mechanisms actually developed earlier.
concepts.increase: Stronger demand can encourage production and hiring across interacting firms. As more contracts reach reset dates, more prices can respond to higher nominal demand; this does not specify a universal multiplier.
concepts.decrease: Weak demand can reinforce mutually cautious spending or production. Lower nominal demand can take time to pass through staggered reset dates, leaving real activity weaker during adjustment.
concepts.edge: Naming an alternative does not establish that it applies empirically, derive its welfare result or prove the same neutrality result as another model. Without an explicit model, do not claim a particular numerical slope or adjustment duration.
concepts.example: If two firms can revise prices this month but a third waits until next month under its existing schedule, aggregate prices need not jump to every desired new price immediately. This illustrates staggering without requiring a new course formula.

check.prompt: Does the lecture’s mention of staggered pricing supply a unique numerical speed of adjustment?
check.answer: No. It names an alternative microfoundation; timing and quantitative effects require additional assumptions not supplied on that slide.

lessons.title: Inflation, unemployment and expectations
lessons.subtitle: Use surprises, natural rates and history to interpret the tradeoff.

source.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 9 - The Expectations-Augmented Phillips Curve.pdf

concepts.title: The expectations-augmented curve
concepts.explain: The stable relationship in the model is between unexpected inflation and cyclical unemployment. Expected inflation and the natural unemployment rate determine where the short-run curve lies.
concepts.formula: π=πᵉ−h(u−u*), h>0; in a π-versus-u graph the slope is −h and intercept is πᵉ+hu*. Use the same percent or decimal convention for all rates.
steps: Compute cyclical unemployment u−u*.
Multiply by −h.
Add expected inflation.
concepts.increase: If u rises above u*, actual inflation is below expected inflation.
concepts.decrease: If u falls below u*, actual inflation is above expected inflation.
concepts.edge: At u=u*, π=πᵉ, not necessarily zero. Stable πᵉ and u* are required for a stable observed short-run tradeoff; anchored expectations means πᵉ need not follow every actual inflation movement. u* includes frictional and structural unemployment. The baseline equation has no additional residual supply-shock term; if one is introduced in an extension, the correct-expectations conclusion needs that term to be zero too.
concepts.example: With πᵉ = 3%, h = 0.5 and u−u* = 2 percentage points, π = 2%.

check.prompt: Does zero cyclical unemployment require zero actual inflation?
check.answer: No. It requires actual inflation equal to expected inflation.

concepts.title: Positive, negative and zero surprises
concepts.explain: The sign of actual inflation alone does not determine the output or unemployment gap. Compare actual inflation with what was expected.
concepts.formula: π−πᵉ = −h(u−u*)
steps: Subtract expected inflation from actual inflation.
Use the opposite sign for the cyclical unemployment gap.
Relate unemployment to output via Okun’s law.
concepts.increase: A positive inflation surprise implies u below u* and output above potential in the model.
concepts.decrease: A negative inflation surprise implies u above u* and output below potential.
concepts.edge: Zero surprise means π=πᵉ and therefore u=u* in the baseline equation; π can be positive, zero or negative. Positive inflation below expectations implies a negative surprise, and deflation milder than expected implies a positive surprise. Connecting a price-level surprise with an inflation surprise uses the same known previous price as the base; changing that base or adding an unmodeled disturbance is another experiment.
concepts.example: Actual inflation 2% with expected inflation 4% is a −2-point surprise. Actual inflation −1% with expected −3% is a +2-point surprise.

check.prompt: If actual inflation is 1% and expected inflation is 5%, is unemployment above or below its natural rate?
check.answer: Above, because inflation is lower than expected.

concepts.title: Expected inflation shifts the curve
concepts.explain: Holding the natural rate and slope fixed, higher expected inflation raises actual inflation at every unemployment rate. This is a shift of the short-run curve, not movement along it.
concepts.formula: At fixed u,u*, Δπ=Δπᵉ. At fixed π,u*, Δu=Δπᵉ/h. The slope remains −h.
steps: Freeze the unemployment gap.
Change expected inflation.
Translate the entire short-run curve vertically.
concepts.increase: Higher πᵉ shifts SRPC up by Δπᵉ at each u, equivalently right by Δπᵉ/h at each π. Maintaining the same unemployment requires more actual inflation.
concepts.decrease: Lower πᵉ shifts SRPC down and left. At the same unemployment, actual inflation is lower; at the same inflation, unemployment is lower by the corresponding expectation change divided by h.
concepts.edge: Actual inflation alone is not a curve shifter when πᵉ,u* and h stay fixed: it is a movement along the curve. Anchored expectations do not automatically rise or fall with every temporary observed inflation change; specifying adaptive or another expectation rule is an additional assumption.
concepts.example: If πᵉ rises from 2% to 4% with the gap unchanged, predicted actual inflation rises 2 percentage points.

check.prompt: Does an increase in actual inflation necessarily shift the curve?
check.answer: No. With πᵉ and u* fixed, it can be a movement along the existing curve.

concepts.title: A changing natural rate
concepts.explain: The natural rate reflects frictional and structural unemployment when output is at full employment. Changing labor-market matching or institutions can shift it independently of aggregate demand.
concepts.formula: At fixed πᵉ,h: Δπ=hΔu* for fixed u, while Δu=Δu* for fixed π. LRPC is vertical at u=u*.
steps: Identify the change in structural or frictional conditions.
Move the natural-rate position.
Recalculate the cyclical gap using the new u*.
concepts.increase: A higher natural rate shifts the short-run curve up/right and the long-run curve right.
concepts.decrease: A lower natural rate shifts the short-run curve down/left and the long-run curve left.
concepts.edge: A rise in actual u alone does not establish a rise in u*: it can reflect a cyclical demand gap. At correct expectations, actual u must match the new natural rate in this baseline model; using the old u* creates a false gap. Structural improvements can lower u* without requiring inflation to rise.
concepts.example: With actual u = 6%, changing u* from 4% to 5% reduces cyclical unemployment from 2 to 1 percentage point.

check.prompt: Why must the gap be recalculated after a structural change?
check.answer: The relevant benchmark u* has changed, so the same actual u represents a different cyclical condition.

concepts.title: Supply shocks and the shifting tradeoff
concepts.explain: A supply disturbance can raise inflation expectations and increase structural mismatch, raising the natural unemployment rate. Both effects shift the short-run Phillips curve upward/right.
concepts.formula: Supply shock → πᵉ↑ and/or u*↑ → SRPC up/right
steps: An adverse supply shock can create a burst of inflation that raises expected inflation, shifting SRPC upward.
Changing relative sector profitability displaces workers; mismatched skills or locations can increase structural unemployment and u*, shifting SRPC right.
At a fixed actual u, combine the two shifts: Δπ=Δπᵉ+hΔu*. At a fixed π the horizontal shift is Δu*+Δπᵉ/h.
Do not label two higher observed rates as a movement along one unchanged downward-sloping curve.
concepts.increase: An adverse energy shock can produce higher inflation and higher unemployment together.
concepts.decrease: A favorable supply improvement can reduce price pressure, but πᵉ falls only if expectations respond. Better matching can reduce u*. If both fall, SRPC shifts down/left; if one stays fixed, only the other channel operates.
concepts.edge: The source explains supply shocks through πᵉ and u*, not an extra additive shock v. If expectations are anchored and mismatch does not change, these specific shift channels are absent; do not automatically infer their magnitudes from the oil price alone. A shift permits stagflation but does not determine the final equilibrium without aggregate-demand conditions.
concepts.example: Energy-intensive sectors shrink while energy suppliers expand. Workers may not instantly match to new jobs, so natural unemployment can rise.

check.prompt: How can both inflation and unemployment rise?
check.answer: The short-run curve can shift up/right due to expectations or supply-side changes.

concepts.title: Deriving the curve from SRAS
concepts.explain: The lecture starts from the surprise-output relation and interprets the price variable as the logarithm of the price level for the inflation step. Use p=ln(P_level) to avoid confusing an index level with a rate. Subtract the same known previous log price from both actual and expected current log prices. Then use Okun’s negative mapping from output gaps to unemployment gaps. This is a change of variables plus an economic relationship, not a claim that raw price levels equal inflation.
concepts.formula: Y−Y*=b(p−pᵉ). Define π_log=p−p₋₁ and π_logᵉ=pᵉ−p₋₁, so π_log−π_logᵉ=(Y−Y*)/b. If (Y−Y*)/b=−h(u−u*), then π_log=π_logᵉ−h(u−u*).
steps: Rearrange the log-price SRAS as p=pᵉ+(Y−Y*)/b.
Subtract the same known p₋₁ from p and pᵉ. This makes the inflation surprise equal to p−pᵉ exactly for log inflation.
If instead working with ordinary percentage inflation and raw price levels, divide their surprise by the common previous price: π−πᵉ=(P_level−P_levelᵉ)/P_previous. Rescale b accordingly.
Use an Okun coefficient with consistent output-gap and unemployment-rate units. Normalizing output by Y* or expressing rates in percentage points changes coefficient values, not the negative sign.
At zero surprise Y=Y* and u=u*; a positive surprise gives Y>Y*,u<u*; a negative surprise gives Y<Y*,u>u*.
concepts.increase: A positive price surprise raises output and creates a positive inflation surprise with lower cyclical unemployment.
concepts.decrease: A negative price surprise lowers output and creates a negative inflation surprise with higher cyclical unemployment.
concepts.edge: Log-price differences are continuously compounded inflation; ordinary percentage inflation is exp(π_log)−1 and is approximately π_log only for small changes. Expected log price is not generally the log of expected price under uncertainty. Keep the forecast convention and shared previous-price base explicit. Okun’s law is an empirical/model relation, not an accounting identity guaranteed in every setting.
concepts.example: If the previous price index is 100, expected current index is 102 and actual is 104, ordinary inflation is 4% versus expected 2%, a 2-point surprise. The log surprise is ln(104/102)≈0.01942, or 1.942 log percentage points. Both have the same sign but are not numerically identical. A model using log prices must calibrate b and h in those units.

check.prompt: What extra operation is needed if the SRAS price variable is a raw index and inflation is ordinary percentage growth?
check.answer: Subtract the common previous index and divide by that previous index; merely subtracting produces an index-point difference, not a percentage rate.

concepts.title: Anticipated and surprise policy
concepts.explain: An unexpected demand expansion moves the economy along a short-run Phillips curve. A fully anticipated policy adjusts expected inflation, shifting the curve and leaving unemployment at its natural rate in the misperceptions model.
concepts.formula: Surprise policy changes π−πᵉ; anticipated policy can change π and πᵉ together
steps: State whether the policy was anticipated.
Decide whether expectations stay fixed or change.
Distinguish movement along a curve from a shift.
concepts.increase: Unexpected expansion raises inflation and lowers unemployment temporarily. Anticipated higher money growth raises expected and actual inflation without a lasting employment gain.
concepts.decrease: Starting from equilibrium, an unexpected contraction or slower money growth lowers inflation relative to its expected/baseline path and raises unemployment temporarily. This is disinflation relative to that path; actual inflation can remain positive and the price level can still rise over time. A fully anticipated lower-inflation policy changes π and πᵉ together and leaves u=u* in the flexible-price misperceptions model.
concepts.edge: The positive/negative gap conclusions start from u=u* with no other disturbance and fixed natural structure. An unexpected demand expansion from a recession can simply narrow an existing positive unemployment gap. Anticipated-policy neutrality is model-specific; sticky wages/prices can cause real adjustment costs even when policy is announced. Money-growth-to-inflation proportionality also requires the other long-run money-demand/growth determinants to be held fixed.
concepts.example: With h = 1, an unexpected 2-point inflation increase implies a 2-point fall in u relative to u*. If πᵉ rises by the same amount, the gap is zero.

check.prompt: Can permanently higher anticipated inflation permanently reduce unemployment below u* here?
check.answer: No. Expected inflation catches up and the short-run curve shifts.

concepts.title: The natural-rate hypothesis
concepts.explain: Demand disturbances alter output and unemployment temporarily, but after expectations and prices adjust, unemployment returns to the natural rate. This produces a vertical long-run Phillips curve.
concepts.formula: Long run π = πᵉ and u = u*
steps: Allow expectations to catch up to actual inflation.
Set the surprise term to zero.
Locate unemployment at its natural rate.
concepts.increase: Permanently higher money growth produces higher long-run inflation, not permanently lower unemployment.
concepts.decrease: Permanently lower money growth produces lower long-run inflation, not permanently higher unemployment under the natural-rate hypothesis.
concepts.edge: The Classical and lecture Keynesian frameworks both return to a supply-determined long-run allocation after adjustment under a fixed natural structure, even though their short-run mechanisms differ. u* can shift for structural reasons, so vertical does not mean fixed forever. Hysteresis is a separate hypothesis under which demand history itself changes the natural benchmark.
concepts.example: An economy can have u = 5% with inflation 2% or 8% if expectations match actual inflation and u* = 5%.

check.prompt: What makes the long-run curve vertical?
check.answer: Inflation surprises disappear while unemployment is pinned to the natural rate.

concepts.title: The natural rate is estimated
concepts.explain: The natural rate is not observed directly. Different estimates and revisions can change the inferred output gap and therefore the policy recommendation.
concepts.formula: Estimated cyclical unemployment = observed u − estimated u*
steps: Observe actual unemployment.
Compare plausible estimates of the natural rate.
Assess whether the sign of the gap is robust.
concepts.increase: A higher estimate of u* makes a given actual unemployment rate look less recessionary or more overheated.
concepts.decrease: A lower estimate makes the same actual unemployment rate look more recessionary.
concepts.edge: The lecture’s 1994 illustration has a 5.75% point estimate and approximately 4.8%–6.6% uncertainty range while actual unemployment was about 6%; it is historical, not a current estimate. An estimate revision can change the diagnosed gap without any contemporaneous real structural shock. A confidence range straddling observed u prevents a robust sign claim; averaging two estimates does not make uncertainty disappear.
concepts.example: If u = 6% and plausible u* spans 4.8% to 6.6%, the cyclical gap ranges from +1.2 to −0.6 percentage points.

check.prompt: Can an imprecise natural-rate estimate support certainty about the sign of the gap?
check.answer: Not when plausible values lie on both sides of observed unemployment.

concepts.title: History can change the natural rate
concepts.explain: Hysteresis means a temporary shock leaves a persistent effect after the shock has disappeared. Prolonged unemployment can erode skills, weaken attachment or change bargaining power, shifting the natural rate itself.
concepts.formula: Temporary demand loss → persistent change in u* and Y*
steps: A temporary adverse labor-demand shock creates unemployment and may reduce the group of employed insiders.
Long unemployment can erode skills or make them obsolete, weaken work/search attachment, or alter attitudes toward unemployment.
Benefits and employment-protection arrangements can interact with search or hiring incentives; the lecture discusses these as possible persistence mechanisms, not universal causal estimates.
Under insider–outsider wage bargaining, the smaller remaining insider group may support wages that prevent outsiders from being rehired after the original shock ends.
Compare the post-recovery natural rate and labor-market functioning with the original benchmark. Europe’s persistent unemployment pattern is suggestive, but the graph alone does not identify a cause.
concepts.increase: A severe or prolonged recession can raise u* through skill loss, lost job-search attachment or insiders excluding outsiders.
concepts.decrease: Preventing long spells of unemployment or restoring skills and matching can reduce the damage that would otherwise persist. A positive demand episode does not automatically undo skill loss or insider exclusion by exactly the reverse path; recovery depends on the mechanism and institutions.
concepts.edge: Hysteresis is stronger than a slow cyclical recovery: a temporary disturbance changes the later natural rate or productive employment after the original disturbance is gone. Persistence in a graph alone could have other explanations. The simple baseline Phillips equation does not itself generate hysteresis; a law of motion for u* or a persistence mechanism is an added hypothesis.
concepts.example: After layoffs, fewer insiders influence wage bargaining. They may favor higher wages that keep outsiders unemployed even after the initial demand shock ends.

check.prompt: What evidence would distinguish hysteresis from a purely temporary gap?
check.answer: Unemployment or the estimated natural rate remains persistently altered after the original disturbance has ended, with a plausible persistence mechanism.

concepts.title: Why the original Phillips tradeoff shifted
concepts.explain: The original Phillips relationship linked nominal wage growth to unemployment. A later US inflation–unemployment plot for the 1960s suggested a stable inverse tradeoff and encouraged a policy-menu interpretation. The 1970s and later plots show that one fixed curve does not describe all periods: high inflation and high unemployment can occur together. Friedman and Phelps predicted the importance of inflation expectations before the 1970s breakdown.
concepts.formula: The augmented relation concerns π−πᵉ versus u−u*, not a universal fixed relation between π and u.
steps: Distinguish nominal wage inflation in the original study from price inflation in the later plots.
Separate a fitted correlation over one period from a policy-invariant causal tradeoff.
Allow expectations and the natural rate to change when comparing different decades or supply conditions.
concepts.increase: Higher expected inflation or a higher natural unemployment rate shifts the short-run curve up/right, allowing higher inflation alongside higher unemployment across periods.
concepts.decrease: Lower expected inflation or improved matching can shift the curve down/left, allowing inflation and unemployment to decline together without contradicting a negative within-curve slope.
concepts.edge: An inverse plot over a particular period is compatible with roughly stable expectations and u*. A scattered or shifting plot alone does not identify which shock caused the shift; oil shocks, expectations and institutions need separate evidence.
concepts.example: One economy observed at u=5% and inflation 2% under low expectations can later have u=6% and inflation 7% after its curve shifts. Comparing those observations is not a movement along an unchanged curve.

check.prompt: Why does 1970s stagflation undermine a fixed policy menu but not the expectations-augmented framework?
check.answer: Expectations and the natural rate can shift the curve, so the stable relation is conditional on those determinants rather than a permanent tradeoff between observed levels.

concepts.title: Institutions and policies aimed at the natural rate
concepts.explain: Lecture 9 separates reducing cyclical unemployment with demand management from reducing natural unemployment by improving labor-market functioning. Search, matching, skills, relocation, flexibility and benefit design can affect frictional or structural unemployment. Under hysteresis, preventing or reversing long unemployment spells may also affect the later natural rate, but a sustained demand strategy is controversial and can create inflation pressure.
concepts.formula: A lower u* shifts LRPC left and, holding πᵉ and h fixed, SRPC down by h times the reduction in u*.
steps: Identify the friction: missing skills, slow matching, location barriers, hiring/firing incentives or outsider exclusion.
Match the policy to that mechanism rather than assume all unemployment is deficient demand.
Distinguish an improvement in u* from a temporary fall in u below unchanged u*.
Assess tradeoffs: benefit protection, hiring caution, worker security and inflation risks are not resolved by the Phillips equation alone.
concepts.increase: More persistent mismatch or stronger barriers to hiring can raise u* in the stated mechanism. More generous unemployment support may reduce hardship but can alter search incentives; its net effect is not established solely by the diagram.
concepts.decrease: Better job information, training and mobility can lower frictional/structural unemployment if they resolve the relevant constraint. A well-designed change in labor rules or benefits can improve matching, but effects depend on implementation and other institutions.
concepts.edge: A lower actual unemployment rate is not proof that the natural rate fell. Under the baseline model, sustaining u below unchanged u* requires positive inflation surprises; repeated predictable inflation is not a free permanent employment gain. The hysteresis argument for sustained high demand requires additional evidence about how employment history changes u*.
concepts.example: If retraining genuinely lowers u* from 6% to 5% and h=0.5 with expectations fixed, LRPC moves left one point and SRPC moves down 0.5 inflation points at every actual u. A one-point cyclical drop in u without that structural change instead moves along SRPC.

check.prompt: Why cannot an observed unemployment decline alone establish successful structural reform?
check.answer: Actual u can fall because demand temporarily moves it below an unchanged natural rate. Establishing a lower u* requires evidence of improved matching or another lasting structural mechanism.

choices.text: Every price doubles after money doubles with unchanged real output
choices.feedback: That illustrates neutrality.

questions.explanation: Hysteresis requires a persistent effect after the originating disturbance has ended. Skill erosion provides such a mechanism.

questions.prompt: In the insider–outsider account, layoffs remove some workers from wage bargaining. Why can employment remain depressed after the initial shock?

choices.text: Remaining insiders may choose wages that protect their interests while keeping outsiders unemployed
choices.feedback: A smaller insider group can favor wages above the level that would rehire outsiders. The initial temporary shock changes later bargaining and can alter the natural rate.

choices.text: All unemployed workers automatically retain equal bargaining power
choices.feedback: The mechanism depends on losing insider influence.
Persistence need not require the original demand shock to continue.

choices.text: The real wage must fall to market clearing immediately
choices.feedback: That would undo the stated institutional mechanism.

choices.text: Money becomes neutral by an accounting identity
choices.feedback: The account concerns persistent labor-market behavior, not a monetary identity.
